Starting from observations of an unknown nonlinear dynamical system, we first learn an implicit spectral predictor using Observation Spectral Filtering (OSF), a convex method that competes with the best linear observer for the system. We then apply spectral-to-LDS distillation to convert this predictor into an explicit recurrent linear dynamical system. Our main theorem shows that the average prediction error of the distilled LDS decomposes into an exponentially-small distillation term and the OSF learning term governed by the Luenberger complexity of the best observer. The guarantee is dimension-free: it depends on observer complexity rather than on the latent dimension needed to represent the nonlinear system. To our knowledge, this yields the first end-to-end provable method for extracting a best-in-hindsight LDS representation of nonlinear dynamics through convex learning followed by provable distillation. Experiments on linear LDS benchmarks and MuJoCo behavior cloning show that the train-then-distill pipeline produces compact LDS predictors that match or outperform directly trained baselines.

</details>


### [126] [Perturbation Sensitivity at Convergence: A Simple Signal for Identifying Spuriously Correlated Samples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05419)
*Nilesh Kumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-convergence signal identifies spurious vs non-spurious samples without group labels; a fixed input perturbation reveals fragility of non-spurious samples; two-forward-pass detection and rebalancing markedly improve worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds (57.3% → 80.8%), approaching group-labeled upper bound (85.8%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Spurious correlations enable high average accuracy but fail on subpopulations; current group-id methods require early intervention or labeled groups. The work aims to detect affected samples without group annotations and without early stopping, reducing reliance on labeled data.

Method: Train a converged model. Apply a fixed input perturbation and observe that predictions flip more often for samples not aligned with the spurious correlation. Identify 'suspect' samples that flip less frequently. For detection, perform two forward passes per sample. Use detected samples to rebalance training (without using group labels).

Result: Two forward passes per sample suffice to detect spurious-signal samples without group annotations or early stopping. Rebalancing using detected samples yields substantial worst-group accuracy gains: Waterbirds improves from 57.3% to 80.8%; ground-truth group labels achieve 85.8%.

Conclusion: A practical, label-free, post-convergence detection method can identify and rebalance samples affected by spurious correlations, eliminating the need for group annotations or early-stopping intervention while substantially closing the gap to group-labeled upper bounds.

Abstract: Models trained by empirical risk minimization on data containing spurious correlations achieve high average accuracy while failing on subpopulations where the correlation does not hold. Existing methods for identifying the affected samples without group annotations rely on signals from early training, which requires locating the epoch at which to intervene, a hyperparameter typically selected using group-labeled validation data. We show that a usable signal is available after convergence, when loss no longer distinguishes the two populations. Samples consistent with the spurious correlation are classified by a shared rule, while the remaining samples are fit through configurations specific to individual inputs and are correspondingly more fragile. Applying a fixed perturbation to a converged model's inputs flips the predictions of the latter far more often than the former. The resulting procedure requires two forward passes per training sample, no group annotations at any stage, and no early-stopping epoch. Using the detected samples to rebalance training raises worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds from 57.3% to 80.8%, against 85.8% with ground-truth group labels.

</details>


### [127] [IFlowNets: Extending Generative Samplers to Learn Strategies in Incomplete Information Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05422)
*Conor M. Artman,Nicholas Di,Scott Perkins*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Information Flow Networks (IFNs) and IFlowNets to extend generative flow networks to incomplete information games, proving current GFlowNet constraints are inadequate for valid strategy densities, and showing IFlowNets generalize AFlowNets; preliminary results competitive with OS-MCCFR and RL methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap in generative sampling for incomplete information games and fix density-constraint issues in GFlowNets, enabling valid strategy densities and training objectives.

Method: Proves inadmissibility of existing GFlowNet density constraints in incomplete information settings; introduces IFlowNets as a generalization that ensures valid densities for strategies; compares performance to Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo CFR and RL-based approaches in three standard game environments.

Result: IFlowNets strictly generalize AFlowNets and achieve comparable or superior performance and speed to OS-MCCFR and standard RL methods in preliminary experiments.

Conclusion: IFlowNets offer a valid, more general generative framework for incomplete information games, with promising early results; further rigorous evaluation and theoretical analysis are warranted.

Abstract: While many algorithms blend reinforcement learning (RL) with counterfactual regret (CFR) methods to leverage tradeoffs in computational speed and performance, there are fewer investigations into generative sampling frameworks in game theoretic applications in incomplete information games. We extend a generative flow network framework, Adversarial Flow Networks (AFlowNets), to incomplete information games, called Information Flow Networks (IFNs). We prove that previously established constraints for generative flow networks in complete information games are inadmissible for obtaining valid densities (corresponding to player strategies) and a valid training objective. We show that our proposed generalization, IFlowNets, alleviates this issue and strictly generalizes AFlowNets. In preliminary results for three standard game environments, IFlowNets perform comparably to or better than Outcome Sampling Monte Carlo Counterfactual Regret (OSMCCFR) and standard RL-based methods in performance and speed.

</details>


### [128] [Why the Third Axis Is Freedom](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05423)
*Michael Timothy Bennett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: XM reframes exploration in generative training as a pursuit of freedom, not a separate expressivity axis; theoretically and empirically, freedom governs generalization, and selecting for freedom improves XM, especially under distribution shift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether the proposed Explo­rative Modeling (XM) exploration creates a genuine third axis of generative expressivity or if it actually encodes 'freedom' as the true determinant of generalization; to unify prior claims that model behaviour constraints, not form, drive generalization.

Method: Theoretical analysis: derive XM loss as a function of miss probability and the number of outputs K; prove that weaker models generalize and that freedom selection can outperform MDL by large margins. Empirical study: Forward XM experiments varying K to measure freedom; construct XM candidate pools; compare validation selection with a freedom selector that uses unlabelled parent contexts; assess performance under distribution shift.

Result: XM optimization increased or saturated measured freedom as K grew; higher K improved freedom across context-dependent targets; in 29 of 30 cases, the freedom selector outperformed XM, indicating the freedom-based approach is competitive. The paper argues that generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy that omits the extension structure essential for generalisation.

Conclusion: Freedom, not the breadth of representational form, drives generalization in XM; XM is a means to realize freedom, and explicit freedom selection improves XM robustness under distribution shift.

Abstract: In generative training, a model produces an output and is penalised for its difference from an example. With one output per comparison, a model that produces one common answer can outperform a model retaining a broader repertoire. Explorative Modeling (XM) produces $K$ outputs per comparison and updates on the closest, claiming exploration as a "third pretraining axis" associated with generative expressivity. Here I show the third axis is actually freedom, meaning the weakness of the constraint implied by a model's behaviour. Previous work showed freedom is a property of function rather than form. Parameters, architecture, minimum-description-length (MDL), and data can vary while the behavioural constraint remains unchanged. It was formally proved that weakest models are likeliest to generalise, and freedom selection beat MDL by 110-500\% in induction experiments. I prove average XM loss depends on the chance a candidate misses an acceptable region, with exploration raising miss probability to power $K$. For $K>1$, match probability rises with freedom. I then demonstrate empirically that XM optimises for freedom. In a Forward XM experiment, larger $K$ increased or saturated measured freedom, and increased freedom at every tested value under context-dependent targets. I trained XM candidate pools and compared validation selection with a freedom selector that read unlabelled parent contexts. Freedom won in 29 of 30 cases. Generative expressivity is a mode-count proxy for freedom, that discards the extension structure that gives freedom its generalisation significance. XM is a means, freedom an end, and selecting for freedom improved XM under distribution shift.

</details>


### [129] [EvoHarness-RL: Learning Self-Evolving Runtime Harness for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05446)
*Xuying Ning,Dongqi Fu,Tianxin Wei,Hanqing Zeng,Yuanchen Bei,Bingxuan Li,Zihao Li,Qifan Wang,Xiang Shen,Yifan Wu,Jiayi Liu,Hong Li,Yinglong Xia,Xiangjun Fan,Hanghang Tong,Jingrui He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Trainable harness policies orchestrate external state for long-horizon LLM agents; EvoHarness-RL learns Belief, Progress, Experience to coordinate with an external workspace, achieving high success and revealing dynamics of harness annealing and evolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon agents depend on external execution support, but current approaches rely on hand-crafted prompts and heuristics to manage state and access control. There is a need to learn offline harness policies that can construct and update external state online.

Method: Introduce Belief-Progress-Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Use supervised harness fine-tuning to teach the base agent the harness action space and state construction; apply cost-aware GRPO (a policy optimization method) to learn coordination policies for selective read/update/consolidation of external state. Evaluate on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM.

Result: EvoHarness-RL achieves 96.9% task success on ALFWorld. The study identifies harness annealing (policy internalization of recurring harness-use patterns leading to reduced external calls) and harness evolution (progress updates and consolidation yielding a compact, task-adaptive state substrate).

Conclusion: Trainable harness policies that construct and coordinate with external harness workspaces improve long-horizon agent performance beyond merely adding more tools or memory; external-state management can be learned offline and enacted online for better efficiency and robustness.

Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents increasingly rely on external execution support to maintain state, track progress, invoke tools, verify outcomes, and reuse experience across interactions. However, effective harness use raises two coupled challenges: state formation from noisy interaction traces and runtime control over external-state access. Existing agents usually handle both through prompts, heuristics, or domain-specific conventions, leaving the external workspace and its usage policy manually engineered. To address this, we study the problem of harness policy learning, where agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution. We introduce EvoHarness-RL, which exposes Belief, Progress, and Experience (BPE) as policy-facing harness state. Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the base agent the harness action space and how to construct useful external state, while cost-aware GRPO explores coordination policies to selectively read, update, and consolidate that state during long-horizon interaction. Instantiated on ALFWorld with a Qwen3-8B LLM, EvoHarness-RL reaches 96.9% success and reveals two key dynamics: harness annealing, where training internalizes recurring harness-use patterns into the model policy and shifts the agent from frequent harness calls toward selective external-state access, and harness evolution, where progress updates and experience consolidation refine the harness into a compact, task-adaptive state substrate. These results suggest that long-horizon agents benefit from trainable policies for constructing and coordinating with external harness workspaces, beyond simply adding stronger tools or larger memories.

</details>


### [130] [Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotopes for Identifiable and Refinable Predictive Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05454)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ) for multi-source uncertainty: discrete mode, bounded drift, and stochastic noise; provides closed-form likelihood via convolution; couples future steps; identifiable; distinct from Gaussian mixtures; enables per-mode risk and multi-modal conformal sets; empirical gains over same-encoder mixture baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world prediction tasks exhibit distinct uncertainty sources that are not well captured by Gaussian mixtures or conformal regions; need a representation that isolates sources, yields analytic likelihood, and propagates across steps.

Method: Introduce HProbZ as an output head consisting of three generators (binary mode selector, bounded drift generator, stochastic noise generator) combined into a zonotope; share the bounded generator across steps to couple multi-step predictions; derive closed-form likelihood via convolution; prove identifiability up to permutation; compare density to finite Gaussian mixtures; provide per-mode risk and conformal sets analytically.

Result: Empirical evaluation on representative benchmarks shows improved predictive performance relative to same-encoder mixture baselines; HProbZ offers structural properties (identifiability, per-mode risk, conformal sets) absent in mixtures or convex-conformal approaches; density is representationally distinct from finite Gaussian mixtures.

Conclusion: HProbZ delivers a unified, analytically tractable, multi-source uncertainty representation with favorable empirical performance and explicit multi-modal inference tools, addressing limitations of existing heads.

Abstract: Probabilistic prediction heads in neural networks typically output either a Gaussian mixture or a single conformal region. Neither separates the distinct sources of uncertainty often present in real prediction tasks: a discrete choice among modes, bounded systematic drift within the chosen mode, and irreducible stochastic noise. We introduce the Hybrid Probabilistic Zonotope (HProbZ), an output head that represents these three sources as binary, bounded, and stochastic generators of a zonotope, and admits a closed-form likelihood by convolution. Sharing the bounded generator across prediction steps couples future predictions algebraically, so observing one step refines the predictive distribution at every remaining step in a single forward pass. We establish that the three generators are identifiable from the likelihood up to permutation, and that an HProbZ density is representationally distinct from any finite Gaussian mixture. The same shared structure provides analytic per-mode risk and distribution-free multi-modal conformal sets at inference time. Empirical analysis on representative prediction benchmarks supports the effectiveness of the design relative to same-encoder mixture baselines, while offering structural properties that mixture or convex-conformal predictors do not jointly provide.

</details>


### [131] [Matrix Zonotopic Attention: A Context-Adaptive Value Projection for Set Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05472)
*Zhen Zhang,Amr Alanwar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) to quantify input-dependent directions needed to represent permutation-invariant targets, shows depth separation for context-rigid attention, and proposes Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn) with a context-adaptive matrix-zonotope value component. Finds MZAttn matches standard attention at initialization, preserves permutation equivariance, and offers selective advantages on high-rank, sparsely combinatorial targets in set-prediction tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the expressivity limits of standard multi-head attention for permutation-invariant set targets by linking architectural depth to the intrinsic complexity of the target (via TDOF) and by enabling a context-adaptive value projection that remains equivariant and initialization-friendly.

Method: Define TDOF as a measure of input-dependent directions required by a target operator. Perform a depth-separation analysis showing that context-rigid attention needs depth proportional to the target's TDOF, while a single layer with a context-adaptive value family suffices for the same target. Propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn): replace fixed value projection with a center matrix plus a sum of generator matrices gated by input-dependent coefficients (a zonotope). Prove the construction reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialization, preserves permutation equivariance, and offers a data-driven reachability interpretation. Conduct experiments on various set-prediction tasks to test the predictions about when the architecture helps.

Result: The depth-separation analysis shows context-rigid attention requires depth scaling with TDOF; a context-adaptive value layer can replicate the same target more efficiently. MZAttn matches standard attention at initialization and remains permutation-equivariant, enabling a data-driven interpretation of reachability. Empirical results align with TDOF predictions: MZAttn provides architectural advantages primarily for targets that depend on the input set in a high-rank, sparsely combinatorial way, with little improvement for aggregate-statistic targets where standard attention already performs well.

Conclusion: TDOF is a meaningful complexity metric for permutation-invariant targets and guides when to allocate expressive, context-adaptive value capacity. Matrix Zonotopic Attention offers a principled, initialization-friendly, permutation-equivariant extension to attention that is especially beneficial for high-complexity, combinatorial set-targets, while remaining competitive on simpler targets.

Abstract: Multi-head attention combines an input-dependent softmax routing with an input-independent linear value projection, so the per-sample operator mapping aggregated values to outputs is the same for every input set. We study the consequences of this asymmetry for permutation-invariant set targets. We introduce the Transformation Degrees of Freedom (TDOF) of a target operator, a complexity measure counting the input-dependent directions an exact representation requires, and present a depth-separation analysis showing that context-rigid attention needs depth proportional to the target's TDOF, whereas a single layer with a context-adaptive value family can represent the same target. Building on this analysis, we propose Matrix Zonotopic Attention (MZAttn), which replaces the fixed value projection with a context-adaptive matrix-zonotope family: a centre matrix plus a sum of generator matrices weighted by input-dependent gates. The construction reduces to standard multi-head attention at initialisation, preserves permutation equivariance, and admits a data-driven reachability interpretation. Experiments on a range of set-prediction tasks are consistent with the TDOF prediction that the architectural advantage is selective: it appears on targets that depend on the input set in a high-rank, sparsely combinatorial way, and is small on aggregate-statistic targets where parameter-matched standard attention is already competitive.

</details>


### [132] [KV-Skill: Forging Expertise in the Model's Native Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05475)
*Zhaowei Han,Xiang Zhang,Bing Han,Kai Liu,Danqi Hu,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KV-Skill introduces a modular external operator framework for frozen LMs, enabling task knowledge to be captured either from text (Registration) or task outcomes (Reward learning) and deployed separately from the backbone. It achieves strong, consistent improvements across diverse benchmarks with a shared interface and evidence of robustness and scalability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the brittleness and sharing difficulties of weight-based task knowledge and the limitations of prompt-stored knowledge, by externalizing and modularizing task knowledge as factorized operators that can be loaded and reused across models without altering the backbone.

Method: Two complementary pathways: (1) Registration converts a written skill into a text-derived operator using a shared per-backbone interface, (2) Reward learning derives a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. No prompt positioning is added. Evaluations span 10 benchmarks, 4 backbones, and 3 model families, comparing against text-based skills and soft-prefix / LoRA baselines; includes a post-hoc analysis of operator directions and a demonstration of a single interface hosting multiple KV-Skills.

Result: KV-Skill consistently improves task performance over the source text skills and existing methods. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, Registration yields 77.2 accuracy vs 23.4 for the source text skill and 52.0/64.5 for competing methods. Across matched reward-training budgets, KV-Skill outperforms soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA in seven of eight settings. A post-hoc analysis shows text-derived operators retain most benefits with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while random directions fail. A single shared interface can host three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting.

Conclusion: External factorized operators (KV-Skill) enable efficient, modular acquisition and deployment of task knowledge from text or experience, decoupled from the LM backbone, with strong empirical gains and robustness across architectures, motivating broader adoption of external knowledge interfaces.

Abstract: Task knowledge is commonly stored either as text in the prompt or as an update to model weights. Text is modular but must be interpreted on every use, while weight adaptation makes the resulting capability difficult to load, remove, or share independently. We introduce KV-Skill, a design space of external factorized operators that a frozen language model reads through a lightweight interface. KV-Skill supports two complementary paths. Registration converts an authored text skill into a text-derived operator and trains a shared per-backbone interface. Reward learning develops a compact latent operator directly from task outcomes, with or without an authored skill. Neither path adds positions to the prompt. Across ten benchmarks and four backbones from three model families, converting text to a KV-Skill consistently makes the same procedural knowledge more effective. On Qwen3.5-4B LiveMath, registration reaches 77.2 accuracy, compared with 23.4 for the source text skill, 52.0 for SkillOpt, and 64.5 for SoftSkill. Under matched reward training and parameter budgets, KV-Skill gives the best result in seven of eight matched settings against soft prefixes, prefix tuning, and LoRA. A post-hoc rank analysis further shows that text-derived operators retain nearly all of their benefit with one task-aligned direction per injection layer, while matched random directions fail. Finally, one shared interface retains three independently loadable KV-Skills without measurable forgetting. These results show that task knowledge can be acquired from text or experience, compressed into an external operator, and deployed separately from the backbone. Code is available at: https://github.com/shawnzhg/KV-Skill

</details>


### [133] [Align-RAG: Alignment Is All You Need for TSFM In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05571)
*Mohammad Asadi,Soheil Hor,Bardiya Akhbari,Jack W. O'Sullivan,Tahoura Nedaee,Layne C. Price,Raviteja Anantha,Euan Ashley,Ehsan Adeli*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Training-free alignment for retrieval-augmented forecasting on frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) outperforms trained fusion adapters across multiple benchmarks; per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift enable dynamic use of retrieved context without fine-tuning; improvement in MSE on Chronos-Bolt and other TSFMs; alignment shifts resemble closed-form ridge predictor; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Challenge: retrieval-augmented forecasting often relies on learned adapters to fuse retrieved context into the backbone, implying a need for retraining per domain. This work asks whether a training-free alignment can enable dynamic use of retrieved data within frozen TSFMs.

Method: Apply a closed-form, per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before feeding into a frozen backbone. No learned parameters. Compare to trained retrieval adapters. Analyze why alignment works by comparing backbone-induced prediction shifts to a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs; use a futures-shuffle control to rule out futures-averaging. Evaluate on Chronos-Bolt with seven datasets; also test zero-shot MSE across four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures.

Result: Align-RAG achieves avg -3.75% MSE improvement over the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on Chronos-Bolt across seven datasets. It also yields 2.5% to 13.7% MSE improvement in zero-shot MSE on four other frozen TSFMs with different architectures, without any per-backbone tuning.

Conclusion: Frozen TSFMs are capable of leveraging retrieved context through simple, closed-form alignment without training. This alignment-based approach should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before training any fusion modules.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented forecasting promises to adapt frozen Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) to new domains without fine-tuning, but recent methods typically rely on learned fusion modules, i.e., trained adapters that merge retrieved examples into the backbone's forecast, based on the assumption that frozen backbones cannot dynamically incorporate retrieved context on their own. We show this assumption is unnecessary. We introduce Align-RAG, a training-free method that applies a closed-form per-pair amplitude rescaling and integer-lag phase shift to retrieved past-future windows before they enter a frozen backbone's context. With no learned parameters, Align-RAG outperforms the state-of-the-art trained retrieval adapter on a frozen Chronos-Bolt on all seven datasets of the standard benchmark (avg -3.75% MSE), showing that the gains previously attributed to learned fusion are recoverable without any training. Align-RAG further improves zero-shot MSE on four additional frozen TSFMs with various architectures by 2.5% to 13.7% per backbone with no per-backbone tuning. To probe why alignment helps, we compare the frozen backbone's prediction shift under aligned demonstrations to the closed-form ridge prediction shift on the same pairs. We find that aligned demonstrations induce prediction shifts that track a closed-form ridge predictor on the same pairs, with a future-shuffle control ruling out a futures-averaging account. Together, these results indicate that frozen TSFMs already support dynamic in-context use of retrievals, and that closed-form alignment should be the default baseline for retrieval-augmented forecasting before any fusion module is trained. Code available at: https://github.com/masadi-99/align-rag

</details>


### [134] [LC-GRPO: Bridging Train-Inference Gap for Flow-Based GRPO with Langevin Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05600)
*Yingqing Guo,Hui Yuan,Zijian He,Mengdi Wang,Zheng Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LC-GRPO adds a Langevin correction to a flow-based GRPO framework, aligning stochastic training with deterministic ODE inference by correcting ODE steps to target the current timestep's marginal distribution; theory shows reduced Wasserstein error and empirical gains in reward optimization without sacrificing sample quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a mismatch between ODE-based inference for flow models and SDE-based training in reinforcement learning, causing divergences in finite-step discretizations and blurry stochastic rollouts that hinder policy optimization.

Method: Apply a two-step rollout: first an inference-aligned Euler ODE step, then a Langevin correction that targets the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The score is derived from the flow velocity, avoiding extra score models, yielding an isotropic Gaussian transition with tractable likelihood. A single Langevin correction can reduce Wasserstein error compared to a flawed Euler step, and at matched noise levels can outperform Euler–Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE.

Result: The approach yields theoretical guarantees of reduced Wasserstein error under suitable conditions and empirical improvements in reward optimization across SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo for text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, while preserving generation quality and narrowing the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

Conclusion: LC-GRPO with Langevin correction improves alignment between training and inference in flow-based GRPO, provides a tractable, score-free correction step, and empirically enhances policy optimization while maintaining sample quality.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models are typically sampled by solving a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), whereas online reinforcement learning requires stochastic rollouts for policy exploration and optimization. Existing GRPO methods for flow models therefore replace the inference-time ODE with a stochastic differential equation (SDE) during training. Although the ODE and SDE share the same marginal distributions in continuous time, their finite-step discretizations can differ substantially. In particular, SDE rollouts often become blurry as the exploration noise increases, creating a mismatch between the samples used for reinforcement learning and those generated by the test-time ODE sampler. We introduce LC-GRPO, a flow-based GRPO framework with Langevin correction. Each rollout transition first takes an inference-aligned ODE Euler step and then applies a stochastic Langevin correction targeting the marginal distribution at the resulting timestep. The required score is recovered directly from the flow velocity, requiring no additional score model, while the resulting transition remains an isotropic Gaussian with a tractable likelihood for policy optimization. We theoretically show that, under suitable conditions, one Langevin correction step reduces the Wasserstein error of an imperfect ODE Euler step. At a matched randomness level, we further show that the proposed transition can be more accurate than the standard Euler--Maruyama discretization of the reverse SDE. Experiments on SD3.5-Medium, FLUX.1-Dev, and HunyuanVideo demonstrate that LC-GRPO consistently improves reward optimization across text-to-image and text-to-video tasks, preserves generation quality, and substantially narrows the gap between stochastic training rollouts and deterministic test-time ODE inference.

</details>


### [135] [GAUGE: Granularity-Adaptive Counterfactual Gating of Evidence for Incomplete Multimodal Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05608)
*Yunping Shi,En Yu,Kairui Guo,Jie Lu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GAUGE: a fine-grained, counterfactual gating method for incomplete multimodal classification using Taylor-based evidence scores to modulate unit-level evidence without changing the backbone, achieving strong results across six benchmarks and with a theoretical Taylor remainder bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address incomplete multimodal inputs where coarse imputation and fusion retain misleading components within recovered modalities, compromising prediction reliability; need a mechanism to selectively gate reliable vs. unreliable evidence at a fine-grained level.

Method: Impute missing modalities with a frozen imputer; encode observed and recovered inputs as fine-grained evidence units; compute prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores for the counterfactual effect of replacing each unit with a reference representation in a single forward-backward pass; map scores to continuous gates; convert gates into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without changing the backbone; no explicit per-unit intervention in the model architecture.

Result: GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across six benchmarks under diverse incomplete-input settings; demonstrates robust and reliable unit-level evidence control.

Conclusion: GAUGE provides a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness, supported by a Taylor remainder analysis that bounds the error of the first-order approximation relative to the exact counterfactual effect.

Abstract: Multimodal classification typically assumes all modalities are available, yet real-world inputs are often incomplete. Imputation and dynamic fusion can mitigate such incompleteness, but existing methods operate at a coarse modality level and thus cannot retain reliable components while suppressing misleading ones within the same recovered modality, compromising prediction reliability. To address this issue, we propose GAUGE, a lightweight counterfactual gating framework for incomplete multimodal classification. GAUGE first imputes missing modalities with a frozen imputer and encodes observed and recovered inputs uniformly as fine-grained evidence units. Rather than intervening on each unit explicitly, GAUGE scores the counterfactual effect of replacing every unit with a reference representation through prediction-aware Taylor evidence scores, all obtained in a single forward-backward pass. These scores are mapped to continuous gates, which are converted into additive attention-logit biases for unit-wise evidence modulation without altering the backbone architecture. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that GAUGE outperforms strong baselines across diverse incomplete-input settings. Furthermore, a Taylor remainder theoretical analysis characterizes the error of the first-order approximation relative to the exact counterfactual effect, establishing GAUGE as a principled and scalable framework for fine-grained evidence control under modality incompleteness.

</details>


### [136] [Reasoning Errors Have a Region and a Direction in the Residual-Stream Trajectory of LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05660)
*Hamed Damirchi,Ignacio Meza De la Jara,Damith Ranasinghe,Yuhang Liu,Javen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A three-stream detector reads reasoning validity by combining motion signals with restricted state views, outperforming displacement-only and single-layer probes on unseen benchmarks and also detecting factual completion/verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reliably distinguish sound reasoning from flawed reasoning in language models. Displacement-based trajectories lack origin state, while full-state probing reintroduces shortcut-prone information; a middle ground is needed that preserves enough context to interpret motion without exposing full states.

Method: Introduce a three-stream detector: (1) motion stream capturing layerwise residual-stream displacements, (2) a coarse region reader using vector quantization to obtain a restricted location view, and (3) a fine direction reader over normalized, multi-layer states. The combination restores sufficient state context to interpret motion without full-state probing.

Result: On unseen reasoning benchmarks, the method increases selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state-of-the-art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. It also reads factual completion and fact verification more effectively than competing detectors. Ablations show motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals.

Conclusion: Reading reasoning validity via state-conditioned motion is more effective than using static states or decontextualized trajectories alone, and the three-stream architecture offers a robust, generalizable signal across tasks.

Abstract: As language models are increasingly used for tasks that require verifiable reasoning, reliably distinguishing sound reasoning from flawed reasoning has become an important practical problem. Recent trajectory-based methods seek this signal in layerwise residual-stream displacements, which capture how representations change while attenuating some stable, token-specific information. However, displacement omits the state from which an update originates, whereas restoring the full state risks reintroducing shortcut-prone information. We identify this trade-off and propose a three-stream detector that combines motion with two restricted views of location. A coarse region reader based on vector quantization and a fine direction reader over normalized multi-layer states. This design restores enough state context to interpret the motion without returning to full-state probing. On reasoning benchmarks unseen during training, our method improves selection accuracy by up to 12% over the displacement-only state of the art and 21% over single-layer probing baselines. Although trained only on reasoning benchmarks, it also reads factual completion and fact verification, ahead of every detector we compare against, which places the signal on correctness rather than on a kind of reasoning. Ablations further show that motion, region, and direction provide complementary signals. These results suggest that reasoning validity is better read from state-conditioned motion than from either static states or decontextualized trajectories alone.

</details>


### [137] [Potential Matching Optimal Transport: Continuous Normalizing Flows for Exact $p$-Wasserstein Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05666)
*Lishuo Zhang,Ruizhi Huang,Yang Yu,Lei Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PMOT introduces a potential-flow approach to p-cost optimal transport by parameterizing the CNF velocity with a scalar potential in a generalized Benamou--Brenier form. It achieves zero-loss exactness under certain regularity, termination matching, and uniqueness assumptions, recovering the p-optimal map and dynamics. Empirically, it matches p-OT references on synthetic data, remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional data, and enables flexible sample-based terminal matching via an MMD-based color transformation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Leverage a principled potential-flow formulation to handle general p-cost OT, enabling exactness results and flexible terminal distribution matching while remaining learnable and scalable via CNF-based flows.

Method: Parameterize the velocity field via a scalar potential within the generalized Benamou–Brenier framework for exponent p; train the potential gradient using a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges between the model endpoints; ensure exact terminal matching under regularity/uniqueness assumptions; allow flexible terminal distributions.

Result: Proves zero-loss exactness: any zero-loss solution satisfies the gBB optimality system and recovers the p-optimal transport map and dynamics; experiments show PMOT learns p-specific maps aligned with p-OT references; competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data; MMD-based color transformation demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

Conclusion: PMOT provides a principled, scalable potential-flow method for general p-cost OT with exactness guarantees under stated assumptions, yielding accurate p-specific maps and versatile terminal matching for density modeling and color transformation.

Abstract: We introduce Potential Matching Optimal Transport (PMOT), a potential-flow framework for general $p$-cost optimal transport with $c_p(x,y)=\|x-y\|^p$. PMOT parameterizes the CNF velocity field with a scalar potential in the generalized Benamou--Brenier form for the chosen exponent $p$. It trains the potential gradient with a self-induced matching loss along straight bridges determined by the model's own endpoints, while allowing flexible terminal distribution matching. Our main result establishes zero-loss exactness: under the stated regularity, exact terminal matching, and uniqueness assumptions, any zero-loss solution satisfies the generalized Benamou--Brenier optimality system and recovers the corresponding $p$-optimal transport map and dynamics. On synthetic benchmarks, PMOT learns $p$-specific maps that agree with the corresponding $p$-matched OT references. It also remains competitive as a likelihood-based density model on high-dimensional tabular data, and an MMD-based color transformation experiment demonstrates flexible sample-based terminal matching.

</details>


### [138] [When Does Consensus Mean Correctness? Measuring the Agreement-Accuracy Coupling with Semantics-Preserving Re-Rendering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05670)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Render-equivalence can yield a reliable, label-free target for measuring and training model correctness in multimodal tasks, using exact program-derived answers from figures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To obtain a direct, label-free reliability signal for model correctness, overcoming the lack of exact ground truth in perturbed natural images by using render-equivalence in scientific figures, where re-drawn figures preserve semantic meaning and have an exact answer key.

Method: Introduce RENDEQ to generate render-equivalence sets by re-rendering scientific figures from programmatic data, then compare re-rendering vs resampling across three open-weight vision-language models (VLMs). Evaluate stability of agreement and standard metrics across three replication instantiations; analyze impact of style factors, particularly plotting libraries; and investigate the effect of fine-tuning on cross-render consensus.

Result: Re-rendering outperforms resampling in accuracy and reliability; agreement-based signals beat a baseline (mean token log-probability) on two of three models and tie on the third; a buggy replication traced to a rendering pipeline caused initial failure; error dispersion is dominated by a single style factor (the plotting library) by a large margin; fine-tuning on cross-render consensus reverses the effect, reducing accuracy across all replications.

Conclusion: Agreement is informative only when errors are diffusely distributed; optimizing for agreement can reduce error diffuseness and hurt actual accuracy, implying that blindly maximizing agreement is not a universally valid objective for model reliability or training.

Abstract: A model's agreement across perturbed inputs is used both as a label-free reliability signal and as a self-training target, on the premise that agreement tracks correctness. That coupling is rarely measured directly: natural-image perturbations preserve meaning only by assumption, and no exact answer key localizes errors. Scientific figures remove both obstacles, a figure is drawn from data by a program, so redrawing it yields images that are semantically equivalent by construction and share a programmatically exact answer. We build RENDEQ, a generator of such render-equivalence sets, and measure the coupling on three open-weight VLMs, checking every finding across three independent instantiations. Re-rendering beats resampling on both accuracy and reliability. Agreement beats an evidence-carrying baseline, mean token log-probability, on two of three models and ties on the third, reversing an intermediate, buggy replication traced to a rendering-pipeline failure. The dispersion behind this is concentrated in one style factor, the plotting library, more than double the next-largest factor and an order of magnitude above the noise floor. Fine-tuning on the model's own cross-render consensus inverts: accuracy falls in every one of five replication runs, the opposite sign to published results on natural images. Agreement certifies correctness only above a threshold set by how diffuse a model's errors are, and an objective that rewards agreement destroys exactly that diffuseness.

</details>


### [139] [Consistency Has a Computable Blind Spot: A Commutation Theory of Label-Free Reliability for Vision-Language Figure Reading](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05675)
*Rasul Khanbayov,Hasan Kurban*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A theory linking invariance and equivariance for label-free reliability in vision-language models, identifying a calculable blind spot, and introducing a training-free detector (Equivariance-Consistency Score) with the REND-EQUIV dataset; empirical validation shows detectability depends on the interaction of the perturbation relation and the fault class.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address a known blind spot in label-free reliability tests: certain reading errors persist under input perturbations and cannot be detected by invariance-based tests.

Method: Develop a formal framework around perturbation edits, commutativity (centralizers) and their relation to invariance and equivariance; define matched invariance/equivariance edits; prove completeness results for affine reading errors; show limitations for label permutations and mitigation via cyclic relabeling; instantiate as Equivariance-Consistency Score and release REND-EQUIV; conduct experiments across three models and a hand-labeled population; use a second invariance-family method to attribute the blind spot to the relation; apply cyclic relabeling to real data.

Result: Two matched edits are provably complete for affine reading errors; no suite of swap edits is complete for label permutations, with cyclic relabeling closing much of that gap. The Equivariance-Consistency Score detects blindness without labels or training data (label-free, training-free). The predicted ordering holds across three models and a hand-labeled population; a second invariance-family method localizes the blind spot to the relation rather than the implementation; cyclic relabeling yields its predicted gains on real data.

Conclusion: Detectability in label-free reliability is a joint property of the perturbation relation and the fault class, not of the relation alone. The proposed Equivariance-Consistency Score and REND-EQUIV provide practical, data-free tools, and the results unify observations across metamorphic-testing literature.

Abstract: Label-free reliability for vision-language models rests on invariance: perturb the input and a faithful reader's answer should not change. This has a known blind spot, a systematic misreading survives the perturbation and gets certified wrong, which we show is computable, not just real: an error is invisible to an edit exactly when the two commute, so the errors a suite cannot reach form its joint centralizer, a set that shrinks as edits are added and can be written down rather than guessed at. We act on the complementary relation, equivariance: edit a figure's data and the correct answer must change by a computable amount. Two matched edits are provably complete for affine reading errors; no suite of swap edits is complete for label permutations, and cyclic relabeling closes most of that gap. We instantiate the theory as the Equivariance-Consistency Score, a label-free, training-free detector, and release REND-EQUIV, pairing matched invariance and equivariance sets over identical data. The predicted ordering holds across three models and a hand-labeled population immune to the one circularity in how it is selected; a second invariance-family method confirms the blind spot belongs to the relation, not to any implementation; and cyclic relabeling delivers its predicted gain on a matched real sample. The same characterization explains a reported inversion of this ordering in the classifier metamorphic-testing literature: detectability is a joint property of the relation and the fault class, never of the relation alone.

</details>


### [140] [SEAM: Global consistency beyond local accuracy in scientific machine learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05702)
*Gnankan Landry Regis N'guessan,Bum Jun Kim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEAM is a generator-agnostic framework that tests global consistency of local explanations by modeling regions as a finite explanation-sheaf and detecting channel-level obstructions across overlaps, enabling exact repairs or residual empirical attributions; validated on PDEs and out-of-distribution FNO monitoring, it provides a global explanation-consistency audit for scientific ML.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Local explanation checks (per subdomain, split, or prediction) do not guarantee a globally coherent explanation. There is a need for a computable, cross-region consistency test that integrates local explanations into a unified scientific account, robust to distribution shift and generator differences.

Method: Introduce SEAM-Ω, a finite explanation-sheaf framework where each region is represented by a structured explanation with state, closure, observation channels, and optional contract metadata. Compare neighboring explanations on overlaps to produce channel-resolved obstructions; enforce repairs under account-permitted revisions; split exact feasibility vs residual-aware regularized records; separate inconsistency from non-identifiability; prove theorems on minimum-cost intervention and detectability; validate on 19 experiments with synthetic PDE systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator monitoring.

Result: SEAM identifies incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, localizing failures to specific channels and overlaps; provides exact feasibility or residual attribution; demonstrates a global explanation-consistency audit capability beyond local checks.

Conclusion: SEAM adds a global, generator-agnostic audit to ML solvers and scientific models, enabling verification that local explanations cohere into a single coherent scientific account, and offering principled intervention strategies under distribution shift.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning commonly validates models at the level of a subdomain, a benchmark split, or an explanation for one prediction. Yet such local checks cannot establish whether the resulting explanations can be assembled into one globally admissible explanation. We introduce Scientific Explanation-Admissibility Machines (SEAM), a generator-agnostic framework that makes this local-to-global consistency question computable across regions, sensors, regimes, and model components. The finite explanation-sheaf instantiation SEAM-$Ω$ represents each region by a structured explanation with state, closure, and observation channels together with optional contract metadata; compares neighboring explanations on their overlaps; and converts disagreement into a channel-resolved obstruction. This obstruction locates inconsistency and tests competing declared accounts by restricting each repair to the revisions that one account permits. Exact feasibility refutes or retains an account; when exact repair is unavailable, residual-aware regularized records provide a separately labeled empirical attribution. The framework also separates inconsistency from non-identifiability and monitors learned generators under distribution shift. We establish theorems for minimum-cost intervention and conservation-contract detectability, together with companion results for identifiability and closure recoverability. Across nineteen experiments involving synthetic partial differential equation systems and out-of-distribution Fourier neural operator (FNO) monitoring, SEAM detects incompatible explanations even when local predictions are accurate, and attributes failures to specific channels and overlaps. SEAM adds a global explanation-consistency audit to existing solvers and learning models, testing whether their local explanations form a coherent scientific account.

</details>


### [141] [Spectral Aliasing Pretext: A novel task for Self-Supervised fault diagnosis in rotating machinery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05705)
*Victor Gialis,Maxime Metz,David Esteve,Abdenour Soualhi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAP is a self-supervised pretraining method for fault diagnosis that uses spectral aliasing to create a pretext task for a Transformer; it yields stable, discriminative representations, and linear probing with limited labels outperforms full supervised fine-tuning on the CWRU dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeled vibration data for machinery fault diagnosis is scarce in industrial settings. A self-supervised approach that leverages abundant unlabeled data and robust frequency-domain representations can reduce labeling requirements.

Method: Undersample signals to produce folded spectra (spectral aliasing) and train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. The model learns frequency-domain invariants related to faults without destructive data augmentations. Evaluation uses linear probing (train only a linear layer on frozen features) and full fine-tuning as a baseline.

Result: SAP yields stable, highly discriminative representations. In linear probing, it achieves high classification performance with very little labeled data and low variance. Full fine-tuning does not improve stability or accuracy.

Conclusion: SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis when labeled data are limited, potentially reducing labeling costs in industrial settings.

Abstract: Deep learning is a new way for machinery fault diagnosis but requires extensive labeled data, a scarce resource in industrial settings. We propose Spectral Aliasing Pretext (SAP), a self-supervised learning method that pretrains models on unlabeled vibration data by exploiting spectral aliasing. We deliberately undersample signals to create folded spectrum, then train a Transformer to reconstruct the original unfolded spectrum. This pretext task forces the model to learn frequency-domain invariants characteristic of mechanical faults, without potentially destructive augmentations. Experiments on the CWRU dataset show that SAP learns stable and highly discriminative representations. In a linear probing setting, SAP quickly achieves very high classification performance with only a small fraction of labeled data and low variance. In contrast, full fine-tuning, including fully supervised training, does not lead to more stable or better results. Overall, these findings suggest that SAP combined with linear probing can be more effective and reliable than fully supervised training for fault diagnosis with limited labeled data.

</details>


### [142] [CircuitSteer: Geometrically Aligned Multi-Layer Steering via Sparse Autoencoder Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05732)
*Mehrshad Saadatinia,Parsa Razmara,Ardalan Aryashad,Ali Abbasi,Seyedarmin Azizi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CircuitSteer uses Sparse Autoencoders to identify multi-layer semantic circuits in LLMs and applies multi-point, geometry-aligned interventions to steer behavior across layers while preserving fluency, outperforming single-layer methods on toxicity, emotion intensity, sycophancy, and refusal across two model families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing steering approaches rely on fixed single-layer interventions and often fail to sustain behavioral changes across layers, limiting robustness and coverage. A distributed, multi-layer circuit-level steering framework could enable more reliable and fluent behavior control.

Method: Train Sparse Autoencoders to extract coherent circuits distributed across multiple layers via feature co-activation; construct a feature flow circuit using co-activation and alignment of decoder directions; isolate multi-layer subcircuits responsible for a target behavior; synthesize dense steering vectors from sparse features; apply multi-point interventions to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory across layers.

Result: Empirically, CircuitSteer consistently yields fluency-preserving interventions across toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal tasks on two model families; outperforming contrastive activation addition and other baselines by providing robust multi-layer control and broader coverage.

Conclusion: Multi-layer circuit steering with geometric alignment of features provides more robust and effective behavioral control in LLMs than static single-point interventions; code is available for reproduction.

Abstract: Controlling the behavior of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for AI alignment. Existing steering methods, such as Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), typically rely on fixed single-layer interventions derived from aggregate activation differences. These methods impose a single intervention across semantically diverse inputs and often fail to sustain consistent behavioral changes across layers, limiting the effectiveness of the steering. In this work, we introduce CircuitSteer, a novel framework that leverages Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to identify and manipulate coherent semantic circuits distributed across multiple layers. By constructing a feature flow circuit based on feature co-activation and the geometric alignment of decoder directions, we isolate the specific multi-layer subcircuits responsible for a target behavior. We then synthesize dense steering vectors from these sparse features and apply multi-point interventions to guide the model's internal semantic trajectory. We evaluate CircuitSteer using contrastive examples across a diverse set of tasks, including toxicity, emotion-intensity, sycophancy, and refusal, spanning two model families. Across all models and datasets, CircuitSteer is the only method to consistently produce fluency-preserving interventions; competing methods either sacrifice text quality or lack coverage, failing entirely on complex behaviors like sycophancy and refusal. These results demonstrate that multi-layer circuit steering, enabled by enforcing geometric alignment among selected features, yields strictly more robust and effective behavioral control than static single-point interventions. Code is available at https://github.com/mehrshad-sdtn/CircuitSteer.

</details>


### [143] [Multivariate Time Series Forecasting needs Cross Variable Loss](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05742)
*Kuiye Ding,Yifan Hu,Hanchen Wang,Hao Xue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Direct Forecasting (DF) objectives miss cross-variable and lagged dependencies in multivariate time series forecasting. The authors identify this objective gap and propose CvLoss, a plug-in structural regularizer on a cross-variable graph that enforces consistency of forecast residuals across synchronous and asynchronous interactions. CvLoss improves diverse forecasting backbones and competing objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multivariate forecasting, future variables co-evolve via shared dynamics. DF with point-wise loss does not explicitly constrain cross-variable residual structure, leading to mismatches when cross-variable and lagged dependencies are important.

Method: CvLoss is a plug-in structural regularizer that imposes a cross-variable graph constraint on forecast residuals. It penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, promoting consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions.

Result: CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

Conclusion: CvLoss effectively addresses the objective gap in multivariate forecasting by enforcing cross-variable residual consistency, and is broadly compatible with existing forecasting architectures.

Abstract: Multivariate time series forecasting presents unique challenges because future variables often co-evolve under shared system dynamics. While existing studies mainly focus on cross-variable dependencies in historical observations, dependencies among future values are much less explored. Specifically, modern forecasting models largely follow the Direct Forecasting (DF) paradigm, generating multi-step forecasts with point-wise objectives that do not explicitly constrain cross-variable structure. In this work, we show that the DF objective is mismatched in the presence of cross-variable and lagged dependencies, revealing an objective gap. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{C}ross-\textbf{V}ariable \textbf{Loss} (CvLoss), a plug-in structural regularizer that constrains forecast residuals on a cross-variable graph. CvLoss penalizes inconsistent edge-wise residual differences over forecast patches, encouraging consistency across both synchronous and asynchronous interactions. Our experiments show that CvLoss consistently improves competitive forecasting models, outperforms representative learning objectives, and is compatible with a variety of forecasting backbones.

</details>


### [144] [Equipment-centric workpiece localization in near real-time using deep learning-based vision and event-driven finite state machines](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05744)
*Dohyeon Kong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A vision-driven, equipment-centric 3D localization framework for hot forging that infers workpiece locations from observed handling equipment using multi-camera data, 3D pose estimation, keypoint-guided attention, and event-driven FSMs; achieves scalable, interpretable tracking with reasonable accuracy and latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In hot forging, extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing disrupt direct workpiece tracking. An equipment-centric approach leverages observable handling actions to infer locations for traceability and process coordination.

Method: Estimate floorplan-space 3D coordinates of equipment from multiple static 2D cameras; recognise grasp and release actions; validate activities with event-driven finite state machines; continuously update workpiece states; integrate a keypoint-guided attention mechanism into a 3D CNN to focus on relevant equipment regions; support visualization and quantitative analysis of transfers.

Result: Evaluation in an operational factory shows 100% event-detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window; mean localization error of 317.8 mm; mean system latency of 21 seconds; framework connects perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates feasibility of continuous, interpretable workpiece tracking in harsh manufacturing environments by leveraging equipment-centric perception and event-driven reasoning, with practical potential for traceability and process optimization; further work could target improving localization accuracy and reducing latency, as well as generalizing to other processes.

Abstract: Continuous workpiece localization is essential for traceability and process coordination in hot forging, but direct tracking is unreliable because of extreme temperatures, surface degradation, and irregular routing. This study presents an equipment-centric framework that infers workpiece locations from handling equipment observed by multiple static 2D cameras. The framework estimates floorplan-space 3D equipment coordinates and recognizes grasp and release activities. Event-driven finite state machines validate these activities as discrete handling events and continuously update workpiece states and locations. A keypoint-guided attention mechanism integrated into a 3D convolutional neural network improves activity recognition by focusing on functionally relevant equipment regions. Evaluation in an operational hot forging factory achieved 100\% event detection accuracy within a 33-second tolerance window, a mean localization error of 317.8 mm, and a mean system latency of 21 seconds. The framework connects vision-based perception with interpretable event-driven reasoning and supports visualization of workpiece transfers and quantitative analysis of equipment operations.

</details>


### [145] [Accelerating nanodrug development in continuous flow systems using informed prediction models based on low-cost surrogate nanoparticles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05761)
*Kai Dahms,Eilien Heinrich,Jochen Schmid,Michael Bortz,Iryna Savych,Regina Bleul*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Shape-constrained predictive modeling predicts nanoparticle size and PDI across process conditions in microfluidic liposome/LNP synthesis, reducing empirical screening.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Empirical optimization is costly due to sensitivity of nanoparticle properties to process parameters; lack of predictive frameworks slows development.

Method: Develops a shape-constrained model informed by experimental data from microfluidic synthesis under varying lipid concentration, flow rate, and aqueous/organic mixing ratio, integrating expert knowledge; validate with minimal empirical data.

Result: Accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity across process conditions; reduces experimental workload and supports efficient process development.

Conclusion: Shape-constrained modeling is a practical framework for rational manufacturing of nanomedicine systems; potential generalization to other nanoparticle platforms.

Abstract: The development of nanotherapeutics often involves extensive empirical optimization due to the sensitivity of nanoparticle properties, such as size and polydispersity index (PDI), to minor changes in process parameters. Factors like formulation concentration, flow rates, and mixing ratios can significantly influence clinical efficacy and therapeutic outcomes. The absence of predictive mathematical frameworks has made iterative experimental screening necessary, increasing both costs and development time.
  This study introduces and validates a predictive modeling approach based on shape constraints, aiming to enhance the estimation of nanoparticle characteristics across various process conditions. Using controlled microfluidic methods, liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios.
  The shape-constrained model, informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge, was subsequently validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data. Results reveal that shape-constrained modeling facilitates accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows. This framework supports rational and efficient process development for manufacturing nanomedicine systems.

</details>


### [146] [Neuro-Symbolic Closed-Loop Control of Laser Powder Bed Fusion with an In-Loop Ontology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05773)
*Gisuk Hong,Jaebong Cho,Hyunbo Cho*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A geometry-conditioned neuro-symbolic closed-loop controller for laser powder bed fusion uses an ontology and a DL reasoner to set predictive-control targets, linking geometry-derived constraints to observable signals. It demonstrates significant dross reduction on IN625 using an Eagar–Tsai surrogate, with ratio calibration as the principal next step.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate quality defects (dross) in LPBF by combining symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to map geometric/process contexts to controllable references within a closed-loop controller.

Method: Integrate a standards-aligned ontology inside the control loop; use a Description Logic reasoner to translate process objectives/constraints into references and bounds for the controller. Map a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio to an observable width bound (with Gaussian-process uncertainty). Apply an Eagar–Tsai surrogate tuned to NIST AM-Bench IN625. Active constraints include a lack-of-fusion floor, a monotone guard beyond calibrated range, and an energy-density cap; operate by changes in geometry, solving a small per-scan quadratic program.

Result: Geometry-aware control eliminates dross that a geometry-blind controller produces, achieving zero dross with a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring; degrades gracefully under plant mismatch; can retarget to new alloys/constraints by editing ontology data rather than code; demonstrates architectural feasibility and identifies ratio calibration as the key next step (experimental calibration of the depth–width ratio).

Conclusion: The proposed architecture is feasible for combining symbolic ontology-driven constraints with data-driven learning in LPBF control, enabling geometry-aware, constraint-aware closed-loop control and easy retargeting to new materials through ontology edits.

Abstract: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which a standards-aligned ontology operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe, and a description-logic reasoner converts them into the references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross, a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality yet cannot be measured during the build, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width, with the ratio and its calibrated uncertainty supplied by a Gaussian process. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints-adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, a monotone guard beyond the calibrated range, and an energy-density cap where a process window is declared while running only on changes of geometric context and otherwise leaving a single small quadratic program on the per-scan path. In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture eliminates the dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code. The results establish architectural feasibility, experimental calibration of the ratio is the principal next step.

</details>


### [147] [GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05783)
*Paweł Batorski,Przemysław Spurek,Paul Swoboda*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GROM offers a one-shot, analytical ridge-regression-based unlearning method for LLMs that directly edits targeted weights with a closed-form additive update, enabling fast, gradient-free removal of specified knowledge while preserving performance on retained data and resisting low-bit quantization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the computational burden and ineffectiveness of iterative, backpropagation-based unlearning methods, and to provide an exact, data-preserving, robust alternative that remains effective under quantization.

Method: Formulate unlearning as a ridge-regularized least-squares problem and derive a closed-form additive update for selected weight matrices in a layer. The update is computed from gradient-free forward passes only (no backpropagation, no iterative convergence) and applied to enforce suppression of unwanted content while preserving behavior on retained data.

Result: GROM is orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning, achieving state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP. It preserves overall model performance and resists low-bit quantization attacks that recover removed content. Code is publicly available.

Conclusion: Analytical, one-shot weight edits can outperform iterative unlearning methods in speed and robustness, suggesting a viable path for safe, scalable model apologies. Further work should assess generalizability across architectures, task settings, and deeper analyses of forgetting metrics and potential edge cases.

Abstract: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

</details>


### [148] [Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05797)
*Stefan Krsteski,Charlotte Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes ex ante difficulty prediction for 17 agentic benchmarks; shows AUC alone can mislead, uncovers token-level entropy as a predictive signal, and uses residuals to reveal environment flaws.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable estimating task difficulty from description before costly rollouts, aiding benchmark calibration and progressive curricula, especially in long-horizon domains.

Method: Empirically evaluate ex ante difficulty across 17 benchmarks in coding, mathematics, ML, web navigation, function calling, and other domains; analyze AUC, token-level entropy as features, and residuals between predicted and observed difficulty to diagnose environment issues such as contamination and infeasibility.

Result: AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates; token-level entropy is a useful predictive signal; residuals between expected and observed difficulty expose hidden environment flaws.

Conclusion: Ex ante difficulty prediction is viable with richer signals; residual analysis helps diagnose environment issues and informs benchmark design and training curricula.

Abstract: Task difficulty dictates an agent's likelihood of success, and estimating it without rollouts means forecasting this directly from a task description before executing costly simulations in stateful environments. Reliable estimates would therefore allow environment designers to calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula. This becomes increasingly important as agents move into long-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error is a severe computational bottleneck. Prior work on early prediction is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments, often relying on narrow features and inaccurate evaluation metrics. We study \textit{ex ante} difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We show that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and show how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

</details>


### [149] [Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Reinforcement Learning for Visual Continuous Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05989)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OG-SPR combines latent multi-step self-prediction with next-observation prediction via lightweight adapters to learn representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation dynamics, improving sample efficiency in visual RL on DM Control Suite, especially in hard domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current dynamics-based representation learning in model-free visual RL relies on either latent self-prediction or observation prediction, each with limitations. A representation may be temporally predictive at latent level but not grounded in observation dynamics, or vice versa. Limited data exacerbates these issues; a hybrid approach could leverage strengths of both objectives.
