Method: OG-SPR trains a model-free visual RL agent with two auxiliary objectives: (1) multi-step latent self-prediction to encourage temporal predictability in latent space, and (2) next-observation prediction to ground the representation in observation-level dynamics. To avoid over-constraint, two lightweight adapters are introduced for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporal signals without being forced to satisfy the self-prediction objective directly. Evaluated on 28 visual-control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite.

Result: OG-SPR yields improved aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive methods, with especially pronounced gains in challenging tasks such as dog and humanoid agents. The paper also notes that forcing latent self-prediction on the shared representation can over-constrain it and may not always help.

Conclusion: A hybrid objective that preserves latent temporal predictability while grounding representations in observation dynamics—enabled by adapters—offers better sample efficiency for model-free visual RL in continuous control tasks, addressing limitations of using either predictive objective alone.

Abstract: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Recent dynamics-based representation learning methods have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-free visual RL by learning dynamics-aware representations through auxiliary prediction performed either in latent space (self-prediction) or observation space (observation prediction). However, state-of-the-art methods from both categories still struggle on challenging visual control tasks when training data is limited. We posit that relying on either predictive objective alone may be insufficient. In contrast, observation prediction grounds learned representations in observation-level dynamics, but does not directly regularize the temporal predictability of latent representations over extended horizons. In this paper, we propose Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR), a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation-level dynamics. OG-SPR incorporates two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. We empirically show that directly imposing latent self-prediction on the shared representation may over-constrain it and does not necessarily improve performance. To address this issue, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite show that OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

</details>


### [150] [Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05819)
*Alfred M. Pastor,Maribel Castillo,Jose M. Badia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A learning-to-rank approach for selecting efficient tensor-network contraction plans for GPU-based quantum circuit simulations, using features derived from contraction sequences and gradient-boosted ranking models trained from GPU measurements.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contraction-plan selection is a key bottleneck in tensor-network simulations: plan quality largely drives runtime, and GPU performance depends on parallelism, memory traffic, and geometry, making automatic plan ranking valuable.

Method: Represent each contraction plan by structural features extracted from its pairwise contraction sequence; train gradient-boosted ranking models (listwise and pairwise) on GPU timing measurements; evaluate on diverse circuit families with in-distribution and shift test sets; compare to random and MinFill baselines; test cross-GPU robustness by applying source-trained models to a second device without retraining.

Result: Rankers generally identify better contraction plans; the listwise model yields the strongest overall decision quality; plans show some stability across GPUs, enabling model transfer without retraining but with degradation; learning-to-rank reduces the search space for contraction plans and is practical, though backend dependence remains.

Conclusion: Learning-to-rank provides a practical method to accelerate contraction-plan selection for tensor-network simulations, offering improved plan quality and partial portability across GPUs, while acknowledging backend-specific effects.

Abstract: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining. The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.

</details>


### [151] [Evidential Rule Learning for Interpretable Classification with Abstention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05859)
*Javier Fumanal-Idocin,Javier Andreu-Perez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FERL: a fast, interpretable fuzzy-rule learner producing evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) in one pass; Lipschitz-stable; outperforms SOTA rule learners on 30 tabular datasets; strong credal-class metrics, OOD/novelty detection, and interpretable anomaly naming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for interpretable models that not only predict well but also provide evidence behind decisions and abstain when uncertain, avoiding post-hoc calibration and multiple inference passes.

Method: Learn fuzzy rule models with native evidential outputs (belief/plausibility/abstention) in a single deterministic pass using only fuzzy memberships; no auxiliary heads or held-out sets; proven Lipschitz stability.

Result: FERL achieves statistically significant accuracy gains over 30 datasets; achieves best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers with higher set coverage; matches or surpasses dedicated detectors for near-OOD AUROC; approaches strongest detector performance on concept-bottleneck disjoint evaluation while excelling in AwA2-specific metrics and providing attribute-level anomaly naming.

Conclusion: FERL delivers interpretable, robust, evidential rule-based classification with fast inference, stability guarantees, and strong performance across standard predictive, OOD/novelty, and anomaly-explanation tasks.

Abstract: Interpretable classification often requires more than accurate predictions for real-life deployment: models should be transparent about the evidence behind their decisions and abstain when they cannot decide reliably. We introduce Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL), a method that learns interpretable, accurate fuzzy rule models whose outputs are evidential. Unlike post-hoc calibration, FERL's belief, plausibility, and abstention capabilities arise directly from the fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, with no auxiliary head, held-out set, or repeated inference. Our theoretical analysis further shows that FERL is Lipschitz stable, which means that its evidential outputs vary smoothly with the input. Against state-of-the-art rule learners, FERL is statistically significantly more accurate across a 30 tabular-dataset benchmark ($+2.6\%$ average accuracy over the second best). Its native set predictions attain the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers ($u_{65}/u_{80}=0.80/0.83$ vs.\ $0.79/0.80$ for the naive credal classifier), at higher set coverage ($0.92$ vs.\ $\le0.82$). FERL also matches dedicated out-of-distribution detectors on tabular near-OOD detection ($77.7$ vs.\ $77.4$ AUROC for the strongest baseline). Under detector-class-disjoint concept-bottleneck evaluation, its it is within $2.3$ AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector on both CUB and AwA2, while attaining the best AwA2 AUPR-Out ($68.3$) and novel-class rejection ($57.2$), while being able to name which attributes are anomalous.

</details>


### [152] [Beyond Feature Importance: A Comparative Analysis of Pattern Detection Methods in Cluster Interpretation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05880)
*Benjamin Connor,Anna Jurek-Loughrey,Lu Bai,Muhammad Fahim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comparative evaluation of post-hoc methods (RF feature importance, LIME, PCA) for pattern detection in clustering; none reliably detects all injected pattern types, highlighting a need for dedicated pattern-detection methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interpreting cluster patterns is essential in data analysis, particularly in high-stakes domains like healthcare. Existing explainability tools emphasize feature importance or local explanations, but do not target pattern-level cluster interpretation.

Method: Use synthetic datasets with predefined injected patterns and assess three common post-hoc methods: Random Forest surrogate with permutation feature importance, LIME, and principal component analysis (PCA).

Result: Each method can recover relevant features to some extent, but no single method consistently detects all types of injected patterns.

Conclusion: There is a gap between current explainability tools and the requirements for pattern-level cluster interpretation, underscoring the need for dedicated pattern-detection methods.

Abstract: Interpreting clustering outcomes remains a fundamental challenge in data analysis, particularly in domains such as healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. While numerous explainability techniques exist, they are primarily designed to assess feature importance or provide local instance-level explanations rather than to identify structured patterns present within clusters. This work presents a comparative evaluation of commonly used post-hoc analysis methods for pattern detection in clustering results. To enable controlled evaluation, we introduce a suite of synthetic datasets in which predefined patterns are systematically injected. Three widely used techniques are evaluated: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis. Results demonstrate that although each method can successfully recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. These findings high- light a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, motivating the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies.

</details>


### [153] [Alternating Levenberg-Marquardt Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-Enhanced Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05892)
*Yulun Wu,Matthieu Barreau,Miguel Aguiar,Karl H. Johansson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-level PINN framework (FALM-PINN) that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting via a Fourier-enhanced basis and Levenberg–Marquardt-based nonlinear least squares; yields major accuracy gains and proven convergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs suffer from spectral bias and representation–coefficient coupling, especially for high-frequency, multi-scale, and nonlinear PDEs. A decoupled optimization approach aims to improve accuracy and convergence.

Method: Upper-level learning of a Fourier-enhanced basis to enrich latent space with high-frequency components; lower-level fitting of projection coefficients via nonlinear least-squares solved by Levenberg–Marquardt; alternating optimization with proven global convergence; linear PDEs reduce to a single-step convex problem.

Result: Numerical experiments on challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show relative L2 errors up to two orders of magnitude (≈100x) lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: The FALM-PINN framework is general for nonlinear and coupled PDEs, offering improved accuracy and convergence; rounds out PINN methodology with a theoretically grounded decoupled optimization and a practical Fourier-enriched basis.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often fail to accurately resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency or multi-scale solutions, as well as strongly nonlinear problems. Two factors underlie this difficulty: spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to underfit high-frequency features; and representation-coefficient coupling, the entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization objective. In this work, we propose the Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg--Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN), an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, while the lower-level problem resolves the coupling by fitting the projection coefficients on this basis, solving a nonlinear least-squares problem with the Levenberg--Marquardt algorithm. The framework applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems, and reduces to a single-step convex optimization problem for linear PDEs. We prove global convergence of the alternating training scheme in both cases. Numerical examples on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show that FALM-PINN achieves relative $L^2$ errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [154] [CohortHijack: Robustness of Single Cell Annotation to Companion Cell Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05900)
*Arash Vashagh,Yasmin Vashagh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CohortHijack shows that carefully removing non-target cells from the query cohort can change refined cell-type labels in single-cell annotation without altering the target's expression or the base model, revealing a vulnerability in neighborhood-refinement and majority voting methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: assess robustness and security of single-cell annotation pipelines against targeted, non-disruptive perturbations of the query cohort that preserve the target’s expression profile.

Method: Introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. Compare random vs. structured removal, using greedy, multi-start, and beam search strategies. Datasets: PBMC3K and Paul15. Classifiers: logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM. Also evaluate CellTypist majority voting.

Result: Structured removal outperformed random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets, while removing only a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations show the effect disappears when neighborhood refinement is disabled. In CellTypist majority voting, independent predictions remained unchanged, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals.

Conclusion: Query cohort composition is a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation, highlighting the need for robustness evaluations and defenses against cohort perturbations in neighborhood-refinement and voting-based labeling.

Abstract: Many single-cell annotation tools refine an initial cell label using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. We study whether this refinement can be manipulated without changing the target cell. We introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. We evaluate random and structured removal methods, together with greedy, multi-start, and beam search, on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Structured removal was consistently stronger than random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. We also evaluated CellTypist majority voting, where independent predictions remained unchanged across all evaluations, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals. These findings identify query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation.

</details>


### [155] [BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05928)
*Yuhao Wang,Zelin Zang,Yuxuan Liu,Zhen Lei,Stan Z. Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Block-level JEPA for single-cell data; predicts graph-connected gene-block representations rather than individual genes, yielding robust, high-rank embeddings with improved throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse; existing self-supervised methods focused on token/gene-level reconstruction may miss coordinated biological programs. Leveraging gene blocks defined by protein interactions and coexpression evidence can improve representations and downstream task performance.

Method: JEPA-style teacher-student framework with block-level targets: blocks defined by protein association and corpus-derived coexpression; student forecasts each target-block representation from remaining genes; a slowly updated teacher supplies the target from the full gene set; linear attention for efficiency; evaluated on CellBench tasks and hPancreas benchmark; compared against token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls.

Result: Block-level embeddings show higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth; frozen BioM-JEPA retains expression, pathway and neighborhood information; achieves the lowest aggregate perturbation–response error among evaluated models; representation diagnostics align with canonical pancreatic programs and perturbation relationships; in a one-epoch hPancreas run (batch=8), 5.75× higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76× higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation.

Conclusion: Graph-connected gene blocks are effective prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology, enabling robust, scalable embeddings with favorable throughput characteristics.

Abstract: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes. Here we present BioM-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that instead predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network infers each target-block representation from the remaining genes in a cell, while a slowly updated teacher supplies the corresponding target from the full observed gene set. Under the reported extraction procedure, block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth in the tested diagnostics than token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls. Across CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among the evaluated models. Representation diagnostics were also consistent with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional relationships between genetic perturbations. Linear attention avoids constructing a quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrix; in a matched one-epoch hPancreas experiment at batch size 8, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75-fold higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76-fold higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation. Together, these results support graph-connected gene blocks as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology.

</details>


### [156] [How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05980)
*Sid Ali Hamideche,Louis Adrien Dufrene,Quentin Lampin,Guillaume Larue*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Linear mappings reveal partial cross-model alignment but are not universally effective across diverse text embeddings; compatibility depends on model architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether latent universality holds across heterogeneous, independently trained embedding models and assess AI-to-AI latent communication via lightweight translators.

Method: Train and evaluate simple linear translators across nine embedding models with varying architectures, pooling strategies, and training objectives; assess cross-model compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval metrics.

Result: While translators recover meaningful shared structure for some compatible model pairs, they fail for others. Compatibility is determined jointly by architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution; heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings.

Conclusion: Simple linear mappings are not universally sufficient to relate heterogeneous embedding spaces; successful cross-model transfer occurs only for a subset of compatible configurations, underscoring the importance of model characteristics in latent space compatibility.

Abstract: We investigate whether simple transformations can translate representations across heterogeneous text embedding models. Understanding how independently trained models organize semantic information is an enabler for AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text. Focusing on lightweight translators such as linear mappings, we test the literature hypothesis of latent universality in a realistic text setting beyond simplified benchmarks. Across nine embedding models differing in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective, we evaluate compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval. Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Overall, the results show that heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in some literature.

</details>


### [157] [THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05982)
*Pui Chung Siu,Claudia Cabrera,Mani Mudaliar,Arkaitz Zubiaga*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Temporal heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph (THBKG) with time-stamped edges enables retrospective evaluation of therapeutic target–disease links and improves prediction of Phase II→III progression, especially for cases lacking direct evidence; includes explainable, decision-aligned predictions and is released for ongoing validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inadequate target–disease linkage accounts for a large fraction of Phase II failures; no existing biomedical knowledge graph captures evidence profiles as of a past date, hindering retrospective assessment.

Method: Construct THBKG with 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across 19 relation types; attach the year each edge’s evidence changed; define a decision-aligned benchmark to predict Phase II→III progression using graph propagation; develop a path-based explainer for the decision-time subgraph; provide retrospective validation and release the dataset.

Result: Graph propagation on THBKG outperforms direct-evidence baselines under the decision-aligned protocol; relative top-ten performance gains of 4.3–4.5 across therapeutic areas; major gains (72.8% of pairs) with no direct target–disease evidence; encoders rank 5–6x above chance; explainable via a path-based subgraph decomposition.

Conclusion: THBKG serves as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses through retrospective validation and supports explainable, evidence-grounded predictions for advancing candidates.

Abstract: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

</details>


### [158] [A Unified Risk View of Uncertainty: Posterior Risk for Disentanglement and Evaluation Beyond Proxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05995)
*Frieder Wizgall,Georg Tirpitz,Moritz Seiler,Kerstin Ritter,Bálint Mucsányi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unified uncertainty defined as pointwise posterior risk; introduces a theory-backed benchmark with semi-synthetic data to compute oracle epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty; shows that accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unclear, inconsistent definitions of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty across literature hinder evaluation of uncertainty estimates; ground-truth epistemic uncertainty is often unavailable, so current benchmarks rely on proxy tasks (e.g., out-of-distribution detection) that provide incomplete uncertainty targets.

Method: Proposes that uncertainty equals pointwise posterior risk, combining Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-dependent deviations from the posterior mean. Develops a theory-backed benchmark that enables direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes.

Result: Empirically, accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals meaningful differences between methods, identifying approaches that align with oracle uncertainty targets and showing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

Conclusion: The unified definition provides a foundation for a fine-grained, theory-backed evaluation of uncertainty estimates. The benchmark enables direct computation of oracle uncertainties without proxy tasks and helps diagnose method performance across datasets and modeling choices.

Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimates are critical in safety-sensitive applications, where understanding the sources of predictive uncertainty is essential. This often requires disentangling epistemic uncertainty from aleatoric uncertainty, yet these uncertainty types are not defined consistently across the literature, making it difficult to assess whether a method produces accurate uncertainty estimates. Evaluation is further complicated by the fact that ground-truth epistemic uncertainty is typically unavailable. Existing benchmarks therefore mostly rely on proxy tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not provide complete ground-truth uncertainty targets and offer limited insight into the structure and quality of uncertainty estimates. We propose a unified definition of uncertainty as pointwise posterior risk, the expected loss of a predictor under the distribution of plausible ground-truth functions given the data. This view combines Bayesian uncertainty over functions with estimator-dependent deviations from the posterior mean, capturing effects such as misspecification and optimization error. This formulation constitutes the foundation of a theory-backed benchmark that enables direct computation of oracle epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty using semi-synthetic datasets with real covariates and known generative processes. By avoiding proxy evaluations, the benchmark enables fine-grained analysis of uncertainty estimates. Empirically, we find that accurate prediction does not guarantee reliable uncertainty disentanglement. The benchmark reveals practically useful differences between methods, identifying approaches with meaningful alignment to oracle uncertainty targets while exposing sensitivity to datasets and modeling choices.

</details>


### [159] [Do Tabular Foundation Models Agree with Themselves?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06004)
*Christian Klötergens,Vijaya Krishna Yalavarthi,Lars Schmidt-Thieme,Tom Hanika*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TFMs do not produce faithful joint distributions for tabular data under two proposed consistency criteria (marginalization and factorization); all tested TFMs violate these across classification and regression datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ground-truth joint distributions for tabular data are unknown, making posterior-faithfulness hard to assess; the paper seeks criteria to judge whether a model's joint predictions could arise from any joint distribution.

Method: Introduce two consistency requirements—marginalization consistency and factorization consistency—and evaluate TFMs on real-world tabular datasets to see if their predicted joint distributions satisfy these properties for both classification and regression.

Result: All TFMs examined violate both marginalization and factorization consistency across all datasets and tasks, indicating unfaithful joint representations.

Conclusion: Current TFMs' joint predictions are not faithful to any consistent joint distribution; the paper calls for revised modeling or evaluation frameworks that enforce these consistency properties.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are currently the best approach to tabular prediction problems. They are constructed as transformers that approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution based on a pre-training prior. These univariate predictors can be converted into multivariate ones autoregressively by sampling one target and adding it to the features.
  However, the faithfulness of the resulting joint has not been investigated. Furthermore, TFMs cannot be evaluated against the posterior itself, at least not on real-world datasets, because the ground-truth distribution is unknown. We therefore propose asking a different question: could a model's predictions result from any joint distribution? To answer this question, we pose two requirements that any such model must satisfy. The first is marginalization consistency, which demands that marginalized conditionals are equal to directly predicted marginals. The second is factorization consistency, which demands that different factorization orders result in equal joint distributions. Every TFM that we evaluate violates both of these requirements for both classification and regression across all datasets.

</details>


### [160] [ProDVI: Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06015)
*Xinwei Liu,Junyuan Liang,Jianting Zhang,Wuhui Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ProDVI uses LLM-generated, executable dynamics priors to pretrain the value-network encoder, improving RL sample efficiency without needing datasets, simulators, or meta-learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address sample inefficiency in model-free RL and the limitations of relying on pre-collected data, high-fidelity simulators, or meta-learning to initialize agents.

Method: Prompt a code-generating language model to produce Python functions encoding coarse environment dynamics; generate synthetic transitions from these priors; use them to train a dynamics-prediction objective that pretrains the state-action encoder of the value network within an actor-critic framework; the priors serve as initialization rather than faithful environment simulators.

Result: Empirical improvements in sample efficiency on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite tasks using ProDVI with standard model-free RL baselines.

Conclusion: LLM-informed dynamics priors can provide useful inductive biases for RL initialization; inaccuracies in priors can be corrected by online learning, and the approach avoids requiring external datasets or simulators.

Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) is notoriously sample inefficient. One contributing factor is that RL agents are typically initialized from scratch, forcing them to acquire task-relevant knowledge through online interaction. Existing approaches obtain informative initializations through pre-collected datasets, high-fidelity simulators, or meta-learning over related tasks, but these prerequisites may be difficult to access or even unavailable. In this paper, we propose Programmatic Dynamics Priors for Value Network Initialization (ProDVI), a framework that leverages the commonsense and domain knowledge encoded in large language models to initialize RL agents without relying on these resources. Specifically, ProDVI prompts a code-generating language model to produce executable Python functions that encode coarse hypotheses about environment dynamics. These functions are then used to generate synthetic transitions. Based on these transitions, we construct an auxiliary dynamics prediction objective to pretrain the state-action encoder of the value network in an actor-critic framework. The learned representation provides dynamics-aware inductive biases before online RL begins. Importantly, the generated programs are used only for representation pretraining and are not required to faithfully simulate the target environment. While the generated programs may be inaccurate, their induced initialization can be corrected through online learning from real transitions and rewards. Experiments on OpenAI Gym and DeepMind Control Suite tasks show that ProDVI can effectively improve the sample efficiency of model-free RL algorithms.

</details>


### [161] [BioKD: Selective Physiology-to-Video Knowledge Distillation via Reliability Gate for Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06023)
*Bojing Hou,Ruohao Li,Yitong Zhu,Hongjun Liu,Luwen Yu,Yuyang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BioKD is a reliability-aware physiology-to-video knowledge distillation framework for video-based emotion recognition. It uses physiological signals as privileged information during training to guide a video-based student, with a sample-wise reliability gate and progressive distillation to handle noisy supervision, achieving improved valence/arousal performance on DEAP and AMIGOS without extra inference cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video-based emotion recognition suffers from ambiguous social cues and high noise; physiological signals offer privileged information but are impractical at inference. The paper aims to leverage physiology during training to improve a non-intrusive video model while keeping inference non-intrusive.

Method: Physiology-to-video knowledge distillation with a reliability-aware gating mechanism and progressive distillation. A teacher (physiological signals) guides the student (video) during training; gating regulates transfer strength based on reliability and samples; distillation is progressive to stabilize learning; no additional inference cost. Evaluations on DEAP and AMIGOS under trial-wise and subject-wise protocols.

Result: BioKD outperforms baselines in valence/arousal recognition on DEAP and AMIGOS in both trial-wise and subject-wise settings. Reported example: 68.01% trial-wise arousal on DEAP and 65.29% subject-wise. The approach mitigates overconfident teacher errors, beats entropy-only weighting, and incurs no extra inference-time overhead nor the need for physiological sensing at inference.

Conclusion: Reliability-aware physiology-to-video distillation is a viable strategy to enhance video-based emotion recognition with privileged information during training, yielding robust subject-independent performance without extra inference cost. It addresses negative transfer due to unreliable supervision and offers a practical deployment path.

Abstract: To address the limitations of video-based emotion recognition under ambiguous or socially masked behavioral cues, as well as the poor deployability of physiological signals, this paper proposes a reliability-aware physiology-to-video knowledge distillation framework, termed BioKD. The proposed framework leverages physiological signals as privileged information during training to guide a video-based student model in learning deep affective representations, while relying solely on non-intrusive video inputs at inference time. To cope with the high noise and instability of physiological teacher supervision caused by inter-subject variability, signal artifacts, and temporal inconsistency, BioKD incorporates a sample-wise reliability-aware gating mechanism together with a progressive distillation strategy. By adaptively regulating the strength of knowledge transfer, the framework suppresses negative transfer induced by unreliable physiological supervision and enables more stable cross-modal distillation. Experiments on DEAP and AMIGOS show that BioKD consistently outperforms representative baselines under both trial-wise and subject-wise evaluation protocols for valence and arousal recognition. For example, BioKD achieves 68.01\% on DEAP (trial-wise arousal) and 65.29\% under the more challenging subject-wise setting, demonstrating improved performance under a subject-independent evaluation setting. Further analyses show that BioKD effectively mitigates overconfident teacher errors and outperforms an entropy-only weighting strategy, confirming the importance of explicitly modeling supervision reliability. In addition, BioKD introduces no additional inference-time overhead relative to the same video student architecture and removes the need for physiological sensing and multimodal synchronization.

</details>


### [162] [Hybrid-Adaptive Thread Tuning to Mitigate Simulation Execution Bottlenecks in High-Performance Reinforcement Learning Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06025)
*Jiming Su,Hantao Hua,Lujia Yin,Yiping Yao,Feng Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoThread is a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning framework for RL inference in simulation-in-the-loop systems, using a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) and an M/M/1 queue to predict and regulate thread counts under dynamic workloads, yielding notable speedups and throughput gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic simulator workloads and runtime thread contention impede efficient RL inference. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match available resources quickly, causing scheduling overhead and reduced throughput. A fast, accurate, and robust thread-count predictor is needed to mitigate bottlenecks.

Method: A hybrid approach: (1) use a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor; (2) constrain/guide predictions with a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model; (3) perform load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate prediction errors; (4) integrate into simulation-in-the-loop RL inference to allocate threads adaptively with fast response.

Result: AutoThread achieves an average speedup of 18.4% over static strategies, attains average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Code and dataset are publicly available.

Conclusion: The proposed PINO-guided, queue-constrained adaptive threading approach effectively mitigates simulation bottlenecks in RL inference under dynamic workloads, delivering substantial throughput and latency improvements while remaining adaptable to varying workloads.

Abstract: In simulation-in-the-loop decision-making systems, reinforcement learning (RL) inference is often constrained by simulator-side execution overhead, where workloads are highly dynamic and sensitive to runtime thread configurations. Existing multithreaded strategies struggle to match thread resources before or during execution, causing resource contention, scheduling overhead, and reduced throughput. Through empirical analysis, we identify the ratio of task execution time to scheduling time as the key factor determining the optimal thread count. Building on this insight, we propose AutoThread, a hybrid adaptive thread-tuning method for mitigating simulation bottlenecks in RL inference. AutoThread employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) as a thread-count predictor and incorporates a finite-source M/M/1 queueing model to constrain and guide prediction, enabling fast and accurate estimation under dynamic workloads. It further performs load-aware online fine-tuning to compensate for prediction errors and refine resource allocation. Experiments show that AutoThread improves average speedup by 18.4\% over static strategies, achieves average throughput of 1.7x and 1.8x that of XGBoost and Reinforcer, respectively, and reduces execution time by up to 83.8\% compared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/suchenjm/AutoThread.

</details>


### [163] [Dynamic Graph Prompting via Topology-Routed Mixed-Curvature Experts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06031)
*Quanxin Wang,Xuanting Xie,Bingheng Li,Xingtong Yu,Shuo Wang,Ruiyi Fang,Zhao Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CurvPrompt introduces a topology-routed, geometry-aware prompting framework for dynamic graphs, leveraging a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts with adaptive routing to handle geometry under-adaptation and label scarcity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Temporal local topology shifts (edge clustering and degree heterogeneity) dynamically reshape the edge-curvature spectrum, causing a geometry mismatch when using a single embedding space. This geometry under-adaptation motivates geometry-aware prompting for dynamic graphs.

Method: Maintain a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each paired with a learnable prompt; a topology-aware gate routes node–time instances to a sparse subset of experts to create a mixed-curvature representation. Use soft routing during pre-training to learn a continuous topology–geometry mapping and switch to hard Top-K routing with uniform weights during downstream adaptation for stability and efficiency.

Result: Experiments on four benchmark datasets show substantial gains in few-shot link prediction and strong, consistent performance on node classification, validating the effectiveness of geometry-adaptive prompting for dynamic graphs.

Conclusion: Geometry-adaptive prompting with topology-routed, multi-curvature representations effectively addresses geometry under-adaptation in dynamic graphs, enabling personalized, efficient representations under label scarcity.

Abstract: Dynamic graph prompting freezes a pre-trained temporal backbone and adapts it to label-scarce downstream tasks using lightweight prompts. However, existing methods operate within a single, fixed embedding space. In this work, we reveal that temporal shifts in local clustering and degree heterogeneity actively reorganize the edge curvature spectrum---indicating that the optimal representation geometry dynamically evolves with local topology over time. We formalize this unaddressed mismatch as geometry under-adaptation. To overcome this limitation, we propose CurvPrompt, a topology-routed geometry prompting framework for dynamic graphs. Instead of relying on a single space, CurvPrompt maintains a bank of curvature-diverse Riemannian experts, each paired with a learnable prompt. A topology-aware gate dynamically routes each node--time instance to a sparse subset of experts, constructing a personalized mixed-curvature representation. To ensure parameter efficiency and training stability under extreme label scarcity, CurvPrompt employs soft routing during pre-training to build a continuous topology--geometry mapping, and transitions to hard Top-K routing with uniform weights during downstream adaptation. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets show that CurvPrompt significantly advances few-shot link prediction while delivering strong, consistent performance on node classification tasks, validating the necessity of geometry-adaptive prompting.

</details>


### [164] [Does Latent Context Help? A Controlled Evaluation of Inverse Reinforcement Learning in Arctic Shipping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06105)
*Vaishnav Vaidheeswaran,Dilith Jayakody,Biruk Ambaw,Jaswanth Kumar,Md Mahbub Alam,Gabriel Spadon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Nonlinear shared reward outperforms linear rewards; per-vessel latent context harms performance. Apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental features, not hidden preferences. Model evaluation is metric-dependent; no single metric suffices. Implication: test explainability of observable features before adding latent context for trustworthy AI in safety-critical domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether latent {per-vessel} context in meta-IRL captures genuine hidden preferences or merely re-encodes information already present in observed states, to ensure interpretability and robustness in AI-assisted Arctic navigation.

Method: Compare three reward models (linear shared, nonlinear shared, latent-context on top of nonlinear architecture) using 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic seasons. Assess held-out likelihood, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer. Conduct behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation to determine whether vessel-level variation is due to hidden factors. Use multiple metrics to evaluate learned rewards.

Result: Nonlinear shared reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over linear baseline; adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions. Different metrics (predictive accuracy, route fidelity, reward transfer) yield different model rankings; no single metric suffices.

Conclusion: Observable route, environmental, and vessel features largely explain behavioral variation; latent per-vessel context provides limited or negative value. Before incorporating latent context, test explainability with respect to observed features. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted navigation can help Arctic shipping adapt to rapidly changing sea-ice conditions, but reliable deployment requires reward models that are interpretable and robust to changing environments. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a framework for recovering such rewards from vessel trajectories, while recent meta-IRL methods introduce latent context variables to capture behavioral heterogeneity. However, it remains unclear whether these latent representations recover genuinely hidden preferences or simply re-encode information already available in the observed state. We conduct a controlled evaluation on 3,186 AIS-derived voyages from 202 vessels across nine Arctic shipping seasons, comparing a linear shared reward, a nonlinear shared reward, and a latent-context model built on the same nonlinear architecture. The nonlinear reward improves held-out likelihood by 50.9% over the linear baseline, whereas adding vessel-specific latent context reduces performance by 16.5%. Behavioral analysis, context probes, and a pre-registered feature-hiding ablation show that apparent vessel-level variation is largely explained by observable route and environmental conditions rather than hidden vessel-specific factors. Moreover, predictive accuracy, route fidelity, and reward transfer yield different model rankings, demonstrating that no single metric is sufficient to evaluate learned rewards. These findings motivate testing whether the observed route, environmental, and vessel features already explain behavioral variation before adding per-vessel latent context. This supports more trustworthy AI deployment in safety-critical domains.

</details>


### [165] [Kastor: An efficient fine-tuning strategy for generative emulation of PDE simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06107)
*Guillaume Couairon,Alexis Jacq,Yu-Han Wu,Renu Singh,Yana Hasson,Quentin Berthet,Romuald Elie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Kastor introduces a two-stage inference pipeline and a mean prediction regularization (MPR) to convert a deterministic physics foundation model into a fast, accurate generative surrogate for PDE-like simulations, addressing error accumulation and stochasticity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To replace expensive PDE solvers with fast, differentiable surrogates while mitigating error accumulation in autoregressive models and capturing stochastic dynamics.

Method: A two-stage inference: (1) large-stride causal autoregressive model for long-horizon dynamics; (2) non-causal temporal super-resolution to refine outputs. A novel training objective, Mean Prediction Regularization (MPR), constrains the model to predict the deterministic distribution mean under null noise conditioning. Additional gains from spatial gradient matching. Evaluations on diverse simulations of The Well benchmark show improved forecasting accuracy, spectral fidelity, and efficiency.

Result: The approach yields improved accuracy and stability for Functional Generative Networks (FGN) and diffusion-based emulators, outperforming competing methods in forecasting accuracy, spectral consistency, and computational efficiency. Reported gains include a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting error versus Walrus-based finetuning and superior VRMSE on 8 of 10 datasets.

Conclusion: Kastor provides an effective, scalable generative surrogate framework for physical simulations, combining two-stage inference, MPR, and gradient matching to achieve high accuracy, stability, and spectral fidelity across diverse datasets while reducing computation compared with existing baselines.

Abstract: Machine learning offers a promising avenue to accelerate physical simulations by replacing computationally expensive traditional Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solvers with fast, differentiable surrogate models. However, standard auto-regressive ML emulators often suffer from error accumulation over long horizons and struggle to capture the stochasticity of complex physical systems. In this paper, we propose Kastor, a comprehensive methodology to adapt a deterministic physics foundation model into a highly efficient and accurate generative surrogate. First, we introduce a two-stage inference scheme that combines a large-stride causal auto-regressive model with a non-causal temporal super-resolution network, significantly reducing error accumulation while minimizing computational cost. Second, we present Mean prediction regularization (MPR), a novel training objective that constrains the generative model to predict the deterministic distribution mean under null noise conditioning. This regularization dramatically improves the performance and stability of both Functional Generative Networks (FGN) and diffusion-based emulators. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating spatial gradient matching improves the accuracy and physical fidelity of the simulations as measured by power spectrum density. Extensive evaluations on diverse simulation datasets of the benchmark The Well show that with these components, our model outperforms competing methods in forecasting accuracy, spectral consistency, and computational efficiency. Our model achieves a 42.9% average reduction in forecasting compared to our reference based on the Walrus finetuning methodology, and outperforms Walrus for 8 out of 10 datasets on variance-normalized RMSE (VRMSE).

</details>


### [166] [Is Self-Pretraining really useful to improve diagnosis in medical Time Series?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06122)
*Omar Coser,Antonio Orvieto,Paolo Soda,Loredana Zollo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-PreTraining (SPT) improves transformer performance on medical time-series across diverse tasks, with gains of 0-6 percentage points, especially for deeper models; no task-specific architectural changes required and benefits persist under data-limited conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether SPT gains observed in long-context transformers extend to multimodal, multivariate, and simple univariate medical time series, and to evaluate its impact on performance and scalability under limited data.

Method: Evaluate transformer architectures on three medical time-series tasks (rehabilitation robotics—Camargo dataset; stress detection—Non-EEG Stress; Parkinson's gait—Gait Parkinson's Disease). Compare training from scratch vs. Self-PreTraining using four masking-based objectives promoting temporal and cross-modal representations. Systematically vary model depth to assess capacity interaction with pre-training benefits.

Result: SPT consistently yields 0-6 percentage point accuracy gains depending on masking strategy, dataset, and architecture. Benefits appear in multivariate and even univariate inputs, and increase with model depth, indicating richer temporal representations are better exploited by larger models.

Conclusion: SPT is a simple, general pre-training strategy that improves transformer performance on medical time-series in data-limited clinical settings without requiring task-specific architectural changes, supporting improved robustness and accuracy.

Abstract: Inspired by recent evidence that transformer architectures benefit from Self-PreTraining (SPT) on long-context benchmarks, we investigate whether similar gains extend to multimodal, multivariate, and even simple univariate medical time series. Our objective is to assess the impact of SPT on the performance and scalability of transformer-based models across diverse medical applications, particularly under limited data conditions. We evaluate transformer architectures on three representative medical time-series tasks: rehabilitation robotics (Camargo dataset), stress detection (Non-EEG Stress), and Parkinson's disease detection (Gait Parkinson's Disease). Models are trained either from scratch or through SPT using four masking-based objectives designed to promote temporal and cross-modal representation learning, and we systematically vary model depth to examine how capacity interacts with pre-training benefits. Across datasets and configurations, SPT consistently improves classification accuracy by 0-6 percentage points depending on masking strategy, dataset and architecture, with gains observed not only in multivariate settings but also when models are restricted to simple univariate inputs. The improvements increase for deeper models that can better exploit the enriched temporal representations learned during pre-training. These findings indicate that SPT is a simple and general strategy that enhances transformer performance on medical time-series tasks without requiring task-specific architectural changes, supporting its potential to improve robustness and accuracy in data-limited clinical settings.

</details>


### [167] [LLM Inference Under Bursty Workload Distribution: Modifying the WAIT Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06135)
*Anjali Gangadhar Katageria,Shobha Rani,Raghu Nandan Sengupta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An online, traffic-adaptive extension to the WAIT scheduling algorithm using interarrival-based intensity estimation and MMPP-based simulations; yields higher throughput than baselines at low arrival-rate shifts with similar latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world LLM-serving workloads are bursty and time-varying, violating Poisson/constant-rate assumptions. A lightweight, model-free adaptation improves throughput without sacrificing latency.

Method: Extend WAIT with online estimation of arrival rate from interarrival times; validate via simulation using Markov Modulated Poisson Process workloads and diverse request types; compare against Sarathi-Serve, ORCA, vLLM.

Result: In low-arrival-rate-shift scenarios, the proposed method achieves higher throughput than baselines while maintaining comparable latency.

Conclusion: Online, traffic-aware adaptation of WAIT effectively handles time-varying requests, offering improvements in throughput with acceptable latency; supported by simulation with MMPP workloads.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Claude are widely used for information retrieval and problem-solving. Recent work has focused on improving scheduling algorithms to boost throughput while maintaining low latency. However, these approaches often assume Poisson request arrivals with constant rates - an assumption that fails to reflect the inherently bursty and dynamic nature of real-world traffic. We propose a lightweight extension to the state-of-the-art WAIT algorithm [1], which adapts to time-varying arrival rates without prior traffic knowledge. The proposed algorithm performs online estimation of request intensity based on observed interarrival times. Using Markov Modulated Poisson Process (MMPP)-based synthetic workloads with diverse request types, we conduct a simulation-based evaluation demonstrating that the proposed method achieves higher throughput than Sarathi-Serve [2], ORCA [3], and vLLM [4] in the evaluated low arrival-rate shift scenarios while maintaining comparable latency.

</details>


### [168] [SkillTFM: Gated Skill Evolution for Training-Free Adaptation of Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06137)
*Yi He,Zhengkang Guan,Anpeng Wu,Peng Cui,Fei Wu,Kun Kuang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces SkillTFM, a training-free adaptation framework for tabular foundation models that uses a verifiable skill bank and gated skill evolution to handle distribution shifts and heterogeneous feature semantics, achieving notable AUC gains across simulated and real datasets and showing backbone-agnostic efficacy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tabular foundation models promise generality but struggle with distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns; fine-tuning or extra labeled data is costly, motivating a training-free adaptation approach.

Method: SkillTFM deploys a verifiable and extensible skill bank that couples boundary evidence identification (to characterize task structure and base-model failure patterns) with gated skill evolution (retrieving/extending reusable skills under explicit validation). The system is demonstrated across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, and evaluated with multiple TFM backbones.

Result: Quantitative gains include AUC improvements of 0.128–0.142 and a nonlinear-boundary AUC rise from 0.699 to 0.898, with consistent performance across different TFM backbones.

Conclusion: SkillTFM provides a general, training-free pathway to adapt TFMs under distribution shifts, validating that a skill-based, boundary-aware mechanism can generalize across backbones and tasks.

Abstract: Tabular data are ubiquitous in real-world applications and are crucial for data-driven prediction and decision-making across science, industry, finance, healthcare, and public services. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose tabular learning, offering reusable predictors across diverse datasets and substantially reducing the need for task-specific training, tuning, and model development. However, their practical deployment remains constrained by distribution shifts, heterogeneous feature semantics, and task-specific patterns that are difficult to capture without costly fine-tuning or additional labeled data.
  To this end, we propose SkillTFM, a training-free system that shifts TFM adaptation from parameter updates to the gated evolution of agentic skills. The core of SkillTFM is a verifiable and extensible skill bank that couples boundary evidence identification with gated skill evolution: the former characterizes task structure and base-model failure patterns, whereas the latter retrieves and extends reusable skills subject to explicit validation. Across simulated boundary settings and real-world electricity-price forecasting, SkillTFM improves AUC by 0.128--0.142, raises nonlinear-boundary AUC from 0.699 to 0.898. Furthermore, experiments across TFM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of SkillTFM.

</details>


### [169] [Threshold-Based Early Stopping of Accumulations in Neural Networks with Binary Activation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06177)
*Quentin Luquet de Saint-Germain,Massil Ait Abdeslam,Jean Pierre David*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Post-training early-stopping for binary activations that predicts the final sign of running sums to skip unnecessary accumulations, enabling substantial arithmetic reduction with modest accuracy loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce computation and energy for binary neural networks by exploiting the fact that partial sums drift toward their final sign, allowing early stopping without retraining.

Method: Characterize the behavior of running accumulations on the training data, predict the final sign as early as possible, and skip remaining terms during inference; operates in a post-training fashion with an idealized weight-ordering assumption; reports savings as a count of skipped operations.

Result: On VGG11 with CIFAR-10, skipping 86.6% of accumulation terms in the deepest convolution yields a 0.37-point accuracy drop; skipping 25% of full-network arithmetic when applying the method to the three deepest convolutions yields a 1.36-point drop.

Conclusion: The approach provides a model-parameter-free post-training reduction in arithmetic for binary networks by exploiting accumulation dynamics; effectiveness depends on the order of weights and dataset behavior, with a trade-off between computation reduction and accuracy; demonstrates substantial potential for constrained deployment.

Abstract: Binary neural networks are very attractive for constrained deployment, enabling small footprint and low-power inference. For binary activations, the dot products become sign-controlled additions or subtractions, but the number of operations is unchanged. Indeed, every neuron or output channel still accumulates all of its input, even though only the sign will be retained, which is often wasteful. As the accumulation progresses, the running partial sum frequently drifts so far from zero that its final sign becomes highly predictable long before the last term is reached; every contribution evaluated after that point changes the value of the sum but not the final output activation. This paper turns this observation into a post-training early-stopping mechanism. We characterize the behavior of the running accumulations on the training dataset and use this information to predict the final sign as soon as possible. No model parameter is retrained. We count the number of operations under an idealized ordering of weights. On VGG11 applied to the CIFAR-10 dataset, the method removes $86.6\%$ of the accumulation terms of the deepest convolution for a $0.37$-point accuracy drop, and $25\%$ of the full-network arithmetic when used on the three deepest convolutions simultaneously, for a $1.36$-point drop.

</details>


### [170] [SAGA: Score-Weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment for Low-Resource Nordic Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06179)
*Hoda Fakharzadehjahromy,Emil Wiman,Andreas Bueff,Hafsteinn Einarsson,Fredrik Heintz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SAGA uses dependency-parser supervision to substitute human preference labels for grammar-focused alignment in low-resource, morphologically rich languages, improving output quality without human labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on costly human preference annotations in policy optimization for LLMs, especially for low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers exist.

Method: Convert parser judgments into delta-DPO preference pairs, aggregate with a composite reward combining parser quality and lexical diversity, filter low-information pairs via a reward-gap criterion, and monitor reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision.

Result: On Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål with GPT-SW3-1.3B, SAGA improves grammatical quality: Danish parse success rises 69.0%→93.8%; Icelandic shows a +4.5 pp improvement on independent Stanza eval (three-run mean +3.3 pp) with native speakers preferring SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons; Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 pp.

Conclusion: Parser-derived supervision is a practical alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages when high-quality dependency parsers are available.

Abstract: Preference optimisation has proven effective for improving large language models but typically relies on costly human preference annotations. Extending these methods to morphologically rich, low-resource languages remains challenging because such annotations are scarce. We present SAGA (Score-weighted Adaptive Generation Alignment), a parser-guided preference optimisation framework that replaces human labels with dependency-parser supervision. SAGA converts parser judgements into preference pairs for delta-DPO, combines parser quality with lexical diversity in a composite reward, filters low-information pairs using a reward-gap criterion, and monitors reward hacking to maintain reliable supervision. Across Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian Bokmål using GPT-SW3-1.3B, SAGA consistently improves grammatical quality without requiring human preference labels. Danish parse success increases from 69.0% to 93.8%, Icelandic achieves a +4.5 percentage-point improvement on an independent Stanza evaluation (three-run mean +3.3 percentage points) while native speakers prefer SAGA outputs in 80% of pairwise comparisons, and Norwegian Bokmål improves by +28 percentage points. These results demonstrate that parser-derived supervision is a practical alternative to human preference annotation for grammatical alignment in low-resource languages where high-quality dependency parsers are available.

</details>


### [171] [Continual Learning in Transition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06216)
*Zhiyan Hou,Dan Zhang,Tao Feng,Liyuan Wang,Wei Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Hongyan An,Junfeng Fang,Haokai Ma,Zhaohui Xu,Haiyun Guo,Jinqiao Wang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Abstract reframes continual learning from a parameter-centric view to system-level adaptation, introducing a tri-axial framework (When, How, Where) to analyze on-policy, post-training, inference-time, and external components, surveying methods and outlining challenges and future directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the shift in continual learning from purely parameter updates to broader system-level adaptation, by mapping existing methods onto the tri-axial dimensions and highlighting cross-cutting challenges and opportunities.

Method: Conceptual framing and survey using a tri-axial (When/How/Where) taxonomy to categorize CL methods across update mechanics (off-policy, on-policy, beyond-gradient), stages (pre-training, post-training, inference-time), and loci (internal parameters vs external structures).

Result: Proposes a comprehensive tri-axial framework for characterizing CL evolution; surveys representative methods; documents a trend toward system-level adaptation and identifies key challenges, implications, and directions.

Conclusion: Continual learning is transitioning from parameter-centric updates to system-level adaptation, necessitating research across update mechanics, temporal stages, and external constraints; future work should explore and integrate on-policy, test-time, and memory/external components to build capable, flexible CL systems.

Abstract: Classical continual learning (CL) has primarily focused on enabling models to update and retain knowledge through parameter-centric mechanisms, e.g., training strategies, architectural designs, and weight adaptation. However, emerging paradigms are reshaping the scope of CL beyond this traditional model adaptation view. For instance, on-policy learning broadens the space of update mechanisms; test-time training extends CL from the training phase to inference; and external harness components such as memory, skill libraries, and interaction protocols extend the evolutionary boundaries of model capabilities far beyond the static parameter space. Collectively, these developments indicate a transition from parameter-centric learning toward system-level adaptation. To characterize this transition, we examine the evolution of continual learning through three dimensions: When, How, and Where learning occurs. The How dimension encompasses off-policy, on-policy, and beyond-gradient optimization mechanics. The When dimension captures evolution across pre-training, post-training, and inference-time stages. The Where dimension delineates updates occurring within internal parameters versus external structural constraints. Anchored by this tri-axial framework, we systematically survey representative methods, trace the ongoing transition of continual learning, and discuss the key challenges, broader implications, and future directions arising from this paradigm shift.

</details>


### [172] [Timestep-Conditioned Transformers for Global Weather Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06241)
*Sam Levang,Fran Bartolic,Ty Dickinson,Chase Dwelle,Paulius Rauba,Viktor Cikojevic*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A single GEM-3 model uses explicit multi-timestep inference to balance short- and long-range forecast performance, with mixed-timestep training improving rollout stability; a ~134M-parameter neighborhood-attention transformer on an equirectangular grid.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the trade-off between short timesteps (better diurnal dynamics, higher error growth) and long timesteps (lower error growth, poorer sub-daily predictions) in fixed autoregressive models.

Method: Adopts multi-timestep inference with a single weight set; train with mixed timesteps for stability; employs a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer (~134M parameters) on an equirectangular grid; base on GEM-2 with architectural enhancements; supports configurable timestep at inference.

Result: Achieves near-state-of-the-art medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training/inference, and decision-relevant diagnostics.

Conclusion: GEM-3 provides a practical, flexible forecasting system that balances predictability and usability across forecast horizons, enabling configurable timesteps without retraining and improving rollout stability.

Abstract: Existing machine-learning weather forecasting models rely on predetermined and fixed autoregressive timesteps. The choice of model timestep involves a fundamental trade-off: shorter timesteps (e.g. 1 to 6 hours) finely resolve atmospheric dynamics within the diurnal cycle but increase error accumulation for a given forecast horizon, while longer timesteps (e.g. 24 hours) reduce error accumulation but limit the usability of short-range forecasts where sub-daily predictability is high. In this work, we present GEM-3, a probabilistic global weather model that addresses this trade-off through explicit multi-timestep inference. With a single set of trained weights, the model timestep can be configured at inference time to balance predictability and usability across a broad forecast horizon. Additionally, we find that mixed-timestep training consistently improves rollout stability relative to timestep-specialist models. Under the hood, GEM-3 is a lightweight neighborhood-attention transformer with ~134M parameters on an equirectangular grid with a number of architectural advancements beyond its predecessor GEM-2. The result is a practical forecasting system that couples near-SOTA medium-range probabilistic skill, stable extended-range rollouts, efficient training and inference, and decision-relevant diagnostics.

</details>


### [173] [A Six-Dimensional Taxonomy of Post-Training Adaptation Techniques with Applications in AI Governance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06246)
*Fardin Afdideh,Fernando Seoane,Farhad Abtahi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a six-dimensional taxonomy for post-training adaptation to unify fragmented literature, clarify terminology, and map relationships across techniques, models, and deployment contexts; provides a framework for documentation and governance; identifies open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistence, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training adaptation literature is fragmented across technique families, model classes, and deployment settings, hindering comparison, reproducibility, and governance. A unified taxonomy enables consistent terminology, tracking of model changes, and informed governance decisions.

Method: Literature synthesis to construct a six-dimension taxonomy (mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, model type); analysis of relationships among techniques (inheritance, supersession, hybridization, layered deployment stacks); mapping of evolution across ML eras (traditional ML → deep learning → foundation models → LLMs → multimodal LLMs); articulation of open challenges and governance implications.

Result: A comprehensive six-dimensional taxonomy that unifies post-training adaptation methods, clarifies conflated terms (e.g., fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, prompting), and delineates relationships among techniques. Provides a vocabulary for documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis, and outlines how strategies evolve across model families.

Conclusion: Identifies open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware workflows, highlighting areas for future research and standardization.

Abstract: Post-training adaptation has become central to modern machine learning practice and includes techniques such as retraining, fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, alignment, retrieval augmentation, model editing, unlearning, calibration, and Multimodal Instruction Tuning. However, the literature remains fragmented across technique families, model classes, and deployment contexts, making it difficult to compare methods or describe how a trained model has been modified. This survey synthesizes the post-training adaptation literature and introduces a six-dimensional taxonomy organized by mechanism, goal, data requirement, persistence, structural scope, and model type. The taxonomy distinguishes commonly conflated terms such as fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, and prompting, and shows how adaptation strategies evolve from traditional machine learning through deep learning, foundation models, large language models, and multimodal large language models. It also maps relationships among techniques, including inheritance, supersession, hybridization, and layered deployment stacks. The resulting vocabulary can support technical documentation, model-change tracking, and governance analysis. The survey concludes by identifying open challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, persistent inference-time adaptation, unlearning, multimodal adaptation, and governance-aware post-training workflows.

</details>


### [174] [MetaboLLM: a metabolomics-specialized large language model for biochemical knowledge integration and predictive metabolite graph construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06253)
*Dohyun Ku,Min Gu Kwak,Francisco J. Pasquel,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Specialized metabolomics LLMs (MetaboLLM) and a graph-enabled variant (MetaboLLM-GIN) improve predictive knowledge tasks and patient-level predictions; achieve state-of-the-art results and offer interpretable metabolite graphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
