Motivation: Metabolomics knowledge is scattered across heterogeneous resources and difficult to translate into predictive representations using generic LLMs; domain specialization and graph-augmented descriptions are needed for better prediction and interpretation.

Method: Continual pretraining and supervised fine-tuning of MetaboLLM with structured retrieval; MetaboLLM-GIN converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs and uses a graph isomorphism network for patient-level prediction. Evaluation spans four backbone families, external benchmarks, and retrieval-based setups, with comparisons to base and medically adapted models and non-retrieval/unadapted configurations.

Result: MetaboLLM outperformed base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUCs for stress hyperglycemia after CABG (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs from unadapted or non-retrieval LLMs. Interpretability analyses yielded biologically meaningful findings.

Conclusion: Domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations that enhance knowledge tasks and patient-level predictions.

Abstract: Metabolomics knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous resources and remains difficult to translate into predictive representations. We developed MetaboLLM, a metabolomics-specialized large language model adapted through continual pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and structured retrieval, together with MetaboLLM-GIN, which converts generated biochemical descriptions into metabolite graphs for patient-level prediction using a graph isomorphism network. Across four backbone families, MetaboLLM outperformed corresponding base and medically adapted models on metabolomics knowledge, relational, and description tasks, and transferred to an external public benchmark. MetaboLLM-GIN achieved the highest AUC for stress hyperglycemia prediction after coronary artery bypass grafting (0.8616) and postmenopausal hormone-regimen classification (0.8123), outperforming conventional models, alternative graph constructions, and graphs generated from unadapted or non-retrieval LLM configurations. Model interpretation further produced biologically meaningful findings in both applications. These results show that domain-specialized language models can organize heterogeneous biochemical knowledge into predictive and interpretable metabolite graph representations.

</details>


### [175] [RxnCLF: Contrastive Transformation-Aware Reaction Foundation Model for Improved Reactivity Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06259)
*Yiting Zheng,Cheng Fang,Anthony Donofrio,Haote Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RxnCLF introduces a self-supervised reaction representation learning framework built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG). Trained on 1.7M Pistachio reactions, it learns a transformation-aware latent space that unifies reactants and products, yielding improved accuracy on multiple yield-prediction benchmarks and showing potential for broader reaction informatics tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data scarcity and the enormous, sparse reaction space hinder generalization of existing encodings (string, fingerprint, graph). A representation that explicitly captures reaction transformations could improve predictive performance and interpretability.

Method: Construct a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that merges reactants and products into a single graph. Use self-supervised contrastive learning to pretrain on 1.7M Pistachio reactions, learning a compact latent space focused on transformation features and context. Fine-tune on yield prediction benchmarks (Buchwald–Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed C–N coupling, and proprietary datasets), comparing to graph and sequence baselines.

Result: RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph- and sequence-based baselines on yield-prediction tasks, achieving higher R2 and best overall performance across evaluated benchmarks.

Conclusion: CRG-based RxnCLF acts as a scalable reaction foundation model with good generalization potential across reaction spaces and applicability to tasks beyond yield prediction, such as regio- and enantioselectivity prediction and reaction condition optimization.

Abstract: Reaction yield prediction remains challenging because labeled data are scarce and reaction space is both combinatorially large and sparsely populated, limiting the generalization of existing reaction representations. String-, fingerprint-, and graph-based reaction encodings only partially capture chemical transformations, making accurate prediction difficult for reactions with complex substrates. We propose reaction contrastive learning foundation (RxnCLF), a self-supervised contrastive framework for reaction representation learning. RxnCLF is built on a condensed reaction graph (CRG) that unifies reactant and product information into a single graph, enabling the model to learn explicit and enriched transformation structure rather than disconnected graphs. Pretrained on 1.7 million Pistachio reactions, RxnCLF learns a compact and continuous latent space that captures both reaction-center features and broader side chain contexts, making it transformation-aware and chemically interpretable. Fine-tuned on multiple yield prediction benchmarks, including Buchwald-Hartwig, Pd-catalyzed BH coupling, and proprietary HTE C-N coupling and amide formation datasets, RxnCLF consistently outperforms graph and sequence-based baselines, improving R2 and achieving the best performance overall. Our results highlight the promise of CRG-based RxnCLF as a scalable reaction foundation model, with the potential to generalize across broader reaction spaces and support diverse downstream reaction informatics tasks, including regioselectivity prediction, enantioselectivity prediction, and reaction condition optimization.

</details>


### [176] [Hypothesis Testing with Conditional Queries: Learnability and the Value of Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06262)
*Zonghuan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive testing in a finite outcome space offers at most a quadratic reduction in query complexity over non-adaptive testing; learnability hinges on positive separation of pairwise conditional probabilities, while zero separation yields a best possible error of 1/2. Non-adaptive procedures can simulate adaptive transcripts with O(N^2(T+log(1/ρ))) queries, and there exist lower bounds showing Ω(N^2) non-adaptive queries, yielding a worst-case adaptivity gap of Θ(N^2).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine when adaptive querying helps in model evaluation tasks that must fix test events in advance, quantify the adaptivity gap, and identify the learnability condition in a finite-outcome, conditional-query setting.

Method: Analyze a conditional-query model with |X|=N. First, establish a learnability criterion based on positive separation of pairwise conditional probabilities between two distribution classes. Then compare adaptive vs fixed-design (non-adaptive) testers, constructing a randomized non-adaptive procedure that pre-selects O(N^2(T+log(1/ρ))) pair queries and simulates the adaptive transcript within ρ in total variation. Prove a matching lower bound via a family with constant adaptive query complexity and Ω_ε(N^2) non-adaptive complexity.

Result: Learnability holds iff the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities. If separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error is 1/2 for every finite query budget. For any T-query adaptive policy and any ρ in (0,1), there exists a randomized non-adaptive procedure with O(N^2(T + log(1/ρ))) pre-chosen queries whose transcript is within ρ of the adaptive transcript (in total variation) across all distributions in the model. There is a matching family with constant adaptive query complexity and Ω_ε(N^2) non-adaptive query complexity, implying a worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap of Θ_ε(N^2).

Conclusion: Interaction yields a quadratic, not exponential, improvement in the required number of tests. Adaptive queries provide a substantial but limited benefit; the exponential branching intuition does not translate into exponential query savings.

Abstract: Model evaluations may fix all tests before observing any responses or select later tests using earlier responses. We study this choice in a conditional-query model on a finite outcome space $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|=N$. We first ask which pairs of distribution classes can be reliably distinguished. We then ask how many additional queries are required to match an adaptive tester when all queried events must be fixed in advance. We show that learnability holds if and only if the two classes have positive separation in their pairwise conditional probabilities. When this separation is zero, the optimal worst-case error is exactly $1/2$ at every finite query budget. For any $T$-query adaptive policy and any $ρ\in (0,1)$, we construct a randomized non-adaptive procedure using $O(N^2(T + \log(1/ρ)))$ pair queries chosen before any response is observed. Its simulated transcript is within $ρ$ in total variation of the adaptive transcript, uniformly over all distributions in the model. We also construct a matching family with constant adaptive query complexity and $Ω_\varepsilon(N^2)$ non-adaptive query complexity. Consequently, the worst-case fixed-error adaptivity gap is $Θ_\varepsilon(N^2)$. Thus interaction can reduce the required number of tests by a quadratic factor, but the apparent exponential branching of an interactive evaluation does not yield an exponential query advantage.

</details>


### [177] [The Tamed Subgradient Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm beyond Convexity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06283)
*Iosif Lytras,Nikolaos Makras,Sotirios Sabanis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SG-TULA is a subgradient-based, taming-enabled discretization of Langevin diffusion for non-smooth, non-convex potentials with superlinear gradient growth, yielding explicit non-asymptotic Wasserstein-2 and excess risk bounds, and demonstrated on GPT-2–like LLM pretraining where it competes with AdamW/Muon.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address sampling/optimization for challenging non-smooth, non-convex potentials with superlinear gradient growth where smoothing is costly and existing subgradient-Langevin methods lack non-asymptotic guarantees; provide explicit constants and practical validation.

Method: Define Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA) that operates directly on subgradients; apply taming to stabilize an explicit scheme in the superlinear regime; derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 with explicit constants depending on dimension and inverse temperature; provide excess risk estimates; verify assumptions with explicit constants for a regularized GPT-2 pretraining potential; include a boosted coordinate-wise variant.

Result: Derived explicit non-asymptotic W2 convergence bounds improving on existing subgradient-Langevin rates; excess risk estimates for the associated optimization problem; explicit constant verification for GPT-2-like potentials; empirical pretraining performance showing competitiveness against finetuned AdamW and Muon, where such non-asymptotic guarantees are not available.

Conclusion: SG-TULA delivers provable guarantees for challenging non-smooth, non-convex problems with superlinear growth and demonstrates practical viability in large-scale pretraining settings, offering explicit-constant analyses and avenues for coordinate-wise variants.

Abstract: We study the problem of sampling from target distributions whose potentials are simultaneously non-smooth, subject to superlinear gradient growth, and non-convex. We introduce the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discretisation of the Langevin diffusion that operates directly on subgradients, without relying on computationally demanding smoothing procedures. To handle the superlinear regime, taming techniques are employed to produce a stable, explicit scheme. We derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, with all constants tracked explicitly in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving upon the currently known rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms. We further provide excess risk estimates for the associated optimisation problem. We verify the assumptions, with explicit constants, for the regularized pretraining potential of a LLM in the GPT-2 lineage and the boosted coordinate-wise variant of SG-TULA pretrains the former competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees are presently available.

</details>


### [178] [Surv-IPTB: An Attention-Based Model for Estimating Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit with Survival Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06288)
*Lev V. Utkin,Stanislav K. Kogan,Andrei V. Konstantinov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An attention-based Surv-IPTB framework estimates individual probability of treatment benefit in survival analysis by reframing IPTB as pairwise binary classification, handling censoring with imprecise probabilities; it outperforms T/S-learner baselines with standard survival estimators on synthetic nonlinear data; code is available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for robust, personalized treatment-benefit estimation under right-censoring in survival analysis, especially for nonlinear treatment effects where traditional meta-learners degrade.

Method: Propose Surv-IPTB: reformulates IPTB as pairwise comparisons across treatment/control, uses attention with learnable query-key transforms to aggregate information; right-censoring is modeled with interval-valued probabilities (imprecise probabilities); trains to output soft class probabilities for censored cases; evaluated on synthetic nonlinear datasets.

Result: Experiments on synthetic data with spiral, bell-shaped, circular feature spaces show robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment-effect strengths; Surv-IPTB consistently outperforms meta-learners (T-, S- learners) combined with random survival forests, CoxPH, and Beran estimators, particularly in nonlinear settings.

Conclusion: The approach offers a scalable, statistically principled solution for personalized treatment-benefit assessment in survival contexts; public code provides reproducibility.

Abstract: This work presents a novel attention-based framework for estimating the Individual Probability of Treatment Benefit (IPTB) in survival analysis contexts. The proposed model, called Surv-IPTB, directly quantifies the probability that a specific patient will experience extended survival time under treatment versus control. We reformulate IPTB estimation as a binary classification problem, leveraging pairwise patient comparisons across treatment and control cohorts. The framework incorporates a principled handling of right-censored observations through imprecise probability representations, where uncertain treatment effects are characterized by interval-valued probabilities. An attention mechanism with learnable query-key transformations enables flexible, data-driven aggregation of pairwise comparisons, while simultaneously learning soft class probabilities for censored cases. Through extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with complex nonlinear structures, including spiral, bell-shaped, and circular feature spaces, we demonstrate that our approach maintains robust performance across varying censoring rates and treatment effect strengths. The model consistently outperforms meta-learner baselines (T-learner and S-learner) equipped with random survival forests, Cox proportional hazards, and Beran estimators, particularly in challenging nonlinear scenarios where conventional methods exhibit significant degradation. The results establish the proposed attention-based framework as a scalable and statistically principled solution for personalized treatment benefit assessment in survival settings. The code implementing the model is publicly available.

</details>


### [179] [BaKron: Efficient Quantization with Kronecker-Factored Hessians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06291)
*Johann Birnick,Rayan Saab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BaKron is an efficient two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian-based adaptive rounding method for neural network quantization. It reduces the computational burden to O(mn(m+n)) for an m×n weight matrix via anti-diagonal parallelism and a recursive divide-and-conquer, while maintaining modularity with respect to base quantizer and Hessian estimator.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GPTQ-style adaptive rounding uses only one-sided information; two-sided Hessian approximations capture correlations across output coordinates, enabling richer curvature-informed quantization, but direct vectorized-GPTQ is expensive. BaKron aims to enable two-sided information efficiently.

Method: BaKron uses anti-diagonal parallelism and recursive divide-and-conquer to perform adaptive rounding on an m×n weight matrix. It requires O(m+n) sequential steps and reduces total work from O(m^2n^2) to O(mn(m+n)). It is modular with respect to the base quantizer and Hessian estimator; provides techniques to compute Hessians efficiently; uses benchmarks.

Result: The method achieves cubic-scaling parity with GPTQ while leveraging richer curvature information; promises practical speedups and accuracy gains; validated by practical benchmarks and experiments across various Hessian choices.

Conclusion: BaKron provides a scalable, modular, curvature-aware quantization solver enabling two-sided Hessian information in a practical framework, with broad applicability and efficient computation.

Abstract: We accelerate a family of algorithms for neural network quantization whose geometry is informed by any Kronecker-factored approximation of the Hessian. GPTQ-style adaptive rounding typically uses one-sided information derived from input activations. Two-sided Kronecker-factored Hessian approximations can additionally capture correlations across output coordinates, but applying GPTQ directly in the vectorized weight domain is computationally expensive. Building on the two-sided adaptive-rounding formulation used by BoA and YAQA, we introduce BaKron, an efficient solver that combines anti-diagonal parallelism with a recursive divide-and-conquer construction. For an $m\times n$ weight matrix, BaKron uses $O(m+n)$ sequential steps while reducing the total work from $O(m^2n^2)$ to $O(mn(m+n))$. Thus, it matches the cubic scaling of GPTQ while exploiting richer curvature information. Moreover, BaKron is modular with respect to both the base quantizer and the Hessian estimator. We also provide practical benchmarks, consider a range of Hessians that BaKron can be called with, find an efficient technique to compute these Hessians, and evaluate the algorithm experimentally.

</details>


### [180] [On-Policy Self-Distillation without Any Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06296)
*Yijiang Li,Bingyang Wang,Yijun Liang,Yunjie Tian,Di Fu,Nuno Vasconcelos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes U-OPSD, an unsupervised on-policy self-distillation using model-generated pseudo-solutions and majority voting to rectify confidently incorrect completions, achieving gains across tasks without external supervision.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Eliminate reliance on ground-truth, external feedback, or larger-model guidance in on-policy distillation, enabling true self-distillation.

Method: Generate multiple rollouts, select a pseudo-solution via majority vote under a self-consistency threshold; condition a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution; distill into prefixes of the model’s longest incorrect completion to guide self-correction.

Result: Consistent improvements over base models across diverse benchmarks and settings; matches or surpasses supervised methods (OPSD, GRPO); notable gains on multi-choice benchmarks in non-thinking mode; in thinking mode, on par with OPSD and outperforming GRPO.

Conclusion: Self-distillation with internal consistency is feasible and effective; U-OPSD provides robust gains across model scales and tasks without external supervision, approaching or exceeding supervised baselines.

Abstract: On-policy (Self-)Distillation (OPD / OPSD) has shown strong potential for post-training large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods still rely heavily on external supervision, including ground-truth signals, environmental feedback, or guidance from larger models, and therefore fall short of genuine "self"-distillation. In this study, we show that on-policy self-distillation can be achieved using only a model's own generations via internal consistency. We propose Unsupervised On-Policy Self-Distillation (U-OPSD). U-OPSD first samples multiple rollouts and constructs a pseudo-solution by majority vote under a self-consistency threshold. It then conditions a teacher distribution on the shortest pseudo-solution and distills it into prefixes of the model's longest incorrect completion, allowing the model to correct itself precisely where it is confidently wrong. Across diverse benchmarks, base models, and training settings, U-OPSD consistently improves over the base models and matches or surpasses supervised methods with ground truth (GT), such as OPSD and GRPO. On AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, MATH500, and AMC23, U-OPSD improves over the base model by 8.5% and 10.7% on Qwen3 non-thinking mode at the 4B and 8B scales, respectively, and outperforms OPSD by an average of 3.2% and 2.3%. In thinking mode, U-OPSD remains on par with OPSD, outperforming it by 0.9% at 4B and matching it at 8B, while surpassing GRPO by 0.7% and 1.1%, respectively.

</details>


### [181] [RRC: Unlocking Generative Reward Models in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Ranking-Based Reward Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06310)
*Chenglong Wang,Ziming Zhu,Yifu Huo,Bei Li,Qiaozhi He,Yan Ding,Xiaoyang Hao,Yuxin Gao,Tianhua Zhou,Xiaojia Chang,Tongran Liu,Jingbo Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We introduce Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) to convert comparative preferences from generative reward models into scalar RL rewards, using self-competitive and anchor-guided ranking, improving RL performance on open-ended dialogue and reasoning tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative reward models excel at ranking but standard RL uses scalar rewards, creating a mismatch that hinders effective RL training. A reward-construction method that leverages relative preferences is needed to align these paradigms.

Method: RRC framework with two strategies: (1) self-competitive ranking—derive rewards from comparisons among sampled responses, (2) anchor-guided ranking—use a small set of reference (anchor) responses to enable scalable ranking-based reward construction.

Result: Empirical results show that RRC substantially improves RL training when using generative reward models, with consistent gains over existing reward-construction approaches across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: RRC bridges the gap between ranking-based generative rewards and scalar RL signals, enabling more effective RL with generative reward models and demonstrating robust gains on dialogue and reasoning tasks; code is released at the provided GitHub link.

Abstract: Recent advances in reward modeling show a paradigm shift from discriminative reward models to generative reward models. However, despite their strong capabilities in response ranking, generative reward models have not realized their potential in reinforcement learning (RL). Our analysis reveals that this limitation arises from a mismatch between the comparative nature of generative reward modeling and the scalar scoring paradigm adopted by existing RL algorithms. To bridge this gap, we propose a Ranking-based Reward Construction (RRC) approach, which enables generative reward models to provide more effective RL learning signals by deriving rewards from relative preference rankings. RRC introduces two complementary strategies: self-competitive ranking, which exploits comparisons among sampled responses, and anchor-guided ranking, which enables scalable ranking-based reward construction with a small set of reference responses. Experiments across open-ended chat and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that RRC substantially improves RL training with generative reward models, achieving consistent gains over existing reward construction approaches. Our code can be found at https://github.com/wangclnlp/RRC.

</details>


### [182] [CalibForge: Adversarial Solver Calibration for Scaling Learnable Terminal Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06352)
*Fanzhe Meng,Guoxin Chen,Jiale Zhao,Shuang Sun,Zhiyu Lin,Wayne Xin Zhao,Ruihua Song,Ji-Rong Wen,Kai Jia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CalibForge autonomously synthesizes calibrated terminal tasks by adversarial solver calibration, producing a dataset of 5,431 tasks and boosting agent performance across multiple benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create executable, verifiable tasks that reveal solver-relative difficulty and enable learnable supervision, addressing the gap between solvability and learnability.

Method: Two solver-calibration strategies: (1) multi-solver calibration targeting disagreement among a heterogeneous solver pool, and (2) contrastive solver calibration targeting a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation. Both revise candidate tasks based on verified solver behavior to define a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability.

Result: Construction of 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Ablations show both strategies outperform authoring/validation alone or single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full set achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0; maximum gains over base model: 24.71pp on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68pp on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04pp on Doc2Repo.

Conclusion: Solver-relative learnability is a practical target for creating effective and transferable agent training data; adversarial and contrastive solver calibration yield more effective supervision than traditional data creation pipelines.

Abstract: Training terminal agents requires executable and verifiable tasks that are not merely solvable, but appropriately challenging for learning. Executable validation establishes feasibility, yet does not reveal how a task behaves relative to a given solver setting. In this paper, we present CalibForge, an autonomous terminal-task synthesis system that uses verified solver behavior to revise candidate tasks through adversarial solver calibration. Multi-solver calibration targets disagreement within a heterogeneous solver pool, whereas contrastive solver calibration targets a designated strong-pass/weak-fail relation; both operationalize a solver-relative learnable zone anchored in demonstrated solvability. Using CalibForge, we construct 5,431 calibrated terminal tasks. Our ablations show that both strategies yield more effective supervision than authoring and validation alone or ordinary single-solver feedback. Models trained on the full collection achieve 32.58% and 47.57% on Terminal-Bench 2.0. The largest improvements over the corresponding base model reach 24.71 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, 27.68 points on SWE-bench Pro, and 30.04 points on Doc2Repo. Together, these results support solver-relative learnability as a practical target for constructing effective and transferable agent training data.

</details>


### [183] [An Optimal Agnostic PAC Algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06363)
*Markus Engelund Mathiasen,Jian Qian,Nikita Zhivotovskiy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Optimal excess risk bound for agnostic PAC learning with binary classifiers of VC dimension d; achieves near-tight sample complexity up to universal constants, matching classical lower bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resolve the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning by providing a tight excess risk bound that scales with d, n, δ, and L*.

Method: Construct a learning algorithm from i.i.d. data and prove a high-probability excess risk bound: L(ĥ) ≤ L* + 7×10^8 [ sqrt( L*(d + log(1/δ))/n ) + (d + log(1/δ))/n ].

Result: Agnostic PAC learner with an explicit, statistically optimal excess risk bound; the bound matches known lower bounds up to universal constants for fixed L*, establishing optimal sample complexity in terms of d, n, δ.

Conclusion: Settles the sample complexity for agnostic PAC learning up to universal constants at every fixed L*, aligning with the lower bounds of Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi.

Abstract: Let $H\subseteq\{-1,+1\}^X$ be a class of finite VC dimension $d\ge1$. Writing $L$ for the binary risk and $L^*=\min_{h\in H}L(h)$, we construct a learner achieving the statistically optimal risk bound: from an i.i.d.\ sample of size $n$, for every $0<δ\le 1/2$, with probability at least $1-δ$, \[
  L(\widehat h)
  \le L^*+ 7\cdot10^8\left(
  \sqrt{\frac{L^*(d+\log(1/δ))}{n}}
  +\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}
  \right). \] This settles the sample complexity of agnostic PAC learning up to universal constants at every fixed $L^*$, matching the lower bounds of Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi [A Probabilistic Theory of Pattern Recognition, Springer, 1996].

</details>


<div id='cs.RO'></div>

# cs.RO [[Back]](#toc)

### [184] [VLAff: Vision-Language-Affordance Model for Unified Actionable Affordances](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05215)
*Jihoon Oh,Kento Kawaharazuka,Kei Okada*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes EgoAffordance dataset and VLAff, a vision-language foundation model that learns actionable, embodiment-agnostic affordances from egocentric human videos to enable zero-shot robot manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Embodiment mismatch between humans and robots makes directly transferring manipulation policies hard. The work targets object-centric, actionable affordances that generalize across embodiments.

Method: Leverages egocentric human videos with 3D Structure-from-Motion and hand mesh reconstruction to extract visual, grasp, and trajectory affordances. Builds EgoAffordance dataset (204k episodes; 5.6M visual affordances; 11.6M grasp/trajectory affordances). Introduces VLAff, a large vision-language foundation model that learns cross-modal correlations across all affordances. Given a visual input and instruction, VLAff outputs visual affordance heatmaps, grasp poses, and trajectories, which are converted to executable actions using 3D scene data.

Result: States-of-the-art in visual affordance prediction. Demonstrates applicability to real robot tasks, including zero-shot manipulation and affordance-guided robot learning.

Conclusion: Advances embodiment-agnostic manipulation by exploiting large-scale egocentric data and a unified vision-language foundation model, enabling direct generation of actionable affordances and practical robot control.

Abstract: Learning manipulation skills from human videos is promising for scalable robot learning. However, the embodiment mismatch between humans and robots makes this challenging. One promising solution is to learn object-centric actionable affordances that are embodiment-agnostic. In this work, we propose a framework that leverages egocentric human videos with state-of-the-art 3D Structure-from-Motion and hand mesh reconstruction to extract actionable affordances such as visual, grasp, and trajectory affordances that explicitly encode where to interact, how to grasp, and how to move. We construct EgoAffordance, a large-scale dataset comprising 204K episodes with 5.6M visual affordances and 11.6M grasp and trajectory affordances. Building on this, we introduce VLAff, a large vision-language model-based unified foundation model that learns cross-modal correlations across all actionable affordances. Given a visual observation and instruction, VLAff generates visual affordance heatmaps, grasp poses, and trajectories, which are then converted into directly executable actions by utilizing 3D scene information. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that VLAff not only achieves state-of-the-art performance on visual affordance prediction, but can also be effectively applied to real robot applications such as zero-shot manipulation and affordance-guided robot learning.

</details>


### [185] [A System for Train Condition Monitoring and Structural Health Assessment of Rail Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05221)
*Maximilian Posner,Martin Dazer,Daniela Lauer,Robert Winkler-Höhn,Mathilde Laporte,Tobias Herrmann,Martin Köppel*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A framework combining structural sensors with AI for real-time vehicle condition monitoring in mainline rail to detect impacts and driving-over events, enabling condition-based maintenance and long-term analytics for design optimization and GoA4 progression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GoA4 deployment in mainline rail is constrained by safety concerns and open environments; existing perception (cameras, radar, lidar) identify objects but struggle with reliably detecting impacts and driving-over events; need real-time, reliable structural-state insight for maintenance and safety.

Method: Integrate structural sensor technologies (e.g., accelerometers, strain gauges, vibration sensors; potentially fiber-optic or piezoelectric sensors) with AI-based data analysis to monitor vehicle condition in real time. Applications: (1) automated detection of impacts, structural damage, and driving-over events, (2) condition-based maintenance via continuous monitoring, (3) long-term analytics for design optimization. Real-time processing and anomaly detection via ML/DL on sensor streams, fusion with other subsystems as needed.

Result: Feasibility demonstrated: the integrated sensing and AI framework can detect impacts and structural states, support predictive maintenance, and provide data insights for design optimization. Indicates potential to enhance safety and facilitate transition to GoA4 in mainline rail.

Conclusion: The proposed approach offers a viable path to improved safety and maintenance in mainline rail and supports automation goals, with future work likely focusing on field validation, sensor deployment strategies, data governance, and integration with train control systems.

Abstract: The ongoing digitalization of rail systems and the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) are fundamentally transforming the design, operation, and maintenance of rail vehicles. While fully automated operation at Grade of Automation 4 (GoA4) is well established in metro systems, its deployment in mainline rail remains limited. This is primarily due to stringent safety requirements and the complexity of open operational environments. Current perception systems based on cameras, radar, and lidar are effective in detecting objects but provide limited capability for reliably identifying impacts, collisions, and driving-over events. This paper presents a novel approach for real-time vehicle condition monitoring and impact detection that integrates structural sensor technologies with AI-based data analysis. The proposed framework addresses three key applications: (1) automated detection of impacts, structural damage, and driving-over events, (2) condition-based maintenance enabled by continuous monitoring, and (3) long-term data analytics to support vehicle design optimization. The results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approach and highlight its potential to enhance operational safety, enable predictive maintenance strategies, and support the transition toward fully automated operation in mainline rail systems

</details>


### [186] [Failing Gracefully: Mitigating Impact of Inevitable Robot Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05313)
*Duc M. Nguyen,Saad A. Ghani,Andrew Marshall,Allison Andreyev,Gregory J. Stein,Xuesu Xiao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Proposes a risk-aware safety formulation for service robots that quantifies both the likelihood and severity of failures’ interactions with surrounding entities, paired with FailBench, a MuJoCo-based simulator for evaluating failure modes and their impact on planning and learned policies in households.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Failures in household service robots are inevitable and can have safety-critical consequences. A quantitative, entity-aware safety framework is needed to guide planning and policy learning to minimize harms while maintaining task efficiency.

Method: Introduce a safety formulation that computes the probability of impactful interactions during failures and the severity of their outcomes across entities. Integrate this with planning to balance safety and efficiency. Present FailBench, a MuJoCo-based simulation framework to study robot–environment interactions under diverse failure modes (sensing issues, actuator malfunctions) in household-like settings.

Result: Claim that the proposed safety formulation and FailBench provide a foundation for developing safer and more robust motion plans and learned policies for real-world household deployment; practical evaluation details are not provided in the abstract.

Conclusion: A risk-aware planning framework paired with a dedicated simulation testbed can advance safe, robust behavior for service robots in cluttered, dynamic home environments, enabling systematic evaluation of failures and mitigation strategies.

Abstract: Service robots operate in household environments shared with humans, pets, and everyday objects, where they are highly susceptible to failures such as software crashes, hardware degradation, or unpredictable interactions. While roboticists strive to minimize failures, some remain inevitable, making it critical to mitigate their potential consequences for safe and reliable deployment. This paper introduces a novel safety formulation that evaluates both the probability of impactful interactions between robots and surrounding entities during failures, and the severity of their outcomes. By quantifying the impact of failures on different entities, our approach enables robots to make informed planning decisions that balance safety with task efficiency. To support systematic evaluation, we also present FailBench, a MuJoCo-based simulation framework for studying robot-environment interactions under diverse failure modes, including sensing issues and actuator malfunctions. Together, our safety formulation and FailBench provide a foundation for developing safer and more robust motion plans and learned policies in real-world household environments.

</details>


### [187] [Unified Planning-Learning Framework for Robust UUV Navigation Under Partial Observability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05365)
*Md Ether Deowan,Eleni Kelasidi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A hybrid planning-learning framework for UUVs that fuses onboard occupancy mapping, clearance-aware global planning, and RL-based local control with a learned latent state and uncertainty-aware distillation; demonstrated with reproducible multi-seed tests in Isaac Sim showing improved robustness and safety under partial observability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underwater autonomy suffers from partial observability, dynamic obstacles, and sensing/communication limitations. There is a need for an integrated, safe, and reproducible pipeline that combines perception, planning, and learning to enable robust UUV operation.

Method: Construct occupancy maps from onboard sonar and depth imagery; employ a clearance-constrained global planner for long-horizon structure; integrate an RL policy for short-range tracking and reactive avoidance; learn a compact latent state capturing environmental structure, obstacle dynamics, and uncertainty; use Behavior Tree (BT) distillation with staged supervision; apply uncertainty-calibrated distillation reweighting based on online latent-model uncertainty; maintain time-to-collision (TTC) and clearance cues in planning and policy features; establish a reproducible multi-seed evaluation protocol in NVIDIA Isaac Sim; benchmark against BT-only and standard RL baselines.

Result: The framework yields improved robustness and safety in dynamic underwater environments, outperforming BT-only and standard RL baselines and providing a reproducible methodology for robust UUV autonomy under partial observability.

Conclusion: A unified hybrid planning-learning architecture with latent-state learning and uncertainty-aware distillation offers a general, reproducible approach to robust UUV autonomy under partial observability, integrating perception, planning, and learning for safer, more reliable operation.

Abstract: This paper presents an observation-only autonomy framework for Unmanned Underwater Vehicles (UUVs) navigation in dynamic underwater environments that integrates persistent occupancy mapping, global clearance-aware planning, and risk-aware local control. The proposed pipeline constructs occupancy maps solely from onboard sonar and depth image observations, adapts a clearance-constrained global planner (GP) to provide long-horizon structure, and integrates a reinforcement learning (RL) policy to handle short-range tracking and reactive avoidance. To further support decision-making under partial observability, the system learns a compact latent state representation from onboard sensor data, encoding environmental structure, obstacle dynamics, and uncertainty. Behavior tree (BT) distillation with staged supervision is introduced to improve safety and training stability, while an uncertainty-calibrated distillation mechanism reweights teacher guidance using online latent-model uncertainty, emphasizing uncertain regimes during learning, with time-to-collision (TTC) and clearance cues remaining explicit in planning and local policy features. To demonstrate the efficacy of the framework, a reproducible multi-seed evaluation protocol is established in high-fidelity GPU-accelerated simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Sim, and performance is benchmarked against BT-only and standard RL baselines. The results obtained demonstrate improved robustness and safety under dynamic conditions, thus providing a general pipeline with a unified hybrid planning learning architecture and a reproducible methodology for robust UUV autonomy under partial observability.

</details>


### [188] [World-to-Wrist: Task-Conditioned Future Wrist Modeling for Fine-Grained Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05369)
*Yuhao Pan,Haosong Peng,Zhengshen Zhang,Zhengyang Yan,Yalun Dai,Fushuo Huo,Chujie Wang,Tianyu Qi,Xiucheng Wang,Nan Cheng,Wenchao Xu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: World-to-Wrist VLA (W2-VLA) and W2-CoT introduce task-conditioned future wrist modeling to Vision-Language-Action for fine-grained manipulation. They treat wrist-local interactions via latent tokens interface, forecast future wrist latents given history and task, and generate structured annotations to supervise. Demonstrated improvements on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks with >80 Hz action rate, in single- and bi-manual settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current VLA models treat main-view and wrist-view as parallel inputs, neglecting wrist-specific local interactions essential for fine-grained manipulation. Anticipating how wrist dynamics evolve under a global task context can improve manipulation precision and contact handling.

Method: Introduce W2-VLA architecture: given current multi-view observations and a task instruction, contextualize a set of latent tokens as an interface between the vision-language model and a wrist predictor. Condition on this interface and observed wrist history to forecast future wrist latents, which are converted into future-aware context for action prediction. Also introduce W2-CoT: a synthesis pipeline producing structured annotations describing manipulation progress, transition cues, and wrist-local evidence to supervise the latent interface.

Result: Empirical results on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks show improvements in fine-grained and contact-sensitive manipulation, across both single-arm and bimanual setups, while maintaining action-generation rates above 80 Hz.

Conclusion: W2-VLA with task-conditioned future wrist modeling and W2-CoT annotations provides more accurate, context-aware action predictions for fine-grained manipulation, enabling faster, more reliable performance across diverse settings.

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often treat main-view and wrist-view observations as parallel visual inputs, overlooking their distinct roles in robot manipulation. Fine-grained manipulation, however, benefits from anticipating how wrist-local interactions may evolve under the global task context. To address this limitation, we present World-to-Wrist VLA (W2-VLA), a VLA model for fine-grained robot manipulation with task-conditioned future wrist modeling. Given current multi-view observations and a task instruction, W2-VLA contextualizes a set of latent modeling tokens as a compact interface between the vision-language model and the wrist predictor. Conditioned on this interface and the observed wrist history, the predictor forecasts future wrist latents, which are transformed into future-aware context for action prediction. In addition, we introduce W2-CoT, a synthesis pipeline that produces structured annotations describing manipulation progress, physical transition cues, and wrist-local evidence. These annotations provide auxiliary supervision that shapes the task-conditioned latent interface. Experiments on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved fine-grained and contact-sensitive manipulation across both single-arm and bimanual settings, while maintaining action-generation rates above 80 Hz.

</details>


### [189] [Sliding Sensors: Configurable Confidence in State Estimation for Continuum Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05410)
*Ella Walsh,Spencer Teetaert,Eric Diller,Timothy D. Barfoot,Jessica Burgner-Kahrs*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Mechanically reconfigurable sensing is proposed to shape uncertainty in state estimation for continuum robots by sliding a sensor along the length; demonstrates improved task-relevant confidence and reduced full-body shape error versus fixed-tip sensing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uncertain environments yield spatially non-uniform estimation uncertainty; global accuracy is not always essential, but confidence at task-relevant locations is critical for safe interaction with continuum robots.

Method: Concept hardware enabling longitudinal translation of a sensor within a continuum robot to reconfigure sensing by moving the sensor along the robot; experiments compare sliding sensor to a fixed tip sensor and assess effects on state estimation confidence and full-body shape error.

Result: Demonstrates that estimation confidence can be reconfigured by sensor location; sliding the sensor back and forth over time reduces full-body shape estimation errors compared to a single fixed-tip sensor.

Conclusion: Mechanical reconfigurability of sensing enables uncertainty shaping in continuum-robot state estimation; sensor relocation along the continuum can achieve improved estimation performance at task-relevant locations.

Abstract: Continuum robots often operate in uncertain environments, where accurate state estimation is essential for safe interactions. Estimate uncertainty is inherently spatially non-uniform: confidence varies depending on where measurements are available. Global estimation accuracy is not always the top priority, but rather achieving sufficient confidence at task-relevant locations along the robot. This extended abstract introduces mechanically reconfigurable sensing enabling uncertainty-shaping in state estimation for continuum robots. We present a concept hardware design demonstrating the feasibility of longitudinal translation of a sensor within a continuum robot. We demonstrate that state estimation confidence can be reconfigured by varying the sensor location, and show a reduction of full-body shape estimation errors when sliding the sensor back and forth over time, compared to a single fixed tip sensor.

</details>


### [190] [ARGUS: Aligning Robot Scene Geometry Under Shifting Views with Large 3D Vision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05579)
*Rishik Sathua,Haonan Chen,Katherine Driggs-Campbell*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ARGUS uses large-scale 3D vision models to canonicalize observations from arbitrary viewpoints, reducing entanglement between scene geometry and viewpoint, boosting data efficiency and performance of visuomotor policies by 4–6x on viewpoint-diverse datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visuomotor policy learning is hampered by entanglement of object geometry with camera viewpoint, limiting generalization across viewpoint-diverse data and their learning efficiency.

Method: An observation pre-processing pipeline that applies large-scale 3D vision models to align images from arbitrary camera viewpoints into a canonical viewpoint before passing them to downstream visuomotor policies, enabling a simplified, viewpoint-invariant observation space. Evaluated across datasets with varying viewpoint diversity.

Result: ARGUS consistently outperforms prior approaches in both limited-view and view-diverse regimes and achieves 4–6x faster convergence by leveraging the canonicalized observation space, indicating reduced learning burden for the policy.

Conclusion: Using 3D vision models to reframe observations into a canonical viewpoint can significantly improve data efficiency and generalization of visuomotor policies on large-scale, viewpoint-diverse robot datasets; potential applicability to broader manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Large-scale visuomotor policies have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of robot manipulation tasks. However, despite this success, manipulation polices often entangle scene geometry with the corresponding viewpoint, learning where objects lie in an image rather than where it lies in the task space. This entanglement inherently limits the corresponding policy's ability to learn from viewpoint-diverse datasets (ex. DROID, BridgeV2) and generalize beyond the viewpoints captured in their training data. In this work, we present ARGUS, an observation pre-processing pipeline that uses large-scale 3D vision models to align image observations from arbitrary camera viewpoints into a canonical viewpoint before passing it to downstream visuomotor policies. Experiments across training datasets with varying levels of viewpoint diversity, from fixed multi-view camera configurations to highly varied camera placements, show that our method consistently outperforms prior approaches across both limited-view and view-diverse training regimes. In efficiency comparisons, ARGUS demonstrates an ability to learn from view-diverse data, converging to high success rates 4-6x faster than previous methods by leveraging a simplified observation space. Overall, our findings show that leveraging large-scale 3D vision models reduces the learning burden on visuomotor policies, enabling more efficient learning from large-scale, viewpoint-diverse robot datasets.

</details>


### [191] [PathCover: A Fast Convex Decomposition along a Path via Randomized Iterative Space Partitioning (RISP) on Point Clouds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05586)
*Kunal S. Narkhede,Abhijeet M. Kulkarni,Guoquan Huang,Ioannis Poulakakis*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PathCover is a real-time framework for generating obstacle-free corridors from raw point clouds by constructing convex polytopes via a randomized, linear-time algorithm (RISP), enabling fast MPC/trajectory planning with finite termination guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autonomous navigation requires rapid, obstacle-free regions for trajectory planning; existing corridor generators fail to meet sensor-rate real-time constraints, creating bottlenecks in planning pipelines.

Method: Introduce PathCover and the RISP randomized algorithm that builds convex polytopes directly from raw LiDAR point clouds in expected linear time under a mild probabilistic elimination condition. Generates sequences of overlapping, obstacle-free polytopes that constrain downstream MPC/trajectory optimization, with finite-time termination guarantees and guaranteed progress along obstacle-free references.

Result: Benchmarks on synthetic and real LiDAR data show an order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining similar corridor volumes. Full pipeline validated in high-fidelity quadrotor simulations and real-world deployment on a quadrupedal robot using live LiDAR perception.

Conclusion: PathCover delivers real-time obstacle-free corridor generation with strong theoretical guarantees and empirically demonstrated performance and applicability to diverse robotic platforms and perception setups.

Abstract: Autonomous robot navigation requires the rapid generation of obstacle-free regions for trajectory planning. However, existing corridor generators struggle to meet real-time, sensor-rate computational constraints. To resolve this bottleneck, we introduce PathCover, a framework driven by RISP; a novel randomized algorithm that constructs convex polytopes directly from raw point cloud data in expected linear time under a mild probabilistic elimination condition. PathCover generates sequences of overlapping, obstacle-free polytopes that safely constrain downstream MPC and trajectory optimization. We mathematically guarantee that the algorithm terminates in finite steps while ensuring continuous progress along any obstacle-free reference path. Extensive benchmarks on synthetic and real-world LiDAR datasets demonstrate an order-of-magnitude speedup over state-of-the-art methods while maintaining comparable corridor volumes. The complete pipeline is validated via high-fidelity quadrotor simulations and physical deployment on a quadrupedal robot navigating constrained environments using live LiDAR perception.

</details>


### [192] [Search-Aided Joint Agent-Environment Reinforcement Learning for Robust Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding with Rotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05588)
*He Jiang,Jingtian Yan,Yulun Zhang,Yimin Tang,Tanishq Duhan,Rishi Veerapaneni,Guillaume Sartoretti,Jiaoyang Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: SJRL combines a single-step search-based planner (Causal PIBT) with joint RL where the environment policy learns edge costs, achieving better coordination in LMAPF-R2 and validating on real robots; outperforms Causal-PIBT on dense maps and mixed-reality scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world LMAPF demands handling robust safety constraints and in-place rotation, which are not captured by oversimplified kinematic models; need integrated planning-learning approach to coordinate many agents in constrained spaces.

Method: Hybrid framework SJRL: augment neural policies with Causal PIBT to resolve collisions; joint RL optimizing both agent policies and environment policies; environment policy learns graph edge costs, enabling global guidance via backward Dijkstra; tested on high-density maps and in mixed-reality warehouse with 8 physical and 248 virtual robots.

Result: Significant improvements over Causal-PIBT on multiple high-density maps; successful validation in mixed-reality warehouse with both physical and virtual agents.

Conclusion: SJRL effectively addresses LMAPF-R2 challenges, offering practical, scalable coordination for densely populated environments and real-world robotic systems.

Abstract: Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding (LMAPF) requires repeatedly planning collision-free paths for agents that continuously receive new goals upon reaching their current ones. While many learning-based planners have been proposed for LMAPF, most rely on oversimplified kinematic assumptions that may overlook motion constraints critical to real-world performance. In this work, we study a more realistic LMAPF model derived from many real-world automated warehouse systems, termed LMAPF-R2, which incorporates robust safety constraints and in-place rotation constraints. These constraints substantially increase coordination difficulty, particularly in highly constrained spaces. To address these challenges, we propose Search-Aided Joint Reinforcement Learning (SJRL). We first augment neural policies with Causal PIBT, a single-step search-based planner that resolves agents' collisions and propagates their intentions. We then introduce a unified RL formulation that jointly optimizes agent and environment policies, where the environment policy learns graph edge costs to provide global movement guidance via backward Dijkstra search. Experiments demonstrate that SJRL achieves significant improvements over the strong search-based planner, Causal-PIBT, across multiple high-density maps. We further validate SJRL in a challenging mixed-reality warehouse environment with 8 physical robots and 248 virtual robots.

</details>


### [193] [KILVO: Kinematic-Inertial-LiDAR-Visual Odometry with Robust Multimodal Adaptation for Humanoid Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05647)
*Jixin Gao,Fucheng Liu,Teng Zhang,Fusheng Zha*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: KILVO is a multi-sensor odometry framework for humanoid robots that fuses inertial data, leg kinematics, LiDAR, and camera within an asynchronous-sequential error-state iterated Kalman filter (ESIKF). It uses inertial prediction, high-rate leg-proprioceptive constraints, and sequential LiDAR-first geometric priors followed by photometric visual updates, with multimodal fault tolerance and a compact contact estimator sharing state information. Demonstrates strong accuracy, efficiency, output rate, and robustness across multiple humanoids, gait patterns, and scenarios; code and data released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable robust, accurate, real-time odometry for humanoid robots by exploiting readily available sensors (joint encoders, IMU, LiDAR, camera) and leverages asynchronous fusion to handle real-world sensor degradation and failures while maintaining high update rates.

Method: An asynchronous-sequential hybrid error-state iterated Kalman filter (ESIKF). Inertial data used for state prediction; high-rate leg kinematics provide proprioceptive constraints; exteroception updated sequentially: first LiDAR point registration for geometric priors, then visual update via photometric error; multimodal adaptation addresses sensor failures; compact contact estimation module shares information with state estimation without extra sensors.

Result: Extensive experiments on public datasets and real-world trials across multiple humanoid robots and gait patterns show competitive accuracy, efficiency, and output rates with strong robustness to sensor degradation and failures; claims to surpass state-of-the-art fusion methods; code and datasets released on GitHub.

Conclusion: KILVO delivers robust, real-time odometry for humanoid robots by tightly integrating multimodal sensors within an asynchronous fusion framework, achieving high performance and resilience, with publicly available code and data.

Abstract: This article presents a kinematic-inertial-LiDAR-visual odometry for humanoid robots, called KILVO. Tailored to the platform features, requirements, and real-world complexity, it fully utilizes the sensors commonly equipped on humanoid robots, including joint encoders, IMU, LiDAR, and camera, within an asynchronous-sequential hybrid error-state iterated Kalman filter (ESIKF). Specifically, inertial data are used for prediction, leg kinematics are processed asynchronously at a high rate and provide proprioceptive constraints, while exteroception is updated sequentially, first by registering LiDAR points for geometric priors and then by updating the visual component via photometric errors. Moreover, the framework is elaborately designed with multimodal adaptation for resilience to sensor failures. A compact contact estimation module is also developed, sharing information with state estimation without additional sensors. Extensive experiments on public datasets and in the real world across multiple humanoid robots, gait patterns, and scenarios demonstrate that KILVO achieves highly competitive accuracy, efficiency, and output rates, with strong robustness against sensor degradation and failures, making it more suitable for humanoid robots than state-of-the-art fusion methods. Our code and datasets are released on GitHub.

</details>


### [194] [JoyAI-RA 0.5: Scaling Robot Manipulation Learning via Dual Action Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05674)
*JoyAI-RA Team*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: JoyAI-RA 0.5 is a generalist Vision-Language-World-Action framework that enables cross-source robotic learning via dual action alignment, fusing latent-action world models with explicit canonical actions to learn physical dynamics from human egocentric video, simulation, and real robots. It achieves strong real-world AgiBot performance, with no plateau as more human pretraining data is added, suggesting human video can be a primary axis for scaling manipulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robotic data are scarce and heterogeneous across supervision and embodiment (human egocentric video, simulation, real robots). Naive pooling causes negative transfer. Human egocentric data scale well but are distant from robot data, motivating a unified framework that can leverage all sources without degrading performance.

Method: Dual action alignment: implicit (latent actions inferred from visual transitions) and explicit (canonical action representation with camera-frame chunk-relative end-effector actions). A world-model learns physical dynamics conditioned on latent actions, guided by visual semantics. An inner-outer-loop reinforcement learning schedule facilitates task adaptation and foundation-policy improvement.

Result: On real-world AgiBot benchmarks, JoyAI-RA shows strong performance on seen tasks and generalizes to unseen variations. Performance improves with larger volumes of human egocentric pretraining data, without signs of plateauing, indicating that abundant human experience can be transformed into transferable training signals.

Conclusion: Abundant but weakly labeled human experience can be converted into a transferable training signal, elevating human video from a weak auxiliary source to a primary axis for scaling manipulation capabilities across heterogeneous data sources.

Abstract: Robot data is scarce, so generalist policies need to learn from heterogeneous sources, including human egocentric video, simulation, and real robots, which differ in supervision and embodiment, with action labels missing or mutually incompatible. Human egocentric data scale best but sit farthest from robot data, and naive pooling causes negative transfer rather than knowledge sharing. We propose JoyAI-RA 0.5, a generalist Vision-Language-World-Action (VLWA) framework that couples physical world-dynamics priors with visual semantics and scales manipulation learning across such data via dual action alignment. Implicit action alignment infers latent actions from visual transitions, enabling action-free human, simulation, and robot data to guide a latent-action-conditioned world model in learning physical dynamics. Explicit alignment grounds reliable human and robot trajectories in a unified physical action space through a canonical action representation and camera-frame chunk-relative end-effector actions. An inner-outer-loop reinforcement stage then pairs efficient task adaptation with foundation-policy improvement. On a real-world AgiBot benchmark, JoyAI-RA performs strongly on both seen tasks and unseen variations. The task score improves consistently as the volume of human egocentric pretraining data increases and shows no sign of plateauing at our largest scale. This suggests that abundant but weakly labeled human experience can be converted into a transferable training signal, making human video not merely a weak auxiliary source but a primary axis along which manipulation capability can be scaled. Project page can be found at https://joyai-ra-05.github.io/.

</details>


### [195] [Nonvisual Classification of Ground-Condition by Artificial Proprioception in an Amoeba-Inspired Autonomous Walking Robot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05684)
*Hyoto Yamaguchi,Zenji Yatabe,Seiya Kasai*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A multimodal proprioceptive sensing system using a 3-axis accelerometer, eight foot pressure sensors, and reservoir computing enables nonvisual ground-condition classification (flat vs rough) for an amoeba-inspired quadruped robot, with on-site gait switching and analysis of sensor contributions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable robust, nonvisual ground-condition awareness for legged locomotion to guide gait adaptation in dynamic environments.

Method: Integrate 3-axis accelerometer, eight foot pressure sensors, and reservoir computing (RC) for real-time ground-condition classification without image sensing; account for large sensor-output fluctuations due to walking; classify ground as flat or rough and adapt gait accordingly; assess each sensor's contribution to the classification.

Result: Achieved high-accuracy ground-condition classification despite dynamic robot motion; demonstrated on-board switching of walking gait based on predicted ground condition; provided insight into the relative importance of each sensor in the decision.

Conclusion: Nonvisual proprioceptive sensing with RC is a viable approach for robust ground-condition awareness in legged robots, enabling adaptive locomotion; the study also maps the contribution of individual sensors to the classification performance.

Abstract: Nonvisual classification of ground condition based on a multimodal sensing approach was investigated for an amoeba-inspired autonomous walking robot. To classify ground condition without image sensing and processing, we implemented artificial proprioception by integrating a three-axis accelerometer, eight foot pressure sensors, and reservoir computing (RC). Even when large fluctuations in the sensor outputs are caused by dynamic motions of a four-legged robot in walking, our system can classify the ground condition, flat or rough, with high accuracy. We demonstrate on-site switching of walking gait depending on ground condition in the robot. We also discuss the contribution of each sensor to ground condition classification.

</details>


### [196] [Hijacking Robots with a Piece of Paper: A Systematic Study of Physical Prompt Injection in VLM-Controlled Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05715)
*S. M . Bhagya P. Samarakoon,M. A. Viraj J. Muthugala,W. K. R. Sachinthana,Mohan Rajesh Elara*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Systematic physical prompt injection attacks on VLM-controlled robotics; four-category taxonomy for adversarial in-scene text; benchmark with 20 prompts across layouts and command formulations; tested on GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B; attack success ranges 5-29%; cross-model transfer for authority-impersonation/negation; defenses (prompt-based, two-stage verification, text masking) substantially reduce risk; trade-offs include possible impairment of reading-in-scene tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess vulnerability of vision-language model–based robotic planning to adversarial, human-readable prompts in the visual field, and evaluate lightweight defense strategies to mitigate prompt-injection attacks.

Method: Develop a benchmark with 20 attack prompts evaluated across three physical scene layouts and three command formulations; conduct 5,670 trials on three frontier VLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B); categorize attacks into four types (indirect signage, task redefinition, authority impersonation, conflict injection); analyze attack success, transfer across models, and reasoning traces; evaluate three defenses (prompt-based defense, two-stage verification, text masking).

Result: Attacks succeed across models (27.0% for GPT-4o, 29.4% for Gemini, 5.0% for Qwen3-VL-32B). Authority-impersonating and negation attacks transfer across all models. Successful compromises are usually acknowledged. Defenses manifest differently: Gemini employs explicit rejection, GPT-4o shows perceptual inattention. Mitigations reduce risk: prompt-based defense (75-100% effective, model-dependent), two-stage verification (85-100%), and text masking (100%). Findings indicate real vulnerability to human-readable signage and that simple defenses can substantially reduce risk, with trade-offs for tasks requiring in-scene reading.

Conclusion: VLM-controlled robotic planning is meaningfully vulnerable to physical signage-based prompt injections. Simple defenses substantially mitigate risk while preserving general task capabilities, though some defenses may impair reading-in-scene tasks; defense choice should balance safety with task requirements.

Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed as planners in robotic systems, where they translate natural-language commands into executable actions grounded in visual scene understanding. This tight coupling between perception and instruction-following introduces a new attack surface: adversarial text placed within the robot's visual field can act as an indirect prompt injection into the VLM's reasoning stack. We present a systematic study of physical prompt injection attacks against VLM-controlled sorting, introducing a four-category taxonomy, indirect signage, task redefinition, authority impersonation, and conflict injection, instantiated as a benchmark of 20 attack prompts evaluated across three physical scene layouts and three command formulations that vary in destination specificity and rule explicitness. Across 5,670 trials on three frontier VLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-VL-32B), attacks succeed at 27.0%, 29.4%, and 5.0% respectively, with authority-impersonating and negation attacks transferring across all three models. Analysis of reasoning traces reveals that successful compromise is nearly always conscious (99.9% acknowledgment rate), and that models defend through structurally different mechanisms, explicit rejection for Gemini, perceptual inattention for GPT-4o. We evaluate three simple mitigations: prompt-based defense (75-100% effective, model-dependent), two-stage verification (85-100%), and pre-processing text masking (100%). Our findings show that VLM-controlled manipulation is meaningfully vulnerable to human-readable physical signage, and that simple defenses substantially reduce risk, though defense choice involves trade-offs. The defenses preserve general task capabilities in our benchmark, but they may impair tasks that require reading in-scene labels.

</details>


### [197] [ATP: Anatomical Torque with Passivity-based Control Framework for Safe Upper-Limb Exoskeleton Assistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05723)
*Yu Chen,Gong Chen,Xiang Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Anatomical Torque with Passivity-Based Control (ATP) for safe, generalizable upper-limb exoskeleton assistance using a unified RL-driven muscle controller, online torque refinement, and a passive-energy-tank interaction torque controller, validated in simulations and real-world tests with EMG benefits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend anatomical torque assistance from lower-limb, periodic tasks to complex, nonperiodic upper-limb movements while ensuring safety, passivity, and real-time applicability.

Method: 1) Scalable musculoskeletal simulation trains a unified reinforcement-learning muscle controller to generalize across upper-limb movements and generate anatomical reference torques without heavy biomechanics computations. 2) Online torque-refinement adapts the reference to different movements, suppresses tendon spikes, and adds a learned anomaly score for safe/comfortable assistance. 3) Interaction torque controller drives a cable-driven compliant exoskeleton with an energy tank that preserves passivity and provides theoretical guarantees on torque tracking and system passivity.

Result: Simulations and real-world experiments demonstrate accurate torque tracking and generalization to real-time movements. The controller maintains passivity, resumes tracking after energy-tank replenishment, and reduces targeted muscle activity (EMG) up to 48% compared with gravity compensation and open-loop assistance across static and dynamic tasks.

Conclusion: ATP provides safe, generalizable, anatomy-informed upper-limb assistance with passivity guarantees and tangible reductions in muscle effort, supported by both simulation and human-subject experiments.

Abstract: Providing assistance across diverse movements is a central objective of exoskeletons, and anatomical knowledge can enable responsive support that generalizes across tasks. However, anatomical assistance has mainly been studied for lower-limb exoskeletons, where periodic, weight-bearing motions impose lower demands on torque precision. Extending such assistance to complex, nonperiodic upper-limb movements remains challenging. This paper proposes Anatomical Torque with Passivity-Based Control (ATP) for safe upper-limb exoskeleton assistance. First, a scalable musculoskeletal simulation framework trains a unified reinforcement-learning muscle controller that generalizes across upper-limb movements and generates anatomical reference torques without complex biomechanical computations. Second, an online torque-refinement scheme adapts the reference to diverse movements, suppresses tendon-induced spikes, and incorporates a learned anomaly score for safe and comfortable assistance. Third, an interaction torque controller delivers assistance through a cable-driven compliant exoskeleton without constraining motion to predefined trajectories, while an energy tank preserves passivity with theoretical guarantees on torque tracking and system passivity. Simulations and real-world experiments show accurate tracking of long-duration motion sequences and generalization to real-time human movements. The controller achieves accurate torque tracking while preserving passivity and resumes tracking after energy-tank replenishment. An EMG study with five participants further shows reduced target-muscle activity during static and dynamic tasks compared with gravity compensation and open-loop assistance, with reductions of up to 48% relative to movement without the exoskeleton in a dynamic multi-joint task.

</details>


### [198] [Near-sensor Computing for Rapid Visuotactile Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05725)
*Zhengying Zhu,Ruilin Zhang,Runze Hu,Chenxi Xiao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Near-sensor streaming spectral Poisson solver enables deterministic, energy-efficient tactile geometry reconstruction with sub-millisecond latency, improving reflex loop speed vs host processing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visuotactile sensing performance is limited by host-side processing power, data-transfer delays, and scheduling latency, which hinder fast, reliable robotic responses.

Method: A near-sensor computing framework featuring a fully streaming hardware pipeline implementing a spectral Poisson solver. Operates at 166 MHz with no data-dependent branching or iterative convergence, delivering deterministic latency. 128x128 input frames, 347 mW core power.

Result: First depth value produced after 35,107 input cycles, yielding a fixed latency of 0.211 ms. Across 15 contact geometries, depth error is 0.17% of peak depth. On-chip reflex loop closes in 28.3 ± 4.9 ms, versus 169.9 ± 27.8 ms for a host-based loop using the same actuator.

Conclusion: Near-sensor reconstruction can provide accurate, energy-efficient, and deterministic tactile geometry on timescales suitable for rapid robotic contact responses.

Abstract: Visuotactile sensors reconstruct dense contact geometry from measured surface gradients, but host-based processing increases power consumption and introduces data-transfer delays and variable scheduling latency, limiting the sensing and response speed of robotic systems. To address these limitations, we implement a near-sensor computing framework that includes a spectral Poisson solver as a fully streaming hardware pipeline. The computational core logic has an estimated power consumption of 347 mW and achieves high throughput without data-dependent branching or iterative convergence, thereby providing deterministic latency. Operating at 166 MHz, the pipeline produces the first depth value of each 128x128 frame 35,107 cycles after receiving the first input pixel, corresponding to a fixed latency of 0.211 ms. Across 15 contact geometries, the reconstructed depths differ from a double-precision reference by 0.17 % of the peak contact depth. On-chip decisions based on these reconstructions close a robot protective reflex loop in 28.3 +/- 4.9 ms, compared with 169.9 +/- 27.8 ms for an equivalent host-based loop using the same actuator. These results demonstrate that near-sensor reconstruction can provide accurate, energy-efficient, and deterministic tactile geometry on timescales suitable for rapid robotic contact responses.

</details>


### [199] [In-Context VLA: Endowing Vision-Language-Action Models with Language via In-Context Post-Training and Agentic Tool Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05738)
*Jiarui Yang,Wen Huang,Jiale Zhang,Maowei Hu,Hang Guo*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A critique of free-form textual chain-of-thought (CoT) for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies and a grounded alternative. The paper shows CoT harms low-level control and proposes armethod (ourmethod) with in-context post-training and an agentic tool-use interface to ground language and actively acquire task-relevant information, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks and real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CoT-generated reasoning is ungrounded for low-level manipulation and can disrupt timing; VLA needs to consume grounded language rather than generate it.

Method: (i) In-context post-training: feed structured perceptual evidence as context and supervise only on actions. (ii) Agentic tool-use interface: policy queries detectors, monocular depth, and a vision-language model to gather task-relevant information. Data engine generates diverse, paraphrased, evidence-conditioned spatial descriptions to teach the policy to interpret unseen language.

Result: Consistent state-of-the-art performance and efficiency gains over CoT-based approaches across RoboCasa-GR1, SimplerEnv, LIBERO simulation benchmarks and 8 real-world robot manipulation tasks.
