Existing detectors target single-modality source code or whole-package similarity, yet skill reuse evidence is distributed across authored text, implementation fragments, and operational structure. As a result, they can miss reuse that preserves only one part of a skill. We present SKILLTRACE, a multi-trace provenance auditing framework for LLM-agent skill reuse. SKILLTRACE extracts three provenance traces: Expression, Implementation, and Operational. It represents the Operational Trace as a Skill Operational Graph (SOG) that captures activation, procedure, and resource-flow structure. An LLM assists only the Operational-trace extraction, once at ingestion; at audit time SKILLTRACE compares cached traces deterministically, calibrates each trace against same-function strict negatives, and reports which trace supports a reuse decision. On SKILLTRACE-BENCH, with 820 transformed reuse positives over 100 marketplace anchors and 751 negative controls, SKILLTRACE achieves AUROC 0.938 and F1 0.898. A 36,446-skill wild audit further shows that trace-attributed evidence surfaces actionable reuse review queues beyond repository-level baselines.

</details>


### [224] [Abstract Event Causal Rules: Induction and Application](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05205)
*Ziwei Zheng,Peiqiong Chen,Bang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR) establishes a relation-level causal abstraction to generalize concrete cause-effect pairs; introduces CAC I system to distill AECRs, builds AECR knowledge bases, and AR-GCAE to inject them into CGEP tasks, improving generalization especially for rare/unseen events.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Instance-level causal pairs suffer generalization deficits on long-tail and unseen event combinations; need a principled abstraction to transfer causal knowledge across related events.

Method: AECR as relation-level abstraction; Multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) with similarity-constrained clustering to distill AECRs from noisy data; build two AECR knowledge bases. AR-GCAE injects AECRs into CGEP via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion.

Result: AECRs improve generalization in event causal reasoning and boost event prediction performance, notably for rare/unseen samples.

Conclusion: Abstract causal knowledge via AECRs enhances generalization and practical performance of event-centric reasoning; the framework provides robust causal abstraction and practical knowledge integration.

Abstract: Event-centric intelligent analytical systems heavily depend on explicit causal event knowledge for risk early warning, decision-making support and narrative comprehension. Nevertheless, existing instance-level causal pairs suffer severe generalization deficits on low-frequency long-tail and unseen event combinations. To address this limitation, this work proposes Abstract Event Causal Rule (AECR), a novel relation-level causal abstraction paradigm that transforms concrete cause-effect pairs into generalized abstract causal logic while retaining their intrinsic causal relationships. We design a multi-agent Concrete-to-Abstract Causal Induction (CACI) system coupled with similarity-constrained clustering to distill trustworthy AECRs from noisy raw causal data, based on which two complete AECR knowledge bases are built. To validate the practical utility of abstract causal knowledge, we propose an Abstract Rule-Guided Causal Attention Encoder (AR-GCAE), which injects the retrieved AECRs into the causality Graph Event Prediction (CGEP) benchmark task via rule-guided attention layers and gated representation fusion. Quantitative experimental results reveal that applying AECRs substantially strengthens the generalization capacity of event causal reasoning and brings consistent performance improvements to event prediction, with the most prominent gains observed on rare and unseen event samples.

</details>


### [225] [Otter: A Time-Aware, History-Conditioned Human Chess AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05206)
*Tarun Kumar S*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A 15.3M-parameter time-aware sequential chess model (Otter) predicts human moves using move history and clock pressure, trained on 6.1B positions, achieving 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 accuracy and outperforming Maia 2 with a smaller model; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve human-move prediction by incorporating temporal dynamics and clock pressure, moving beyond position-only models; demonstrate that a smaller, efficiently trained model can surpass larger prior models; enable reproducibility through released code and logs.

Method: Two conditioning signals: (1) move history encoder conditioned on the last 20 moves to capture opening choices, positional drift, and intra-game behavior; (2) a time control module modulating predictions based on clock pressure. Trained on 6.1B positions from 117M Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU, with a 15.3M-parameter model. Evaluated across 11 Elo brackets using top-1 and top-5 accuracy.

Result: Top-1 accuracy 55.23% and Top-5 accuracy 90.95%. Outperforms the prior state-of-the-art Maia 2 with far fewer parameters and less training data. Peak accuracy 57.38% in the 1900–1999 Elo bracket. Code, trained models, and complete training logs publicly released.

Conclusion: Modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move predictions than position-only approaches while using a smaller model; demonstrates data efficiency and reproducibility through public release.

Abstract: Otter is a 15.3M-parameter human chess AI that predicts human move selection by modeling play as a time-aware, sequential process rather than treating each position in isolation. It combines two conditioning signals: (1) a move history encoder that conditions predictions on the last 20 moves, capturing opening preferences, positional drift, and intra-game behavioral tendencies; and (2) a time control module that modulates predictions based on clock pressure. Otter is trained on 6.1 billion positions from 117 million Lichess rapid games over 30 days on a single T4 GPU.
  Otter achieves 55.23% top-1 and 90.95% top-5 move-prediction accuracy, surpassing the prior state-of-the-art human chess model, Maia 2, with far fewer parameters and less training data. Across 11 Elo brackets (<1100 to >=2000), accuracy peaks at 57.38% in the 1900-1999 bracket. These results show that modeling chess as a time-aware, sequential activity yields more human-accurate move prediction than position-only approaches, using a smaller model. Code, trained models, and complete training logs are publicly released.

</details>


### [226] [SearchAuditor: Auditing and Attributing Failures in Long-Horizon Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05212)
*Zhixiang Liang,Yifei Liu,Yidan Huang,Haozhe Zhao,Beichen Huang,Jiaqi Wang,Nan Duan,Qiong Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces SearchAuditBench and SearchAuditor to diagnose and repair failures in long-horizon deep-search agents. Bench provides 1,243 failed trajectories with expert annotations; Auditor localizes, attributes, and repairs failures using evidence-grounded adjudication. Results show modest but consistent gains over baselines (32.3% vs 26.6%), indicating reduced human burden but room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon search agents accumulate errors that propagate through noisy interactions, making it hard to diagnose and repair. Automated auditing can reduce human labor and improve robustness.

Method: SearchAuditBench collects 1,243 failed trajectories from 8 open-weight models across 5 benchmarks with expert-annotated error steps, root causes, and proposed repairs. SearchAuditor is a multi-perspective auditing framework with evidence-grounded adjudication to localize, attribute, and repair failures, evaluated against frontier models and baselines.

Result: End-to-end pass rate for the strongest baseline with frontier GPT-5.5 is 26.6%. SearchAuditor achieves 32.3% end-to-end pass rate across frontier models and can resume failed runs using repairs to improve recovery.

Conclusion: Auditing-based approaches can reduce human effort and improve robustness in deep-search agents, but current gains are incremental, highlighting the need for stronger auditing signals and more capable models.

Abstract: Deep search agents tackle challenging questions through long-horizon web interactions, a process that is both complex and fragile: small reasoning errors may propagate through long, noisy trajectories into fluent but incorrect answers. Diagnosing such failures is difficult, requiring the manual inspection of extremely long execution traces, which could be beyond human capacity. We therefore introduce SearchAuditBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM auditors can localize, attribute, and repair these failures, thereby reducing the human burden. SearchAuditBench comprises 1,243 failed trajectories, averaging 73.1 messages and 65.1K tokens, collected from eight open-weight models on five deep-search benchmarks, each expert-annotated with the critical error step, a search-specific root cause, and a reference repair with grading rubrics. We further propose SearchAuditor, a multi-perspective auditing framework that effectively localizes, attributes, and repairs search-agent failures through evidence-grounded adjudication. Experimental results show that even the strongest baseline, when powered by a frontier model like GPT-5.5, attains only a 26.6% end-to-end pass rate. In contrast, our SearchAuditor consistently outperforms all baselines across different frontier models, achieving an end-to-end pass rate of 32.3%, and resuming failed runs with its repairs enables agents to better recover from errors.

</details>


### [227] [PD-GS: Phoneme-Driven 3DGS for Audio-Driven Talking Heads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05218)
*Ao Fu,Yi Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A phoneme-guided extension to 3D Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS) uses time-aligned phoneme embeddings and a Linguistic Fusion Module to alleviate lip-articulation artifacts (e.g., leaky mouth) while preserving smooth lip dynamics; trained on monocular video, it improves lip geometry on HDTF and reduces closure violations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering but suffers from over-smoothed mouth motion and hard articulatory constraints due to regression from continuous acoustic embeddings. Self-supervised speech encoders provide cues but lack explicit, frame-aligned linguistic targets to disambiguate brief articulation events.

Method: Augment 3DGS with time-aligned phoneme tokens derived from an automatic ASR + forced-alignment pipeline. Introduce a Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM) that adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings via a learned gating mechanism, balancing smooth audio-driven dynamics with phoneme-driven articulation guidance. Train purely from monocular video with image reconstruction and lip-landmark supervision.

Result: On the HDTF dataset, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

Conclusion: Phoneme-driven guidance via the LFM improves articulation fidelity in 3DGS without sacrificing smoothness, demonstrating the value of discrete linguistic targets for accurate lip articulation in neural avatar synthesis; trained from monocular video, it offers strong practicality and potential extension to broader phoneme-based control.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables fast, photorealistic talking-head rendering, yet accurate lip articulation remains elusive: mouth motion is often over-smoothed and may violate hard articulatory constraints such as bilabial closures, producing the notorious ``leaky mouth'' artifact. A key difficulty is that brief, discrete articulatory events are inferred from a continuous acoustic embedding under a regression objective, which biases predictions toward averaged mouth configurations. While modern self-supervised speech encoders provide rich prosodic and phonetic cues, they do not provide an explicit, frame-aligned linguistic target that reliably disambiguates closure-level events. We propose \textbf{Phoneme-Driven Gaussian Splatting (PD-GS)}, which augments a 3DGS talker with time-aligned phoneme tokens obtained from an automatic ASR and forced-alignment pipeline. Our core component, the \textbf{Linguistic Fusion Module (LFM)}, adaptively fuses continuous audio context with discrete phoneme embeddings through a learned gate, allowing the model to preserve smooth audio-driven dynamics while strengthening phoneme guidance on articulation-critical segments. PD-GS is trained purely from monocular video using image reconstruction and lip landmark supervision. On HDTF, PD-GS achieves the best lip geometry among the compared baselines (LMD 2.66) and qualitatively reduces closure violations in challenging phoneme sequences, yielding more linguistically faithful neural avatars.

</details>


### [228] [When Privileged Guidance Misaligns: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05219)
*Junzhuo Liu,Weiwei Li,Jun Ling,Peng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD) aligns privileged on-policy distillation with the learner's execution state by routing guidance to locally matched states and grounding supervision in state-conditioned teacher context, yielding improved task success on ALFWorld and WebShop; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: State-reference mismatch in interactive multi-turn tasks when using privileged distillation; prior methods apply guidance even when the student's state isn't aligned with the reference, causing unreliable supervision.

Method: At each turn, check if current state matches a state along the reference; apply distillation only at matched states; construct state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory; evaluate across ALFWorld and WebShop; ablations to validate routing and context; code available.

Result: Consistent improvement over unconditional full-path distillation; e.g., Qwen3-1.7B: 0.746 -> 0.865 on ALFWorld; 0.574 -> 0.693 on WebShop; controlled routing and context ablations identified as contributors.

Conclusion: State-matched guidance is effective for on-policy privileged distillation; reduces state-reference mismatch; supports robust, state-compatible supervision; code available.

Abstract: Privileged on-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multi-turn agents by allowing a synchronized teacher to re-score the student's response at every turn with access to training-only references, such as successful trajectories. In interactive environments, however, the student's preceding actions continually change the execution state. As the student takes different actions or completes subgoals in a different order, its rollout may reach states not covered by the reference, making the reference an unreliable source of guidance for the state actually reached. Applying privileged distillation indiscriminately therefore creates state--reference mismatch. This mismatch motivates a central objective: providing privileged reference guidance that remains compatible with the student's current execution state. We introduce State-Matched Routing and Contextualized Self-Distillation (SMRC-SD), which explicitly determines when and how a privileged trajectory should guide an on-policy student. At each turn, SMRC-SD verifies whether the student's current execution state matches a supported state along the reference trajectory. Distillation is applied only at matched states, filtering out turns for which the reference lacks locally compatible guidance. For each matched state, SMRC-SD further constructs state-conditioned teacher context from the successful trajectory, grounding supervision in the state actually reached. Across ALFWorld and WebShop, SMRC-SD consistently outperforms unconditional successful full-path distillation. With Qwen3-1.7B, it improves task success from $0.746$ to $0.865$ on ALFWorld and from $0.574$ to $0.693$ on WebShop. Controlled routing and context ablations support both selecting locally supported turns and constructing state-compatible teacher context as contributors to these gains. Code is available at https://github.com/liujunzhuo/SMRC-SD.

</details>


### [229] [Small Foundation Models of Human Cognition and Behaviour](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05224)
*Nick Oh,Fernand Gobet*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Scaling effects in LLMs trained on psych experiment data show in-distribution performance saturates at small to mid-size models, while out-of-distribution generalization benefits from larger scale; information mainly conveyed via stimuli/feedback rather than choice history; models can approximate large baselines but are bounded by training paradigms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determine whether models trained on human behavioral data encode task structure or rely on statistical shortcuts, and how model scale affects in-/out-of-distribution generalization.

Method: Train 14 models (135M–14B) across four architectures on Psych-101 (10.7M trial-level choices, 160 experiments). Evaluate with ablations of four prompt channels (instructions, stimuli, feedback, history) across 27 experiments, and permute trial order to examine sensitivity to task structure.

Result: In-distribution: scale largely saturates; 0.6B–1B parameters match a 70B baseline. Out-of-distribution: larger models show stronger generalization to novel task structure. Ablations show stimuli and feedback content carry ~75.7% of learned information; choice history alone insufficient. Permutation: independence of trials reduces sensitivity; order-sensitive when prior responses determine order.

Conclusion: Small cognitively fine-tuned models can approximate human data and serve as noise-ceiling estimators within training limits; bigger models better capture task structure and generalization beyond training paradigms; model behavior depends heavily on information content and trial structure encoded in prompts.

Abstract: Large language models fine-tuned on human behavioural data have emerged as general-purpose cognitive proxies, but the scale this requires, and whether these models process task structure or exploit statistical shortcuts, remain open questions. We train fourteen models from 135M to 14B parameters across four architecture families on Psych-101, a dataset of 10.7 million trial-level choices from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely matters. The models fall within a narrow band, as though against a ceiling, and 0.6B to 1B parameters suffice to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Out-of-distribution, that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient, with larger models clearly advantaged in generalisation to novel task structure. To determine what information these models use, we run two diagnostics. We progressively strip four prompt channels -- task instructions, experimental stimuli, outcome feedback, and choice history -- across 27 experiments, and permute trial order. Masking the content of stimuli and feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance, demonstrating that choice history alone does not account for performance. Permutation reveals invariance on tasks with independent trials but sensitivity where trial order is determined by prior responses. Small cognitively fine-tuned models therefore show promise as noise ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, though their scope remains bounded by the paradigms seen in training.

</details>


### [230] [Project2Task: Graph-Guided Project-Level Planning for Autonomous Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05225)
*Huirui Xu,Runtao Xu,Shuo Ren,Jiajun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Project2Task introduces a graph-guided, project-level planning layer for autonomous research that decomposes long-horizon projects into bounded, dependency-aware tasks via a lineage graph and a Bernoulli block-model portfolio decomposition, producing executable task contracts independent of downstream executors; evaluated on ~30 tasks across 10 briefs with improvements in quality and downstream task accuracy when integrated with AutoResearchClaw.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-task planning inadequately addresses the long-horizon, multi-task nature of research projects. There is a need for explicit project-to-task planning that defines task boundaries, dependencies, ownership, and artifacts to produce coherent, non-redundant, executable research agendas.

Method: Represent candidate contributions as innovation atoms arranged in a directed lineage graph. Use a lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective to select among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Generate bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repair overlaps and missing fields, and emit dependency-aware task contracts detailing objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. Contracts are executor-agnostic and integrate outputs into a coherent project-level result.

Result: On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding ~30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation yields an average quality score of 7.15 for Project2Task, compared to 4.58 (Brief Baseline) and 5.31 (Topic-only Setting). Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw raises average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759.

Conclusion: Explicit project-to-task planning with graph-guided decomposition and dependency-aware task contracts improves coherence, reduces redundancy, and enables executable, project-level research portfolios; contracts facilitate integration with downstream executors.

Abstract: Research agents can increasingly search literature, propose hypotheses, generate code, run experiments, and draft manuscripts from a single topic. However, a research project is not merely a larger task: it is a long-horizon agenda that must be advanced through multiple bounded tasks with distinct but related objectives, parallel alternatives, and dependency-aware sequences. Existing single-task systems often treat the project as one oversized task, produce a flat set of vague or overlapping tasks, or leave task boundaries and execution order to manual coordination. We introduce Project2Task, a graph-guided project-level planning layer for autonomous research. Given a project brief, it represents candidate contributions as innovation atoms and organizes them in a directed lineage graph. A lightweight Bernoulli block-model objective selects among horizontal, vertical, and hybrid portfolio decompositions. Project2Task then generates bounded tasks with explicit contribution ownership, repairs overlaps and missing execution fields, and emits dependency-aware task contracts that specify objectives, inputs, expected artifacts, evaluation requirements, boundary constraints, dependencies, and execution order. The contracts are independent of any particular downstream research executor and support integration of task outputs into a coherent project-level result. On a benchmark of ten project briefs yielding roughly 30 tasks, manuscript-based portfolio evaluation gives Project2Task an average quality score of 7.15, compared with 4.58 for the Brief Baseline and 5.31 for the Topic-only Setting. Integrating its contracts with AutoResearchClaw increases average downstream task accuracy from 0.536 to 0.759. These results demonstrate the value of explicit project-to-task planning for producing coherent, non-redundant, and executable research-task portfolios.

</details>


### [231] [TriQua: Reconciling Granularity and Context in Factuality Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05228)
*Jin Liu,Steffen Thoma,Achim Rettinger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TriQua introduces a flexible fact decomposition framework that adapts granularity by representing simple claims as standard triples and complex ones as hyperrelational facts with qualifiers, paired with TriQuaScore for factuality. It claims strong alignment with human judgments, robust decomposition quality, and superior evidence-based verification compared to existing decomposition-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the fundamental trade-off in decompose-then-verify factuality evaluation: atomic facts lose essential context, while broader statements lack granularity. A flexible, context-preserving representation is needed to enable accurate retrieval, verification, and explainability.

Method: Decompose facts into either standard triples (for simple claims) or hyperrelational facts with auxiliary qualifiers (for complex claims). Directly annotate concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers to provide fine-grained explainability. Introduce TriQuaScore as a metric to quantify factuality across structured fact units. Evaluate on alignment with human factuality scores, decomposition quality, and evidence-based fact verification, showing TriQua’s robust decomposition and TriQuaScore’s strong correlation with human judgments; TriQuaOutperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based verification.

Result: TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human-annotated factuality scores; TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality; outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

Conclusion: An adaptive, context-preserving fact representation coupled with fine-grained error annotation improves factuality evaluation by enabling precise verification and explainability. TriQuaScore provides an effective quantitative measure, and TriQua demonstrates superior performance over prior decomposition-based approaches in evidence-based verification.

Abstract: The "decompose-then-verify" paradigm for LLM factuality evaluation faces a fundamental trade-off: atomic facts, i.e., one sentence conveying one unit of information, often omit essential context, while broader statements lack the granularity needed for precise assessment. To address this, we introduce TriQua, a framework that flexibly models facts based on their complexity. Simple claims are extracted as standard triples, while complex claims are represented as hyperrelational facts by attaching auxiliary contextual qualifiers. This adaptive structure preserves the necessary context for accurate retrieval and verification without sacrificing atomicity. Furthermore, TriQua's verification process directly annotates concrete errors within specific triples and qualifiers, providing fine-grained explainability for error detection. Alongside the framework, we propose TriQuaScore to quantify the factuality of these structured fact units. Empirical evaluations show that TriQuaScore strongly aligns with human annotated factuality scores, TriQua achieves robust decomposition quality, and outperforms existing decomposition-based frameworks in evidence-based fact verification.

</details>


### [232] [Coherence-Oriented Dream Scene Visualisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05233)
*Azra Açıl,Simon Colton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSV converts dream narratives into a four-panel, temporally coherent visual sequence using LLM-driven segmentation and iterative T2I generation, with regeneration for fidelity; evaluated on 50 DreamBank visualizations using CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dream reports are emotionally vivid but hard to articulate visually; a four-panel, coherent visual representation can aid communication and analysis of dreams. The work integrates language-to-image generation with coherence enforcement and objective multimodal metrics.

Method: 1) Use an LLM prompt to split a dream description into four chronological parts. 2) Generate a panel image for each part with a text-to-image model, enforcing visual coherence across the sequence. 3) Regenerate any image that does not suitably match its text. 4) Evaluate 50 dream visualizations from DreamBank using objective metrics from CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL to assess quality, fidelity, and coherence.

Result: Quantitative evaluation on 50 dream visualizations shows measurable quality, fidelity, and coherence across the four-panel sequences as captured by CLIP, DINOv2, and Qwen2-VL metrics.

Conclusion: DSV demonstrates a viable end-to-end pipeline for converting narrative dreams into temporally coherent visual narratives, with potential applications in dream visualization and cognitive research. Future work could explore richer panel counts, finer-grained temporal segmentation, improved regeneration strategies, and user studies to assess perceptual effectiveness.

Abstract: Dreams can be emotionally intense but difficult to communicate. We describe the Dream Scene Visualiser (DSV) system which turns written dream descriptions into a temporal sequence of four panel images visualising the dream. This starts with a large language model prompted to split a dream description into four chronological parts. Then a text-to-image model produces images for each part with visual coherence maintained across the sequence, and DSV regenerates any image not suitably matching the text. We evaluate DSV over 50 visualisations from dream descriptions in DreamBank, and report quality, fidelity and coherence results via objective measures employing the CLIP, DINOv2 and Qwen2-VL vision-language models.

</details>


### [233] [Search2Skill: Skill Distillation Beyond Knowledge Boundaries Via Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05245)
*Muyang Ye,Tian Lan,Feihu Jiang,Yongshi Ye,Wuyunsiqin,Bin Zhu,Qianghuai Jia,Zhao Xu,Weihua Luo,Ye Wang,Jinyang Zhang,Longyue Wang,Lingfeng Bao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Search2Skill, a framework that identifies agent capability gaps, searches external sources to fill them, and distills retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills, optimized by rubric-based RL.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing self-evolving skill methods rely on the model's internal parametric knowledge or trajectories, which are limited by what the model already knows; domain conventions and procedures often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone.

Method: Automatically identify capability gaps, search external sources to address them, and distill retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills.

Result: Across eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks, Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under streaming and held-out evaluations. Gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

Conclusion: External-evidence-grounded skill learning via Search2Skill yields more generalizable, transferable professional skills than internal knowledge or trajectory-based methods.

Abstract: Reusable skills, which encapsulate the procedural knowledge required to solve real-world professional tasks, offer LLM-based agents a path toward self-evolution in expert domains. Existing self-evolving skill methods construct skills internally from the model's parametric knowledge or trajectories, and are therefore bounded by what the model already knows. However, the domain conventions and standard procedures underlying professional skills often lie beyond this boundary and are hard to elicit from the agent alone. To address this issue, we therefore propose a novel framework, Search2Skill, that automatically identifies the agent's capability gaps, searches external sources to address them, and distills the retrieved evidence into structured, reusable skills. Specifically, Search2Skill is optimized by a rubric-based reinforcement learning scheme that jointly improves when to search, how to search, and how to generate skills. Experiments on eight expert-level domains from three benchmarks show that Search2Skill consistently outperforms both search-augmented and trajectory-based skill-learning baselines under both streaming and held-out evaluation protocols. Further analyses show that the gains arise from skill abstraction rather than raw retrieved evidence, and that the acquired skills transfer across model scales.

</details>


### [234] [LUNAR: Benchmarking Personalized Large Language Models on UNiversal User BehAvioR Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05246)
*Jiahao Zhang,Yongzhi Tong,Zelin Fu,Pengde Zhao,Yanmei Jiang,Jiang Feng,Min Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A cross-domain, longitudinal-behavior LLM personalization benchmark (LUNAR) using a coarse-to-fine synthetic pipeline; shows data access alone doesn't guarantee personalization; emphasizes evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy controls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals and fail to evaluate cross-domain grounding in heterogeneous daily-life activities; there is a need for a benchmark across universal daily-life domains to assess true personalization.

Method: Introduce LUNAR—a benchmark built on a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline that generates synthetic longitudinal app interaction histories across domains (e.g., clothing, food, housing, mobility) grounded in real-world behavioral patterns; fidelity analyses compare distributions to real behavior; evaluate 19 mainstream LLMs and compare direct retrieval of fine-grained records versus compressed memory.

Result: Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks; access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization; neither more context nor larger models guarantee better performance; effective personalization requires selecting and integrating relevant cross-domain evidence; direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records outperforms compressed memory; stronger personalization may come at privacy costs.

Conclusion: Evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control are key challenges for personalized LLMs; the work highlights the trade-offs between personalization performance and privacy, and underscores the need for methods that balance data utilization with privacy protections.

Abstract: Existing personalized LLM benchmarks primarily rely on textual personas or isolated behavioral signals, providing limited evaluation of cross-domain behavioral personalization, where responses must be grounded in heterogeneous daily-life activities. To address this gap, we introduce LUNAR, the first benchmark for evaluating how LLMs personalize responses from longitudinal app interaction histories across universal daily-life domains, including clothing, food, housing, and mobility. To support scalable benchmark construction while mitigating data sparsity and privacy concerns, LUNAR uses a multi-stage coarse-to-fine synthesis pipeline grounded in real-world behavioral patterns. Fidelity analyses show closer alignment with real behavioral distributions than other synthetic benchmarks. Experiments on 19 mainstream LLMs show that access to behavioral logs is necessary but not sufficient for deep personalization: neither more context nor larger models guarantees better performance; effective personalization depends on selecting and integrating relevant evidence across domains. Direct retrieval of fine-grained behavioral records consistently outperforms compressed memory, while stronger personalization can come at the cost of privacy protection. These findings identify evidence selection, cross-domain integration, and privacy control as key challenges for personalized LLMs.

</details>


### [235] [WorldClaw: Agentic 3D Open-World Generation at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05248)
*Chunchao Guo,Jinpeng Li,Yang Li,Zilong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A coarse-to-fine, agentic pipeline (WorldClaw) enables open-world 3D scene generation with global terrain coherence, rich local content, and editable assets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from text while maintaining spatial coherence, detail, and downstream editability.

Method: 1) Planning agents convert a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. 2) WorldClaw builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative/procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. 3) For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and places them on the terrain. 4) Render-based agents refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts.

Result: Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

Conclusion: WorldClaw demonstrates a viable end-to-end framework for open-world 3D generation, integrating planning, terrain synthesis, asset reuse, and render-based refinement to achieve coherent, editable, large-scale scenes.

Abstract: Generating large-scale, freely explorable 3D worlds from open-ended text remains challenging because a system must jointly maintain global spatial coherence, rich local content, and explicit assets suitable for downstream editing and reuse. We present WorldClaw, a fully agentic, coarse-to-fine framework for open-world 3D scene generation. Planning agents translate a text prompt into a structured specification of regions, terrain, assets, materials, and spatial relations. WorldClaw then builds a globally coherent terrain foundation from semantic layouts, reusable assets, generative or procedural materials, and a region-aware height field. For detail-demanding regions, it generates terrain-conditioned compositions, reconstructs editable textured meshes, and recovers their placement on the terrain; render-based agents further refine terrain, objects, appearance, and contacts. Across diverse open-world prompts, WorldClaw produces large-scale scenes with coherent spatial organization, visually compelling local content, and editable instance-level assets while preserving a consistent global terrain structure.

</details>


### [236] [Posture and Sustainment Optimization Under Adversarial Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05256)
*Amelie Norris,Alyssa Lee,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization (CEV) for PSA, using a finite-horizon MDP; RobustCEV against an adaptive attacker; experiments show notable gains over greedy baselines; statistical validation supports results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the unsolved problem of pre-commitment posture allocation in joint operations, where greedy, value-maximizing heuristics ignore geographic coverage and are vulnerable to high-value location targeting; develop robust optimization against adversaries.

Method: Model PSA as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. Introduce Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency. Extend to RobustCEV by iterating against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placements. Validate in three Indo-Pacific experiments with 20 assets and 5 locations; compare to greedy baselines; use 5–20 scenarios; analyze with paired t-tests (Bonferroni) and two-level variance decomposition.

Result: Greedy baseline incurs a 25.1% posture efficiency penalty and 57.3% of scenario-weighted readiness collapse under threat. CEV recovers up to 19.8% efficiency relative to greedy when threat distribution contains geographic signal; robustness gains are achieved with 5–20 scenarios. RobustCEV recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer against an adaptive adversary exploiting deceptive priors. All findings validated with paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, indicating results are structural rather than sampling artifacts.

Conclusion: Adversarially robust, scenario-weighted posture optimization substantially improves pre-commitment posture allocation over greedy methods and resists adaptive adversaries. Gains depend on threat signal content and scenario coverage; the approach is promising but contingent on realistic threat modeling and scalability to larger settings.

Abstract: Pre-commitment posture, the assignment of military assets to theater locations before conflict scenarios resolve, is a critical and formally unsolved problem in joint operational planning. Current practice relies on greedy heuristics that maximize value and ignore geographic coverage and are structurally vulnerable to adversaries that target high-strategic value locations. This paper presents a scenario-weighted adversarially robust posture optimization engine for the Posture and sustainability allocation (PSA) problem, modeled as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process over assets, theater locations, and time steps. We introduce the Composite Expected Value (CEV) optimizer, which places assets by maximizing scenario-weighted expected posture efficiency over a distribution of threat scenarios, and the RobustCEV extension, which iterates against a Bayesian adversary that updates its targeting distribution in response to observed placement. Across three experiments in an Indo-Pacific basing environment with 20 assets and 5 theater locations, we demonstrate that: (1) the greedy baseline incurs a permanent 25.1% posture efficiency penalty due to geographic under-coverage and a 57.3% scenario-weighted readiness collapse under value-correlated adversarial threat; (2) the CEV optimizer recovers up to 19.8% efficiency over greedy when the threat distribution carries a geographic signal, with a curated set of 5 to 20 scenarios sufficient to capture the majority of this gain; and (3) the RobustCEV extension recovers up to 158% efficiency relative to a naive optimizer when an adaptive adversary employs a deceptive threat prior. All findings are validated using paired t-tests with Bonferroni correction and two-level variance decomposition, confirming that the performance gaps reported are structural properties of placement strategies rather than sampling artifacts.

</details>


### [237] [OrchestraBench: Evaluating Multi-Agent Orchestration Failure Modes, Recovery, and Decomposition Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05263)
*Yidian Chen,Yingzi Gu,Natan Vidra,Spurthi Setty,Sharon Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OrchestraBench provides a failure-injection benchmark for multi-agent orchestration, using cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery to diagnose failure, recovery, and decomposition across pipelines; results reveal routing policy weaknesses, latent failure modes, and context dependence, emphasizing detection/attribution for containment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diagnose why and where multi-agent pipelines fail, not just task accuracy, to improve reliability, safety, and containment in production settings.

Method: Seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows; define cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery metrics; use bootstrap CIs and paired tests to compare routing policies; evaluate with a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic; test across multiple domains (Claude agent, loan-approval workflow) and across Sonnet, Opus, Haiku; perform mechanism probes, blind retries, and ablations (trusted-state repair).

Result: Adversarial routing failed on 0% for surface-flag misleading/missing cases; intent-reasoning router achieved 100% matching oracle; three recovery tiers observed across five MAST modes: tool faults fully recovered (1.0), ambiguous delegation partially recovered (0.30), latent/semantic never recovered (0.0); cascade radius grows with pipeline depth (0.9 to 4.7 for depths 3–7); blind retry delays/detection; trusted-state repair gains mainly from trusted-state signal; results are controlled probes, not domain workloads.

Conclusion: Controlled-chain mechanism probes reveal systematic failure modes and contextual dependencies; detection and attribution are necessary for containment; these benchmarks should inform design of robust routing, recovery, and diagnosis in production multi-agent systems.

Abstract: Multi-agent orchestration frameworks are moving from demos to production, yet benchmarks typically report task accuracy without diagnosing why a pipeline failed, where a cascade began, or which routing decision caused the breakdown. OrchestraBench evaluates failure, recovery, and decomposition through a controlled, seed-reproducible failure-injection harness over templated enterprise workflows. It introduces cascade radius and per-failure-mode recovery as primary metrics and compares routing policies with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On a 26-case gold-labelled diagnostic, a keyword/flag router scored 0% on adversarial cases with misleading or missing surface flags, whereas an intent-reasoning model router scored 100%, matching the oracle. Controlled mechanism probes with a real Claude agent over a verifiable arithmetic dependency chain revealed three failure-handling tiers across five MAST modes: tool faults recovered fully (1.0), ambiguous delegation recovered partially (0.30), and three latent or semantic modes never recovered (0.0). This ordering persisted when the computation was reframed as a loan-approval workflow and across Sonnet, Opus, and Haiku, although absolute rates shifted with context. Blind retry reproduced latent faults and increased time to detection, indicating that detection and attribution are necessary for containment. Cascade radius increased with pipeline depth (mean 0.9 to 4.7 across depths 3-7). A trusted-state repair ablation showed that apparent containment gains primarily came from the trusted-state signal rather than autonomous detection. These results are controlled-chain mechanism probes, not domain-workload claims.

</details>


### [238] [Agentic self-driving microscopy benchmarks support qualification but do not necessarily generalize to unseen tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05266)
*Nathan S Johnson,Ian Abshire*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Benchmarking agentic microscope controllers: a 105-config, 1,949-run study shows architecture affects latency, cost, and failures, but surrogate models fail to predict unseen-task performance; benchmarks aid QA but do not yield a universal configuration model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the nascent field of agentic control of physical infrastructure by quantifying how design choices (LLM choice, agent count, delegation, RAG settings) impact microscopy performance and generalization, and assess whether benchmarks can predict performance on novel tasks.

Method: Systematic evaluation of 105 agent configurations (1-, 2-, 3-agent topologies), five LLMs, RAG/context variations, across 53 microscopy benchmarks; total of 1,949 test runs and 49,109 RAG retrievals; development of a trace-logging framework to capture latency, token usage, cost, and failure modes; attempt to train surrogate models to predict unseen-task performance.

Result: Config-level differences observed in latency, token usage, cost, and failure modes. Surrogate models trained on architecture/test results did not reliably predict performance on new, unseen microscopy tasks.

Conclusion: Benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the heterogeneous test suite does not yet support a task-independent global configuration model; suggests a need for standardized, task-aligned evaluation and improved generalization analyses.

Abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly being developed to control a wide range of scientific characterization tools including microscopes and synchrotron beamlines. Research into agentic control of physical infrastructure is nascent and there are few well-established paradigms for how to engineer an agentic system. There are many choices to make when designing a microscopy agent, including the choice of LLM, the number of agents to use, agent responsibilities and delegation rules, retrieval-augmented generation parameters, and more. When designing and optimizing an agentic microscope controller, researchers not only want to ensure that the agent can correctly perform known tasks but also that the agent can generalize to new tasks that it has not encountered before. In this study, we develop a benchmark and trace-logging framework that reveals a) how different choices of agent architecture impact performance at microscopy tasks and b) the limitations of benchmarks for predicting if a particular agent will perform well on unseen microscopy tasks. The framework was used to evaluate one-, two-, and three-agent graph topologies, five LLMs, RAG and context parameters, and operational constraints across 53 microscopy benchmark tests. In total, 105 agent configurations, 1,949 individual test runs, and 49,109 RAG retrievals were recorded. Direct comparisons showed clear differences in latency, token use, cost, and failure mode between configurations. However, surrogate models trained on agent architecture and test results did not reliably predict an agent's performance on new, unseen tasks. These results show that these benchmarks are useful for qualification, regression testing, diagnosis, and direct comparison, but the current heterogeneous test suite does not support a task-independent global configuration model.

</details>


### [239] [CASCADE: An Agentic Regulatory Network Framework for Patient-Data-Validated Downstream Perturbation Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05359)
*Jose A. Bird*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CASCADE can predict the direction of transcriptional changes from perturbations using ARACNe networks; validated by copy-number amplification as a dosage proxy across TCGA and METABRIC, showing strong gene-level concordance for MYC across multiple cancers and partial replication for 15 genes; outcomes are gene-specific, with lineages TFs and CCND2 often failing; an LLM grounding test shows moderate accuracy but with systematic perturbation-type errors for ambiguous queries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Move beyond membership-based validation of regulatory-prediction tools by testing directional accuracy of CASCADE against real tumor data; assess generality across genes and evaluate grounding of natural-language queries to CASCADE calls using LLMs.

Method: Use precomputed ARACNe regulatory networks exposed via MCP to predict transcriptional effects of perturbation. Test directionality by treating focal gene amplification as a dosage-based inverse knockdown proxy in TCGA tumor data. Assess concordance across BRCA, COAD, and STAD, with replication in METABRIC. Compare to MSigDB-based baselines via Fisher's test; extend analysis to 15 genes. Evaluate LLM-based grounding: have two LLMs map natural-language requests to CASCADE calls across 35 queries; measure exact-match rates and analyze failure modes.

Result: MYC knockdown targets show strong concordance between predicted downregulation and expression differences in amplified vs non-amplified tumors (BRCA 90.0%, COAD 72.0%, STAD 85.7%; all p<0.0013); surpass permutation baselines and replicate in METABRIC (87.2%). CASCADE’s accuracy does not exceed curated MSigDB knowledge for MYC/E2F biology but outperforms naive uniform guessing. For 15 additional genes, replication is gene-specific: proliferation regulators tend to replicate; lineage-ident identity TFs and CCND2 often fail. LLM grounding: exact-match rates 71.4% (smaller model) and 85.7% (larger model); some schema/gene-alias issues are mitigated by scale/server corrections, but both models err on perturbation type for ambiguous queries.

Conclusion: CASCADE provides gene-specific directional predictive power with cross-cohort validation, but exhibits gene-class–dependent performance limits and present limitations in natural-language grounding. The work supports cautious optimism for directional prediction in regulatory networks while highlighting the need for deeper mechanistic validation and targeted fixes for ambiguous querying.

Abstract: CASCADE is an agentic framework that predicts downstream transcriptional effects of gene perturbation from precomputed
  ARACNe regulatory networks, exposed via MCP. Prior work validates such tools by checking whether predicted genes are
  known cancer genes (membership); we instead test whether the predicted direction of change matches reality, using
  focal-gene copy-number amplification as a dosage-based proxy for the inverse of knockdown against real TCGA patient
  tumor data.
  For MYC, CASCADE's predicted knockdown targets show strong concordance with real amplified-vs-non-amplified tumor
  expression across three cancer types (BRCA: 90.0%, COAD: 72.0%, STAD: 85.7%; all p<0.0013), well above permutation
  baselines, surviving a PAM50 subtype control and replicating in an independent cohort (METABRIC, 87.2%). Compared
  against curated MSigDB gene-set baselines via Fisher's exact test, CASCADE's accuracy is not shown to exceed existing
  public knowledge of MYC- or E2F-driven biology, though its gene-specific direction-calling clearly outperforms a naive
  uniform guess.
  Extending to fifteen additional genes, validation proves gene-specific rather than universal: proliferation-machinery
  regulators mostly replicate, while lineage-identity transcription factors and one cyclin-D paralog (CCND2)
  consistently fail, a pattern we discuss as a hedged, post-hoc hypothesis.
  We separately benchmark whether an LLM-based agent correctly grounds natural-language requests into CASCADE's real MCP
  tool calls. Across 35 queries, a documented local model reaches 71.4% exact match (85.7% for a larger model); schema
  and gene-alias failures are resolved by scale or server-side correction, but both models confidently default to the
  wrong perturbation type on ambiguous queries, a failure a targeted fix could not resolve because its trigger condition
  never occurs.

</details>


### [240] [Counterfactual Analysis via Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05367)
*Zonghao Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Prompt-engineered GPT-3.5 offers modest predictive gains for counterfactual ROI in online lending, approaching gradient-boosted regression; demonstrates potential for LLM-based counterfactual analysis and decision support.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether large language models can perform counterfactual analysis in decision-critical contexts (online lending) and compare to conventional ML, with focus on ROI under different interest schemes.

Method: Evaluate GPT-3.5 predictions vs advanced ML using standard metrics (R^2). Implement prompt engineering to boost GPT performance; then have GPT generate counterfactual ROIs under varying interest rates; assess coherence and causal reasoning.

Result: Prompt engineering raises GPT-R^2 from 1.97% to 2.84%, near gradient-boosted regression at 3.48%; GPT yields coherent, causally plausible counterfactual ROIs.

Conclusion: LLMs have potential as tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending and other predictive decision-support tasks; further work to improve accuracy and reliability, and to broaden applications.

Abstract: Counterfactual analysis aims to predict potential outcomes under hypothetical scenarios, offering valuable insights for decision-making. This paper investigates the application of large language models (LLMs), specifically the GPT-3.5 model, for counterfactual analysis. We focus on the online lending context, where the counterfactual return on investment (ROI) is crucial for evaluating different interest rate schemes. We begin by assessing the predictive performance of GPT and comparing it with advanced machine learning algorithms. The results show that prompt engineering can significantly enhance GPT's predictions, with the R-squared increasing from 1.97% to 2.84%, closely approaching the 3.48% achieved by gradient-boosted regression. Subsequently, we utilize GPT to generate counterfactual ROIs under a set of alternative interest rates. GPT exhibits logical coherence and causal reasoning in its responses. The findings underscore the potential of LLMs as effective tools for counterfactual analysis in online lending, suggesting broader applications for LLMs in various predictive and decision-making contexts.

</details>


### [241] [DoctorAgents: an agentic framework to iteratively refine AutoML pipeline for small clinical temporal data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05375)
*Ruilin Wang,Bo-Hong Wang,Elizabeth Kourbatski,Jun Bai,Hegang Chen,Ziyang Song,Gilles Boire,Marie Hudson,Yue Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reasoning-driven AutoML for small clinical data via DoctorAgents; LLM-based agents construct, validate, and refine end-to-end ML pipelines with textual gradient descent, outperforming traditional AutoML and yielding interpretable representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clinical ML faces scarce, heterogeneous, temporally complex data and high deployment risk; conventional AutoML relies on brute-force search and lacks explicit reasoning/memory.

Method: Introduce DoctorAgents, a framework of specialized LLM agents (generation, validation, refinement) that autonomously build and optimize ML pipelines. Uses textual gradient descent to backpropagate NL feedback, avoiding exhaustive search.

Result: Empirical evaluation across diverse clinical tasks shows DoctorAgents consistently outperforms AutoML baselines and produces more interpretable task-specific representations.

Conclusion: Reasoning-driven, memory-enabled AutoML with LLM agents is effective for small clinical datasets, improving performance and interpretability over conventional AutoML; future work could explore scalability and generalization.

Abstract: Clinical machine learning (ML) has the potential to support high-stakes medical decision-making, but reliable deployment is often constrained by scarce, heterogeneous, and temporal complexity. Developing effective ML pipelines for such data remains time-consuming and error-prone, while existing automated machine learning (AutoML) systems only partially address this challenge because they largely rely on brute-force search over predefined spaces and lack explicit reasoning and memory. We therefore reformulate AutoML for small clinical data from exhaustive search to reasoning-driven refinement. We propose DoctorAgents, an agentic AI framework that autonomously constructs and optimizes end-to-end ML pipelines through specialized large language model (LLM) agents for generation, validation, and refinement. DoctorAgents backpropagates natural-language feedback through textual gradient descent to perform targeted updates without exhaustive search. Experiments across diverse clinical tasks show that DoctorAgents consistently outperforms established AutoML baselines while producing more interpretable task-specific representations.

</details>


### [242] [C$^3$PO: Evaluating Cross-Modal Composition and Counterfactual Performance in Omnimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05381)
*Swapnanil Mukherjee,Agyeya Negi,Tanuja Ganu,Ponnurangam Kumaraguru*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: C3PO benchmark for cross-modal reasoning with 3,404 samples across video, audio, image, and text; evaluates information composition and counterfactual conflict; reveals modality dominance as a key failure mode; humans outperform models; suggests sustained cross-modal attention is essential.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address brittleness of cross-modal reasoning in multimodal LLMs due to modality dominance; provide diagnostics to identify when and why cross-modal reasoning fails.

Method: Fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates; IC/CC paired structure with a four-tier design; evaluates information composition and counterfactual conflict; includes attention analyses via probes and mid-layer attention entropy as a predictor.

Result: Humans achieve 88.64% accuracy; best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches 73.17%; open-source models falter under conflict; 86–95% of failures arise from modality dominance (one modality chosen and contradictory evidence ignored); 87–95% of attention concentrated on text; mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration; 56-point gap between equally complex templates; performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not merely combinations.

Conclusion: Multimodal perception alone does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must support sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature reliance on a single modality during conflict resolution.

Abstract: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can process diverse sensory inputs, yet their reasoning remains heavily biased toward a dominant modality, resulting in brittle cross-modal reasoning. We introduce C$^3$PO, a benchmark of 3,404 samples spanning video, audio, image, and text, evaluating two abilities: information composition (fusing dispersed evidence) and counterfactual conflict (resolving deliberate contradictions). C$^3$PO's paired IC/CC structure and four-tier design enable targeted diagnosis of when and why cross-modal reasoning fails. Built through a fully automatic pipeline using 25 logically grounded templates, C$^3$PO reveals that while humans achieve 88.64% accuracy, the best model (Gemini-3.1-Pro) reaches only 73.17%, with open-source models collapsing under conflict. Through attention probes, we find 86-95% of failures stem from modality dominance: models commit to one modality while ignoring contradictory evidence, concentrating 87-95% of attention on text. Mid-layer attention entropy predicts correctness-sustained exploration succeeds, premature collapse fails. The 56-point accuracy gap between equally complex templates reveals that performance depends on modalities' structural roles in conflict resolution, not combinations. These findings show multimodal perception does not guarantee robust reasoning; architectures must enable sustained cross-modal attention to avoid premature

</details>


### [243] [Adaptive Arena-based Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts for Open-Ended Care Plan Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05391)
*Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen,Hoang-Loc Cao,Phuc Ho,Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen,René Richard,Hung Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CANOE is a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework for care-plan coordination that uses arena-based quantitative bipolar argumentation to produce contestable, human-influenced plans. Medically fine-tuned models excel on clinical correctness and safety; CANOE provides transparent explanations and human contestability while deterministically recomputing plans as arguments are edited.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monolithic LLM pipelines struggle with transparency, safety, and synthesis of heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple disciplines; a modular, contestable, multi-agent approach is needed for reliable care planning.

Method: Five-module design: (1) complexity assessment, (2) adaptive team recruitment, (3) role-based argumentative computation via Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), (4) human-in-the-loop contestation, (5) care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting/attacking arguments for candidate interventions; arena-based clash resolution resolves conflicts before propagate; care planners accept/reject/edit/add arguments and the framework deterministically recomputes the final plan.

Result: Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows medically fine-tuned models achieve strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE’s argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

Conclusion: CANOE demonstrates that a neuro-symbolic, multi-agent, contestable argumentation framework can yield transparent, safe, and explainable care plans, with robust clinical performance when combined with domain-tuned models.

Abstract: Care plan coordination demands synthesizing heterogeneous clinical, functional, and psychosocial information across multiple professional disciplines, where monolithic LLM pipelines cannot perform in a transparent or safe manner. We present CANOE (Contestable Argumentative Network-of-Experts), a multi-agent neuro-symbolic framework that addresses these limitations through five modules: complexity assessment, adaptive team recruitment, role-based argumentative computation via an Arena-based Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (A-QBAF), human-in-the-loop contestation, and care-plan synthesis. Role-specialized agents generate supporting and attacking arguments for candidate interventions; conflicts are resolved through arena-based clash resolution before acceptability scores propagate across the argumentation graph. Care planners may accept, reject, edit, or add arguments, and the framework will deterministically recompute the final plan. Evaluation on Discharge Me! and MedicalRAG using ROUGE-L, AlignScore, MEDCON F1, FKGL, and LLM-as-a-judge shows that medically fine-tuned models achieve the strongest clinical correctness and safety, while CANOE's argumentative structure provides faithful explanation and human contestability.

</details>


### [244] [Evaluating and Improving Pedagogical Fit in LLM-Based AI Tutors with the Pedagogical Suitability Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05411)
*Benjamin Barlog,Hudson Craig,Zedong Peng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PSI is a six-sub-score composite metric to assess how well LLM tutoring responses fit learner readiness and curricular progression; PSI-guided regeneration improves weak cases; baseline PSI modest across models; alignment may matter more than model category.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To go beyond answer correctness and measure instructional fit in AI tutoring, addressing learner foundation, course sequence, and timing of concept introduction.

Method: Define PSI (six sub-scores); evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, Qwen3) on 240 scenario-based evaluations with paired standard/defective prompts; apply PSI-guided regeneration to 62 weak cases; manual evaluation of the 62 cases.

Result: Baseline PSI values 0.557–0.638; no clear separation between open/closed models; PSI delta under perturbations ≈ -0.002 with sub-score trade-offs; PSI-guided feedback improved 51/62 cases (82.3%); qualitative evidence that regressions improved; results suggest alignment matters more than model category.

Conclusion: Learner- and curriculum-aware alignment is measurable and improvable; PSI is a useful feedback signal for improving tutoring responses; aligning LLM tutoring with curricular structure may enhance effectiveness even when model type varies.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as AI tutors, but a correct answer is not always a pedagogically appropriate one. In classroom learning, effective help depends not only on correctness, but also on whether a response matches the learner's current foundation, the course sequence, and the timing of concept introduction. Existing evaluations focus mainly on answer quality, leaving this instructional fit under-measured. We present the Pedagogical Suitability Index (PSI), a composite metric of six theory-informed sub-scores that evaluates how well LLM-generated tutoring responses align with learner readiness and curricular progression, and we further use PSI as a structured feedback signal for response improvement. We evaluate four LLM tutors (ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemma4, and Qwen3) across 240 scenario-based evaluations using paired standard and defective prompts, then apply a PSI-guided regeneration protocol to 62 weak-performing cases. Baseline differences across the four tested models were modest overall (PSI range: 0.557 to 0.638), and open-weight and closed models did not exhibit a clear separation in pedagogical fit. Under the tested prompt perturbations, overall PSI remained largely stable (Delta = -0.002), though sub-score trade-offs emerged. More importantly, PSI-guided feedback substantially improved weak-performing cases: 51 of 62 cases improved (82.3%). Focused manual evaluation of the 62 PSI-selected weak cases provides initial evidence that the identified weaknesses are instructionally meaningful and that many PSI-guided regenerations correspond to human-judged improvement. These results suggest that learner- and curriculum-aware alignment may matter more for effective tutoring than model category alone, and that such alignment is both measurable and improvable.

</details>


### [245] [Negotiating Risk Boundaries in AI for Policing Through Mixed-Stakeholder Deliberation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05418)
*Mackenzie Jorgensen,Jo Reilly,Alex Sutherland,Miri Zilka*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Deliberative study on AI in policing shows that a mixed-stakeholder group (community reps, police, academics) generally supports AI adoption across 13 use cases, with strong opposition only to recidivism risk assessment. Foregrounding racial equity did not narrow discussion; instead, participants framed deliberation around three core questions: does the tool work, will it deliver real benefits, and will benefits be shared. The analysis suggests integrating racial bias assessment into the risk–benefit analysis from the outset (likened to the curb-cut effect).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address known racial bias risks in policing AI and the underrepresentation of affected communities in decision-making. Evaluate whether AI adoption across policing use cases is acceptable and under what conditions.

Method: Mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop with 30 participants (community representatives, police officers, academics) evaluating 13 AI use cases in policing, with explicit focus on racial bias. Qualitative deliberation and risk–benefit assessment.

Result: Participants were broadly open to AI adoption; three use cases were rejected, most notably recidivism risk assessment (rejection targeted at premises rather than implementation). Foregrounding racial equity did not narrow deliberation; instead, core questions emerged about tool efficacy, real-world benefit, and universal benefit. The reasoning aligns with an inclusive-design curb-cut effect, suggesting preemptive racial-bias framing improves risk-benefit analysis.

Conclusion: Integrating racial bias considerations early in AI use-case evaluation aids risk-benefit analysis and policy design. Representing affected communities in decision-making can enhance understanding of who benefits and who may be harmed; policy should prioritize tools that demonstrably work and deliver equitable, universal benefits.

Abstract: AI tools are being increasingly adopted in policing in the UK and worldwide. Racial bias is a known and well-documented risk, yet representatives of affected communities are rarely included in decisions about AI adoption. We present results from a mixed-stakeholder deliberation workshop bringing together 30 community representatives, police officers, and academics to assess the risks of 13 AI use cases in policing, with an explicit focus on racial bias. We found that participants were broadly open to AI adoption, rejecting only three use cases outright, most notably recidivism risk assessment, where objections targeted the premise rather than the implementation. Our analysis reveals that foregrounding racial equity did not narrow the deliberation. Instead, discussions gravitated toward a fundamental set of questions: does this tool actually work, will it deliver genuine benefit, and will that benefit extend to everyone? This integrated reasoning, reminiscent of the curb-cut effect in inclusive design, highlights the benefit of incorporating the racial bias lens into the risk-benefit analysis of AI use cases from the outset.

</details>


### [246] [SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05439)
*Yixuan Wang,Licheng Luo,Yu Fu,Kaidi Xu,Yue Dong,Mingyu Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A selective translation framework translates NL instructions into formal specs (STL/LTL/SpaTiaL) and abstains when unreliable, using conformal risk control and two black-box confidence signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prevent unsafe execution by avoiding or abstaining from translating NL intents into incorrect or unreliable formal specifications in safety-critical applications.

Method: Introduce selective translation with two black-box signals: back-translation fidelity (NL <-> formal spec) and dispersion of multiple semantically equivalent translations; apply conformal risk control to convert reliability score into an abstention decision; include a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings to filter out OOD inputs; framework is formal-language agnostic and demonstrated on STL, LTL, SpaTiaL.

Result: Improved translation reliability and robustness under cross-domain shifts; uncertainty-aware abstention reduces risk of executing incorrect specs; demonstrates generality across multiple formalisms.

Conclusion: Provides a foundation for trustworthy NL interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize and abstain from uncertain or unreliable generated specifications; potential for broader adoption across formal languages and safety-critical contexts.

Abstract: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.

</details>


### [247] [Stochasticity Is Not the Hard Part: Reduction and Complexity in Instructional Sequencing over Prerequisite DAGs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05455)
*Zonglin Han,Yichen Chen,Jiawen Jiang,Tongan Shi,Kristian A. Stevens*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Stochastic instructional sequencing collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order-ideals; optimal sequencing is NP-hard in general but tractable under certain transfer-acyclic conditions; a computable diagnostic predicts when optimization matters; empirical data shows both regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when the order of instruction matters, the cost of finding the best sequence, and to provide principled computational tools for sequencing in curricula and adaptive learning.

Method: Model learning as a stochastic shortest-path with state-dependent success probabilities; prove exact collapse to a deterministic SP on the lattice of order ideals; establish NP-hardness via reduction from Feedback Arc Set in Tournaments; identify tractable special cases where transfers are jointly acyclic or width-bounded; define a computable diagnostic mΔ; evaluate on a large intro CS dataset and on constructed hard instances; compare myopic vs exact A* search.

Result: Exact collapse preserves optimal values and actions; hardness persists even with minimal prerequisites, unit costs, and p≥1/2; if transfer preferences are jointly acyclic, any topological order of the residual graph is optimal; fixed prerequisite width yields polynomial-time DP; mΔ bounds sequencing value; empirical tests reveal a 'doubly easy' regime and a hard regime where A* with a consistent heuristic expands only linearly many states.

Conclusion: The paper delineates when instructional sequencing is worth optimizing, presents a computable predictor (mΔ) for the potential gain from optimization, and provides both theoretical hardness results and practical algorithms for special cases, with empirical validation across real and constructed datasets.

Abstract: When a student must learn concepts connected by prerequisite dependencies, when does the order of instruction matter, and what does it cost to find the best one? We study instructional sequencing as a stochastic shortest-path problem in which attempting a concept succeeds with a state-dependent probability and failure leaves the learner state unchanged. We first prove that this stochasticity can be eliminated exactly: the problem collapses to a deterministic shortest-path problem on the lattice of prerequisite order ideals, preserving optimal values and actions. The collapse removes stochastic complexity but not combinatorial complexity: optimal sequencing remains NP-hard -- via reduction from feedback arc set in tournaments -- even with no prerequisite edges, unit costs, uniform binary nonnegative transfer, and success probabilities at least $1/2$.
