Method: Introduce three layers: Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows; Compliance and Policy Layer centralizing policy-as-code aligned with HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act, DISHA/DPDP, ISO security; Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric integrating federated learning, differential privacy, secure enclaves with HIMS flows; use synthetic realistic hospital dataset; open prototype; demonstrate end-to-end triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, compliance logging.

Result: Simulation shows reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation; maintains policy-guarded data access; demonstrates end-to-end orchestration and compliance logging; provides blueprint and prototype for deployment (on-prem/hybrid/cloud).

Conclusion: Offers a practical blueprint to move from isolated tools to a governed, globally compliant AI platform tuned for ROI, scalable across deployment models, and adaptable to hospital contexts.

Abstract: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.

</details>


### [298] [Mind the Gaps: Mixture-of-Minds for Human Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06115)
*Pranav Dahiya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Anacreon is a novel approach to individual-level audience simulation within a narrow domain, using authorship embeddings, cluster-adapted adapters, and chain-of-emotion to generate faithful individual predictions; it achieves state-of-the-art ordinal alignment (0.775) on an external survey with reduced biases, indicating progress toward aggregating data from simulated individuals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the mismatch between population-level predictions and individual heterogeneity; aims to overcome LLM simulators' tendency to flatten diversity and propagate biases by constructing faithful, domain-specific “mixtures of minds.”

Method: 1) Learn an authorship embedding to distinguish individuals. 2) Cluster the real qualitative corpus around seed individuals. 3) Train a dedicated adapter per cluster (a mixture of minds) on a Gemma-4 12B base. 4) Harvest demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text; augment each record with a chain-of-emotion. 5) Reduce prompt brittleness by shuffling response options. 6) Reduce positive bias by balancing the training distribution.

Result: On an external large survey, Anacreon achieves a state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775 (typical individual-level accuracy metric in the field) with a small residual bias.

Conclusion: Anacreon advances individual-level audience modeling within a narrow domain and demonstrates that mixing multiple trained adapters (clusters) with enriched personal data can yield better alignment with observed responses while mitigating brittleness and bias; it's a step toward deriving aggregate insights from simulated individuals.

Abstract: Predicting how a population will answer a new question is a long-standing goal. Statistical methods succeed at the level of the mass but falter at the level of the individual. Large language model simulators inherit this gap. They recover a population's central tendencies while flattening its heterogeneity, and they carry social biases and prompt brittleness that distort individual predictions. This paper introduces Anacreon, an audience simulation model that targets the individual level within a narrow, well-specified domain. Anacreon learns an authorship embedding that separates individuals, clusters a real qualitative corpus around seed people, and trains a dedicated adapter for each cluster, a mixture of minds, on a Gemma~4 12B base. It harvests demographics, psychological traits, and survey responses from public text, and augments each record with a chain-of-emotion. It reduces prompt brittleness by shuffling response options and reduces positive bias by balancing the training distribution. On a large, externally sourced survey, Anacreon reaches a state-of-the-art ordinal alignment of 0.775, the individual-level accuracy measure on which the field has converged, with a small residual bias. The work is a step toward drawing aggregate insight from faithfully simulated individuals.

</details>


### [299] [Poli-Bias: Understanding and Measuring Large Language Model Biases in International Political Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06123)
*Massi-Nissa Abboud,Aladin Djuhera,Elena Cabrio,Holger Boche*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Poli-Bias is a counterfactual framework for auditing political bias in LLMs by swapping country identities in prompts; it decomposes disparities into five dimensions and reveals systematic effects across 13 LLMs, enabling fine-grained assessment of political even-handedness and sycophancy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of measuring political bias in LLMs that manifests in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning; provide a decomposition for nuanced understanding instead of a single bias score.

Method: Use counterfactual paired prompts where country identities are swapped across geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks; analyze response differences across five interpretable dimensions.

Result: Found that country identities and user affiliations systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law across 13 contemporary LLMs; Poli-Bias reveals nuanced, dimension-specific biases.

Conclusion: Poli-Bias offers a fine-grained auditing framework for political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs, enabling targeted evaluation beyond aggregate bias measures.

Abstract: Measuring political bias in large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as it can manifest through subtle differences in framing, argumentation, and legal reasoning that are difficult to capture with a single metric. In this work, we introduce Poli-Bias, a counterfactual framework for measuring whether LLMs treat legally equivalent conflict scenarios differently depending on the countries involved. Poli-Bias compares responses to paired prompts in which country identities are systematically swapped across diverse geopolitical relationships, legal violations, and reasoning tasks. Rather than reducing bias to a single judgment, our framework decomposes response disparities into five interpretable dimensions, revealing how and where unequal treatment manifests. Across 13 contemporary LLMs spanning diverse model families and sizes, we find that country identities and user affiliations can systematically affect how equivalent actions are described, evaluated, and defended under international law. Our results thus establish Poli-Bias as a fine-grained framework for auditing political even-handedness and sycophancy in LLMs.

</details>


### [300] [Contextual Information Policy Optimization for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06128)
*Xingyu Guo,Wei Chen,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CIPO (Contextual Information Policy Optimization) introduces an evidence-oriented RL framework for search agents that ties policy updates to how retrieved external evidence is used, reducing prior-driven reasoning and delivering strong cross-domain results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RL objectives reward final correctness or progress without ensuring that subsequent reasoning is grounded in retrieved evidence, leading to confirmation bias and inefficient use of evidence.

Method: CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning actions influenced by retrieved evidence and combines this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward, without requiring human annotations or an extra reward model.

Result: Empirical evaluation across seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks shows reduced prevalence of prior-driven reasoning and strong performance on most tasks.

Conclusion: CIPO aligns reasoning with retrieved evidence, discourages evidence-detached guesses, and generalizes across domains; it avoids extra annotation or reward-model deployment but may still face challenges related to evidence quality and edge cases.

Abstract: Search agents extend large language models beyond static parametric memory by enabling them to acquire and use ex ternal evidence during multi-step reasoning. For knowledge intensive tasks involving complex or evolving information, their reliability depends not only on retrieving relevant ev idence but also on using it to guide subsequent reasoning. However, existing methods primarily reward final-answer cor rectness or intermediate progress, without directly assessing whether post-retrieval actions are grounded in the retrieved evidence. This misalignment encourages prior-driven reason ing: agents form conclusions based on internal knowledge and use retrieval mainly to confirm them, resulting in confirma tion bias and inefficient evidenceuse.Toaddressthisissue, we propose Contextual Information Policy Optimization (CIPO), an evidence-oriented reinforcement learning framework that explicitly aligns policy optimization with external evidence use. CIPO assigns dense, turn-level credit to reasoning ac tions influenced by retrieved information, while combining this evidence-use signal with a global outcome reward to pre serveanswercorrectness.Withthismanner,CIPOdiscourages evidence-detached guesses and promotes reasoning trajecto ries in which retrieved facts can guide or revise subsequent reasoning. Importantly, CIPO requires neither human process annotations nor an additional reward model. Extensive exper iments on seven in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks show that CIPO reduces the prevalence of prior-driven rea soning and achieves excellent performance on most tasks.

</details>


### [301] [FinEvo-Bench: A Longitudinal Benchmark for Self-Evolving Agents in Professional Financial Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06144)
*Bo Deng,Kang Zhou,Lifan Guo,Chongyang Tao,Xuanren Chen,Chenggang Xie,Renzhao Liang,Feng Chen,Chi Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FinEvo-Bench is a longitudinal benchmark for professional finance tasks (120 tasks across six domains, 20 scenes) that tests self-evolution of agents using four scaffolds, with external scoring and rubric-based evaluation. It demonstrates evolution improves task performance and reduces compliance issues, with skill-only evolution often outperforming memory-based approaches in a Claude Code setting, and rubric feedback outperforming reference answers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of existing benchmarks that evaluate tasks in isolation and fail to measure transfer of experience across tasks and over time in professional workflows requiring compliance and multi-aspect evaluation.

Method: A longitudinal setup with 120 real-case tasks organized into six financial domains and 20 scenes. Each scene provides a professional procedure and a rubric for task quality and compliance. Four agent scaffolds (all using Qwen3.7-Max backbone) operate on independently shuffled, interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate self-evolution gain. Outputs are scored by Claude Code (Claude Opus 4.6). Comparisons include memory vs skill evolution, and rubric feedback vs reference-answer feedback across the scaffolds.

Result: Evolutionary running of agents leads to score gains of 9.33–19.37 points and a reduction in compliance issues by 0.12–0.44 per task across scaffolds. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and the fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task). Codex attains the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Within-scene ranks 4–6 show larger gains than ranks 1–3 by 6.10–8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution outperforms memory-only and memory+skill combination in task quality and compliance. Rubric feedback yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback across all scaffolds.

Conclusion: FinEvo-Bench provides a dual assessment of professional performance and self-evolution ability, showing that prior experience can meaningfully improve later performance, especially when coupled with rubric-based feedback and skill-centric evolution. It demonstrates robust cross-task transfer in professional, compliance-sensitive settings.

Abstract: Most agent benchmarks evaluate tasks independently and cannot measure whether experience from one task helps with later tasks. Existing self-evolution benchmarks do not jointly cover professional workflows, open-ended deliverables, and multi-aspect evaluation. We introduce FinEvo-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark with 120 real-case-grounded tasks, 20 business scenes across six financial domains. Institution-provided professional procedures define the required operations and constraints. Eligible institution-provided and publicly documented cases supply the task facts. Each scene contains six related but substantively distinct cases that share a professional procedure and a manually reviewed rubric for task quality and financial compliance. We compare four self-evolving agent scaffolds using the same Qwen3.7-Max backbone and three independently shuffled, globally interleaved task streams. Paired non-evolving controls estimate each scaffold's self-evolution gain from retained experience, while an independent Claude Code scoring agent backed by Claude Opus 4.6 evaluates all outputs. Letta achieves the highest evolved score (91.65) and fewest compliance issues (0.09 per task); Codex achieves the largest self-evolution gain (+19.37). Across scaffolds, the evolving condition raises scores by 9.33-19.37 points and reduces compliance issues by 0.12-0.44 per task. Paired score gains at within-scene ranks 4-6 exceed those at ranks 1-3 by 6.10-8.70 points. In Claude Code, skill-only evolution produces higher task quality and fewer compliance issues than memory-only and combined memory-skill evolution. Across all four scaffolds, rubric feedback also yields higher scores and fewer compliance issues than reference-answer feedback. FinEvo-Bench measures both professional performance and self-evolution ability: how effectively an agent turns prior experience into later improvement.

</details>


### [302] [PaDoc: Layout-Grounded Parallel Decoding for Document Parsing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06146)
*Hao Yu,Jiabo Zhan,Kang Liu,Linnan Zhao,Dongxu Yue,Rui Chen,Jinglin Wang,Chong Sun,Chen Li,Jing Lyu,Chun Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PaDoc introduces a layout-grounded, region-sufficient, prefix-conditioned factorization to enable concurrent layout and content decoding in a single MLLM, reducing decoding depth and boosting end-to-end document parsing speed while maintaining full-page context; it achieves top OmniDocBench Full performance and superior throughput on GPU with concurrent decoding; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end document parsers serialize pages into a single autoregressive sequence, which lengthens decoding with total content; crop-based two-stage parsers expose region-level parallelism but suffer repeated visual prefill and fragmented page context. A method that preserves full-page context while enabling concurrency is needed.

Method: Treat predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Derive a prefix-conditioned factorization under a region-sufficiency assumption, so the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. Implement in a single MLLM using packed variable-length ancestor attention to preserve standard next-token training visibility, and use masked parallel decoding to create branches served as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse by a vLLM backend.

Result: On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc achieves Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, an Overall score of 94.24, with Text Edit 0.038 and Formula CDM 95.59. On a 384-page subset with one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, delivering 67.4–118% higher valid-page throughput and 39.2–54.9% lower P95 latency relative to a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline.

Conclusion: PaDoc demonstrates a successful integration of layout-grounded branching within a single MLLM, enabling concurrent decoding of layout and content while preserving full-page context, achieving state-of-the-art or competitive end-to-end parsing performance and speed; code is publicly available.

Abstract: End-to-end document parsers provide a unified interface, but serialize page layouts and regional contents into one autoregressive sequence. This formulation forces independent regions onto a decoding path whose length grows with the total content, whereas crop-based two-stage parsers expose region-level parallelism at the cost of repeated visual prefills and fragmented page context. To retain full-page context while removing dependencies, we propose PaDoc, a layout-grounded parser that treats the predicted layout as a branching structure over a shared page representation. Under a region-sufficiency assumption, we derive a prefix-conditioned factorization in which the layout stream and regional content branches advance concurrently, reducing the decoding depth to the longest layout-content path. We realize this factorization within a single MLLM: packed variable-length ancestor attention preserves the visibility under standard next-token training, while masked parallel decoding creates branches that the evaluated vLLM backend serves as concurrent requests with cache-resident shared-prefix reuse. On OmniDocBench Full, PaDoc attains an Overall layout F1 of 91.1 and, among end-to-end parsers, a top-tier Overall score of 94.24 together with the best Text Edit (0.038) and Formula CDM (95.59). On a 384-page subset and one A800 GPU, it is the fastest end-to-end parser at five concurrency levels, improving valid-page throughput by 67.4-118% and reducing P95 latency by 39.2-54.9% relative to a same-backbone Sequential SFT baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/Longin-Yu/Padoc

</details>


### [303] [CogVis: Must Open-Vocabulary Change Detection Perceive the Scene Anew for Every Query?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06150)
*Zijie Wang,Chen Zhong,Wei He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CogVis introduces a cognitive memory-guided OVCD framework that decouples temporal perception from semantic decisions and uses a memory-based calibrator and adaptive region filtering to achieve state-of-the-art results with improved throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) demands recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Existing methods entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, leading to instability and inefficiency. Inspired by human visual change perception, CogVis aims to separate temporal cues from semantic reasoning to improve robustness and efficiency.

Method: CogVis follows a perception-memory-verification paradigm. Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) extracts a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features to decouple temporal evidence from semantic decisions. Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) dynamically estimates an image-query-specific decision threshold to compensate for category-dependent score shifts. Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected change candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability.

Result: Experiments on seven benchmarks across semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment show state-of-the-art performance on all datasets. Inference throughput improves by 28.50% due to shared scene-level change perception that avoids repeating temporal perception across queries.

Conclusion: CogVis validates a perception-memory-verification paradigm for OVCD, achieving robust, efficient change detection across diverse tasks by decoupling temporal evidence from semantic decisions and employing memory-guided calibration and adaptive filtering.

Abstract: Earth-surface monitoring requires change detection models capable of recognizing arbitrary semantic categories. Open-Vocabulary Change Detection (OVCD) addresses this need. However, existing methods often entangle temporal perception, semantic discrimination, and region verification, causing unstable results and redundant computation. Inspired by human visual change perception, we propose CogVis, a cognitive memory-guided framework that reformulates OVCD as a perception-memory-verification paradigm. CogVis first employs a Scene Change Perceptron (SCP) to extract a reusable, category-agnostic change prior from frozen bi-temporal features, thereby decoupling temporal evidence from semantic category decisions. A Semantic Memory Calibrator (SMC) then compensates for category-dependent score shifts by dynamically estimating an image-query-specific decision threshold. Finally, an Adaptive Region Filter (ARF) filters connected candidates using learned semantic, temporal, and structural reliability. Experiments on seven benchmarks spanning semantic change detection, binary change localization, and building-damage assessment show that CogVis achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated datasets. By sharing scene-level change perception, CogVis further avoids repeating category-agnostic temporal perception across queries and improves inference throughput by 28.50%.

</details>


### [304] [iARCS: Iterative Agentic RL for Controllable 3D Scene Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06161)
*Saugat Adhikari,Ashok Prasad Neupane,Pramish Paudel,Ajad Chhatkuli,Danda Pani Paudel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: iARCS aligns a pretrained 3D scene generator to natural-language task requirements via iterative agentic reinforcement learning with universal-reward pretraining and LLM-generated reward programs, yielding constraint-faithful, diverse scenes and improving downstream synthetic data quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic scene generators often optimize perceptual realism but fail to reliably satisfy functional constraints (e.g., accessibility, traversability, spatial rule compliance), limiting usefulness for downstream tasks.

Method: A two-stage approach: (1) universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, and (2) task-specific fine-tuning with reward programs generated by large language models and iteratively refined from training feedback, implemented as iterative agentic RL.

Result: Improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks; effective optimization of task-specific constraints; competitive scene diversity; and evidence that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, demonstrating practical utility for synthetic data generation.

Conclusion: iARCS provides a constraint-aware, task-driven synthetic scene generation framework that can adapt to natural-language requirements and deliver usable synthetic data for downstream tasks, bridging high-level specifications with controllable scene generation.

Abstract: Synthetic 3D scene generation is increasingly used as a data source for computer vision and embodied AI, but existing generators often optimize perceptual realism without reliably satisfying task-critical functional constraints. This mismatch limits the usefulness of synthetic data for downstream training, where accessibility, traversability, and spatial rule compliance are often essential. We present iARCS, an iterative agentic reinforcement learning framework that adapts a pretrained scene generator to natural-language task requirements. iARCS uses a two-stage strategy: universal-reward pretraining to improve physical plausibility and layout quality, followed by task-specific fine-tuning with LLM-generated reward programs that are iteratively refined from training feedback. Experiments show improved constraint fidelity on walkability, reachability, and clearance-focused tasks, effective task-specific constraint optimization, and competitive scene diversity. We further show that data generated by iARCS improves a base generator, supporting its value as a practical synthetic data generation tool rather than only a controllable scene editing method.

</details>


### [305] [Schema-Guided Hierarchical Information Extraction and Semantic Evaluation Using Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06167)
*Modhurita Mitra,Jan-Willem Versteeg,Maarten D. Schermer,Shiva Nadi Najafabadi,Marie L. De Bruin,Lourens T. Bloem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Schema-based zero-shot information extraction from unstructured text with path-based semantic evaluation, achieving high F1 and large efficiency gains; generalizable across AI models, HTA organizations, and languages.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable reliable extraction of complex, structured information from unstructured documents and automated evaluation against gold standards, reducing reliance on expert manual annotation.

Method: Define an information schema (domain knowledge model) for hierarchical, nested attributes with variable cardinality. Extract in a single zero-shot query to a generative AI. Use a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align extracted attributes with the gold standard. Compare attribute values semantically using the AI, and apply a rubric (exact, semantic, useful, non-match) for evaluation. Validate on NICE HTA documents using Claude Opus 3.

Result: Extracted 12 of 14 attributes with F1 > 0.9. Time to extract ~30x faster than human. Demonstrated model generalizability across different AI models, HTA organizations, and languages.

Conclusion: The schema-based framework provides a unified and efficient approach for complex information extraction and automated evaluation, with strong accuracy and broad generalizability. Suitable for scalable HTA workflows and adaptable to multiple domains and AI models.

Abstract: We present a schema-based framework for extracting complex, structured information from unstructured text documents using generative AI, followed by automated semantic evaluation of the extracted information against a gold standard. The schema, serving as an information model encoding domain knowledge, provides a unified, systematic, and consistent framework for extraction of hierarchical, nested information, with attributes of variable cardinality, and subsequent evaluation of the results. Information extraction from a document is performed in a single call to the model, in zero-shot mode.
  In the evaluation step, we introduce a path-based semantic matching algorithm to align the nested, variable-cardinality attributes in the extracted results with those in the gold standard. We use generative AI for semantic comparison of the extracted and gold standard values of an attribute, and introduce a rubric to classify the result of the comparison, according to domain-specific considerations, as an exact, semantic, useful, or non-match.
  We were able to extract 12 out of 14 attributes with an F1 score of $>$90\% from documents published by the health technology assessment organisation NICE, using the generative AI model Claude Opus 3. The time needed to extract the attributes from a document was $\sim$30 times lower than the time taken by a human domain expert. We further demonstrate generalisability of this framework across different generative AI models and transferability across different HTA organisations and languages.

</details>


### [306] [MicroEvo: Knowledge-Guided LLM Sampling for Efficient Microarchitecture Design Space Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06183)
*Jia Xiong,Runkai Li,Chenxu Niu,Guangyuan Gao,Changwen Xing,Yifan Zhang,Xinlai Wan,Jieran Cui,Chen Bai,Yusheng Hua,Ying Wang,Ming Ling,Xi Wang,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MicroEvo introduces a knowledge-guided framework combining large language models and Monte Carlo Tree Search to optimize multi-objective microarchitecture design, addressing large search spaces and evaluation costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Design space exploration for microarchitectures is hampered by vast search spaces and expensive performance, power, area (PPA) evaluations, which limit effective decision-making and Pareto convergence.

Method: MicroEvo integrates LLM-driven evolutionary operators with a Pareto-aware MCTS tree policy, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism to extract/reuse optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt search behavior online.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows up to 36.2% improvement in Pareto-front quality over NSGA-II and 10.6x higher search efficiency, with demonstrated scalability to an industrial-scale core; code available at the provided GitHub repository.

Conclusion: A knowledge-guided Hybrid search framework (MicroEvo) effectively improves Pareto-optimal microarchitectural designs under budget constraints by leveraging LLMs, MCTS, and knowledge reuse.

Abstract: Microarchitecture design space exploration suffers from expansive search spaces and expensive PPA evaluation, leaving only a small simulation budget for design decision-making. Existing methods perform blind search without considering microarchitectural dependencies and fail to learn from the iterative search effectively, leading to wasted evaluations and weak Pareto convergence. In this paper, we propose MicroEvo, a knowledge-guided framework that couples off-the-shelf LLMs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for multi-objective microarchitecture optimization. MicroEvo combines LLM-driven evolutionary operators, a Pareto-aware tree policy that balances Pareto contribution and diversity, an active knowledge accumulation mechanism that extracts and reuses optimization insights, and state-aware directives that adapt the search behavior online. Experiments show that MicroEvo improves Pareto-front quality by up to 36.2% over NSGA-II and achieves 10.6x higher search efficiency, and also demonstrates strong scalability to a complex industrial-scale core. The code repository is available at: https://github.com/GEAR-SEU/MicroEvo-ICCAD-26.

</details>


### [307] [Comparative Approaches to Agent Retrieval over Large Skill Libraries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06196)
*Indivara Kolluru,Nathan Sportsman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid lexical+dense retrieval outperforms a typed-graph approach for on-demand skill loading; adding structural relations does not extend retrieval reach and can degrade performance, due to pre-filter topology; author-written queries overstate hits; main contribution explains when structure helps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently select and sequence skills to load from a large library without loading the entire corpus; identify whether structure (prerequisites, data flow) improves retrieval over a strong ranker.

Method: Compare a hybrid ranker (lexical + dense embeddings) against a typed knowledge graph of workflow relations across 690 skills; evaluate on 117 realistic queries; analyze edge layer and reachability; compare with author-written queries; assess pre-filter topology bound and redundancy of edges.

Result: Hybrid ranker hits top-5 for 73.5% ± 8.0; about 25% unserved. Graph approach underperforms by 11.2 points (p=0.0007). LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing beyond free neighbors; 73% of missed queries are not reachable via graph. 98.6% of typed edges connect skills already surfaced by ranker. Graph enriches semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. Author-written queries overstate hit@5 by up to 44 points.

Conclusion: Structuring retrieval via a knowledge graph does not improve retrieval reach beyond a strong ranker under current pre-filter topology; structural interdependence helps only under certain conditions (when edges add novel reachability beyond existing neighborhood). The study provides a mechanistic explanation of when added structure is beneficial and when it is not.

Abstract: Agents backed by large skill libraries must decide which skills to load and in what order. Loading the entire library into context is expensive and provides no structure for autonomous sequencing. We study two systems for this problem over a corpus of 690 skills: a hybrid ranker combining lexical and dense-embedding retrieval for sparse, on-demand loading, and a typed knowledge graph encoding workflow relations such as prerequisites, data flow, and ordering. On a set of 117 realistic, non-echoing queries, the hybrid ranker retrieves the correct skill within the top five in 73.5% +/- 8.0 of cases, leaving roughly a quarter of queries unserved. When used as the design intended (substituting graph neighbours for additional ranked results at matched token budget), the graph is significantly worse (-11.2 points, p = 0.0007). Its LLM-generated edge layer adds nothing over neighbours obtained free from a local embedding pass, and 73% of the queries the ranker misses are not reachable through the graph at all. We attribute this to a pre-filter topology bound. Because the graph's candidate edges are drawn from the same embedding neighbourhood the ranker already searches, 98.6% of typed edges connect skills the ranker had already surfaced together. The graph can enrich relation semantics but cannot extend retrieval reach. We further show that evaluating on author-written queries overstates hit@5 by up to 44 points, which would have hidden these results entirely. Our contribution is a mechanistic account of why added structure does not improve retrieval over a strong ranker, and identify the conditions under which adding structural interdependence into the retrieval is optimal.

</details>


### [308] [EnvACE: Internalizing Environment Dynamics via World Rehearsal for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06197)
*Zishan Xu,Zhiyuan Yao,Yuxin Chen,Yifu Guo,Zhengxi Lu,Yuquan Lu,Jinyang Huang,Yan Xu,Yasheng Wang,Weinan Zhang,Xingshan Zeng,Weiwen Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EnvACE trains large language model agents with world rehearsal instead of external environment interaction. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsing the environment response, creating an internal world model that improves decision-making and transfer. It achieves strong, transferable performance across multiple benchmarks and benefits from private rehearsal at test time; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on costly real or simulated environments for long-horizon tool-use in LLM agents. Enable scalable, grounded policy learning by internalizing environment dynamics.

Method: Policy executes in two phases per step: (1) generate a tool call (action), (2) role-play the environment to produce the response to that action (rehearsal). The rehearsal conditions subsequent decisions. Both roles are optimized end-to-end using task rewards, yielding an internal world model that supports decision making. At test time, optional private rehearsal uses the internal model within a limited budget.

Result: EnvACE outperforms environment-scaling baselines across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, with strong transfer across model scales. Controlled studies show world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning. Private rehearsal at test time provides additional gains.

Conclusion: World rehearsal enables scalable LLM agent training beyond external environments by internalizing action–environment dynamics; code is publicly available for replication.

Abstract: Training large language model agents for long-horizon tool use typically relies on interactions with real or synthesized executable environments, whose construction and verification are costly, or on external simulators that are difficult to ground. We introduce EnvACE, an agentic reinforcement learning method that replaces external environment interaction during training with world rehearsal. The policy alternates between acting and rehearsal: it first generates a tool call, then plays the role of the environment to produce the response induced by that action, and conditions subsequent decisions on the rehearsed response. Both roles are jointly optimized end-to-end using task-success rewards. Through world rehearsal, the policy internalizes the relationship between actions and their environment responses in its parameters, yielding an agent world model that directly supports decision making. Across BFCL-v4, tau^2-Bench, VitaBench, and FinMCP-Bench, EnvACE achieves strong and transferable performance, outperforming environment-scaling baselines in the overall evaluation. Controlled studies further show that world rehearsal consistently improves policy learning across model scales. At test time, the internalized world model enables private rehearsal before committed execution, yielding further gains under a moderate rehearsal budget without additional external interaction. Our findings establish world rehearsal as a new path toward scaling LLM agent training beyond the constraints of external environments. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Within-yao/EnvACE.

</details>


### [309] [TS-RAG: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06223)
*Yixiong Xiao,Congxi Xiao,Jingbo Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes TS-RAG, a retrieval-augmented generation approach for time series forecasting that uses specially designed reference tokens to fuse input and retrieved similar sequences, achieving state-of-the-art results on real-world benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG's success in NLP motivates leveraging external retrieved time series to improve forecasting, but time series face data scarcity, smaller models, and naive reference concatenation is ineffective.

Method: TS-RAG introduces reference tokens to fuse input and retrieved sequences; retrieves similar sequences and integrates them for forecasting; designed to capture complex temporal dynamics better than naive concatenation.

Result: Experimental results show consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

Conclusion: The proposed TS-RAG framework effectively enhances time series forecasting by incorporating retrieved sequences, addressing data and model limitations in TS forecasting; potential for broader applicability and further refinement.

Abstract: While deep learning models, particularly transformer-based architectures, have shown impressive performance in time series forecasting, the application of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in this domain remains limited. Since RAG has proven effective in enhancing the capabilities of large language models by incorporating relevant external information, retrieving similar time series sequences as references might also improve accuracy in time series forecasting tasks. However, most time series models are constrained by limited training data, smaller parameter scales, and a lack of the extensive generative capabilities found in large language models. Simply concatenating reference sequences into the prompt, as done in language models, may not yield the expected results. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach, TS-RAG, which leverages RAG to enhance forecasting performance. The framework introduces specially designed reference tokens to effectively fuse information from the input sequence with that from retrieved similar sequences, enabling a more robust capture of complex temporal dynamics. Experimental results demonstrate that TS-RAG achieves consistent state-of-the-art performance across several real-world forecasting benchmarks.

</details>


### [310] [DASH: Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons for On-Policy Self-Distillation of Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06243)
*ZhiYan Hou,Xinyu Tang,Hongyan An,Jianjin Zhang,Weizhen Wang,Yunyun Han,Gengsheng Li,Xiangzhao Hao,Haiyun Guo,Wenbin Hu,Jinqiao Wang,Yafeng Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DASH enhances on-policy distillation (OPSD) by using divergence-adaptive gates to weight token-level supervision according to the temporal evolution of divergences, improving mathematical reasoning benchmarks across model scales without extra forward passes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD provides dense token-level supervision but treats all local divergences equally, ignoring the temporal context of how discrepancies accumulate during generation. Exploiting the temporal structure can improve the effectiveness of supervision signals.

Method: Introduce Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons (DASH). For each local distillation signal, compute its gap from the sequence-level mean, map this gap to an adaptive propagation gate, and apply these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation. This yields token-level weights that reflect the realized discrepancy sequence. DASH reuses existing teacher and student distributions from OPSD, requiring no additional forward passes.

Result: Empirical gains on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales, consistently outperforming vanilla OPSD reruns. Gains are achieved without extra teacher or student forward passes; code is released.

Conclusion: DASH leverages temporal context in divergence histories to adapt supervision, providing consistent improvements over OPSD with minimal computational overhead and maintaining compatibility with existing RLVR pipelines.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models using automatically verifiable outcome signals, but these signals are typically sparse and at the sequence-level. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) mitigates this sparsity by querying a privileged teacher at student-visited prefixes and providing dense token-level distributional supervision. Although this dense supervision alleviates signal sparsity, we find that standard OPSD still underexploits the temporal structure of the rollout. It assigns every local divergence the same coefficient, regardless of its position or the divergence sequence in which it occurs. In on-policy autoregressive generation, the same divergence magnitude can follow different discrepancy histories, reflecting different evolutions of the mismatch between the teacher and student. Since the local scalar alone cannot distinguish these temporal contexts, standard OPSD cannot adapt its token-level weights to the realized discrepancy sequence. To address this limitation, we propose Divergence-Adaptive Supervision Horizons (DASH). DASH maps the gap between each local distillation signal and the sequence-level mean to an adaptive propagation gate and then uses these gates to control backward multi-step aggregation. By doing so, DASH adjusts token-level supervision weights according to how local divergences evolve during generation. Experiments on three mathematical reasoning benchmarks across three model scales show that DASH improves over our matched vanilla OPSD reruns on every benchmark at all three scales. DASH reuses the teacher and student distributions that OPSD already computes, so the gains require no additional teacher or student forward pass.
  Code: https://github.com/DBtxy/DASH-OPSD

</details>


### [311] [Improving the Realism of Synthetic Clinical Benchmarks Under Utility Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06265)
*Omid Bazgir,Md Nasir,Jacob Hoffman,Yang Yang,Manu Agrawal,Anusua Trivedi,Vinay Rao Dandin,Chris Gibbons,Christine Swisher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Utility-constrained realism improvement for synthetic clinical benchmarks; demonstrates deterministic realism revisions on a Synthea-based care-gap benchmark while preserving downstream utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Synthetic benchmarks in privacy-sensitive healthcare often pass utility checks yet lack structural realism. There is a need to optimize realism without violating utility constraints to ensure benchmarks reflect real-world data.

Method: Formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement; instantiate on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients processed through demonstration EHR workflows and the same downstream pipeline as operational data; measure realism via missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment; compare two deterministic revisions against a naive densification control; analyze relation between internal realism and source fidelity.

Result: Baseline benchmark is extremely thin (e.g., sampled-pair missingness 79.44%, 12.75% of rows actionable, 38.94% of patients with zero actionable measures, top-three token concentration 100.0%). Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while staying above the utility floor; naive densification preserves unrealistic templating. Internal realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives.

Conclusion: Synthetic benchmark quality should be explicitly optimized for realism with utility treated as a constraint rather than as sole evidence of realism; improving realism under utility constraints can produce more trustworthy benchmarks for enterprise AI in healthcare.

Abstract: Synthetic clinical benchmarks for enterprise AI agents can pass existing utility checks and still remain structurally unrealistic, especially in privacy-sensitive healthcare settings where operational data are hard to access. We study how to improve such benchmarks without breaking the downstream utility checks already used in practice.
  We formulate benchmark revision as utility-constrained realism improvement: dataset changes should increase realism while staying above an operational utility floor. We instantiate this idea on a care-gap benchmark derived from Synthea-generated patients exercised through demonstration electronic health record workflows and then processed by the same downstream pipeline as operational data. Realism is measured through missingness structure, simplicity, structural plausibility, and population alignment.
  The baseline benchmark is extremely thin: sampled-pair missingness is 79.44%, only 12.75% of rows are actionable, 38.94% of patients have zero actionable measures, and top-three token concentration reaches 100.0%. Two deterministic revisions improve these panels while remaining above the current utility floor, whereas a naive densification control preserves unrealistic templating. We further show that internal benchmark realism and source fidelity to an aggregate operational reference are related but distinct objectives. These results suggest that synthetic benchmark quality should be optimized explicitly, with utility treated as one constraint rather than as sufficient evidence of realism.

</details>


### [312] [The Illusion of Visual Tool-Use: A Causal Audit of Thinking with Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06270)
*Zhiheng Wang,Bo Peng,Lai Wei,Chaochao Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Causal auditing reveals that visual tool-use in multimodal LLMs often lacks causal effect on answers; introduces Visual Evidence Gain to isolate observation contributions; identifies policy miscalibrations (Calling Without Looking; Looking Without Planning) and an illusion of visual tool-use where aggregate gains do not reflect causal utility across rollouts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determine whether visual evidence returned by crop-and-zoom tools causally influences model answers, and diagnose miscalibrations that inflate perceived gains.

Method: Model the tool-use scenario as a causal graph distinguishing observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts; perform three levels of interventions—policy (tool-use vs direct inference), trajectory (corrupting observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing individual observations). Introduce a step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, to quantify each observation's causal contribution. Evaluate across six models and five perception benchmarks.

Result: Identified policy miscalibration with two failure modes: (1) Calling Without Looking—returned observations do not causally affect the answer; (2) Looking Without Planning—observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. Trajectory analysis decomposes policy-level accuracy gains, revealing the gain is concentrated in a calibrated minority. Overall, there is an illusion of visual tool-use: aggregate gains do not reflect broad causal effectiveness. Code is available at the provided repository.

Conclusion: Visual tool-use in its current form exhibits limited causal efficacy across rollouts; robust auditing and calibration are necessary. The work provides a concrete causal framework and metrics (Visual Evidence Gain) to guide redesign of visual tools and evaluation protocols.

Abstract: The "thinking-with-images" paradigm equips multimodal LLMs with active visual operations such as crop-and-zoom. However, models using these operations often achieve only marginal or negative gains over direct inference at substantially higher token cost. They may also repeatedly crop irrelevant regions and fail on questions that direct inference answers correctly. We ask whether the returned visual evidence causally affects the answer. To answer this question, we formulate visual tool-use as a causal graph that separates observation-mediated paths from action-induced shortcuts. We then audit it through interventions at the three levels: policy (comparing tool-use with direct inference), trajectory (corrupting all observations during rollout), and step (counterfactually replacing one individual observation under a fixed prefix). Our step-level estimand, Visual Evidence Gain, isolates the contribution of each returned observation. Across six representative models and five fine-grained perception benchmarks, we uncover policy miscalibration with two failure modes. In Calling Without Looking, returned observations have no causal effect on the answer. In Looking Without Planning, observations are informative but the call schedule is incoherent. A trajectory-level diagnostic decomposes the policy-level accuracy gain and shows that the gain is concentrated in a Calibrated minority. We term this discrepancy the illusion of visual tool-use: despite aggregate accuracy gains, visual tool-use is not causally effective across a broad range of rollouts. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauAudit.

</details>


### [313] [QuanTiMedAI: Quantum-Enhanced Time-Series Model guided by Agentic AI for Cardiac Arrest Mortality Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06294)
*Mutasim Fuad Sarker,Adiba Rahman Namira,Wafa Binte Alam,Md Adnan Arefeen,Mahzabeen Emu,Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuanTiMedAI introduces a quantum-enhanced, agentic AI framework for cardiac arrest mortality prediction. It uses an agentic LLM for feature discovery and a compact quantum recurrent network for temporality-aware prediction, achieving AUROC 0.852 on MIMIC-IV with 605 parameters and outperforming baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing mortality models in ICU cardiac arrest rely on static early-admission summaries and fail to capture temporal progression during the ICU stay; there is a need for temporally aware, parameter-efficient predictive models.

Method: An agentic large language model (LLM) guides clinically informed feature discovery, feeding into a compact quantum recurrent network that models temporal dynamics; nonlinear feature enhancement via quantum architecture; evaluated on a MIMIC-IV cohort of cardiac arrest patients; includes structured ablation study.

Result: The quantum-enhanced model attains AUROC = 0.852 using 605 parameters, roughly 2.9% better than a current state-of-the-art baseline; quantum architecture achieves competitive performance with far fewer parameters; ablation confirms contribution of architectural components.

Conclusion: Quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can exceed classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters, with agentic LLM-guided feature selection improving the quality of input features.

Abstract: Cardiac arrest remains one of the most lethal conditions encountered in intensive care units. Despite the growing availability of electronic health record data, existing mortality prediction studies in this population largely depend on static summaries derived from early admission. Such approaches ignore the temporal progression of physiological deterioration and recovery that unfolds throughout a patient's ICU stay. To address this limitation, we introduce QuanTiMedAI, a quantum-agentic framework developed for cardiac arrest mortality prediction using agentic AI guided quantum enhancement time series model. The proposed system combines an agentic large language model (LLM) for clinically informed feature discovery with a compact quantum recurrent network for temporality aware mortality prediction. Our findings demonstrate that agentic LLM-guided feature selection consistently outperforms conventional feature selection approaches, and the proposed quantum architecture achieves competitive predictive performance through nonlinear feature enhancement while keeping the number of parameters very low. Through extensive experimentation on a MIMIC-IV cohort of cardiac arrest patients, QuanTiMedAI's quantum-enhanced architecture attains an AUROC of 0.852 using only 605 parameters, an improvement of approximately 2.9\% over a current state-of-the-art baseline for this task. A structured ablation study systematically validates the contribution of each architectural design choice. These results show that quantum-enhanced sequential modeling can exceed classical recurrent networks while using substantially fewer parameters.

</details>


### [314] [Bias Analysis of L2 Speaking Assessment Systems Using Concept Activation Vectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06300)
*Arya Labroo,Mengjie Qian,Kate Knill*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper analyzes bias auditing of L2 speaking assessment systems using Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) with BERT and Whisper-based graders, comparing linear separability in activation spaces and the effect of using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on recovering concepts and sensitivity; findings show concept recoverability depends on representation/architecture, SAEs increase linear recoverability but reduce activation-space sensitivity, highlighting need to distinguish recoverability from influence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure fairness and interpretability of transformer-based L2 speaking graders by distinguishing whether unwanted concepts are encoded and whether they influence scores; address limitations of CAVs in complex embeddings and explore SAEs for cleaner concept directions.

Method: Apply CAV-based bias analysis to two systems: text-based BERT grader and Whisper-based multimodal grader; evaluate concept encoding vs influence using gradient-based sensitivity; experiment with SAEs to learn CAVs in sparse latent space and map back to activation space; compare linear separability and impact across representations.

Result: Concept recoverability varies with representation/architecture; sensitivity to concepts is architecture-dependent; SAEs improved linear recoverability of concepts but attenuated original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers.

Conclusion: Need to distinguish concept recoverability from concept influence when auditing bias in speaking assessment; caution that improving linear separability may come at cost of actual sensitivity, and that evaluation should consider both aspects across architectures.

Abstract: Automatic speaking assessment systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings to mark second language (L2) learners' speaking tests, making it critical to show that their scores depend on speaking proficiency rather than irrelevant speaker attributes such as first language (L1) or age. Transformer-based foundation models have improved the accuracy of these L2 speaking graders, but their black-box representations make fairness and interpretability analysis more difficult. Building on prior work that used Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to detect bias towards unwanted attributes (`concepts') in feature-based graders, we extend CAV-based analysis to two neural speaking assessment systems: a text-based BERT grader and a speech-and-text multimodal grader based on Whisper. CAVs represent human-interpretable concepts as directions in a model's activation space, allowing us to distinguish between whether a concept is encoded in a model's internal representations and whether it influences the predicted score, the latter quantified using a gradient-based sensitivity metric. Since CAVs rely on linear separability, which is less likely in complex neural embedding spaces, we also investigate whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide cleaner concept directions by learning CAVs in a sparse latent space and mapping them back to activation space. Our analysis shows that concept recoverability depends strongly on the representation and architecture being probed, rather than on the concept alone. Sensitivity to concepts is also architecture-dependent. SAEs make concepts more linearly recoverable, but attenuate the original activation-space sensitivity, especially in low-dimensional layers. These findings highlight the need to distinguish concept recoverability from concept influence when auditing bias in speaking assessment systems.

</details>


### [315] [HarnessOpt-Bench: Evaluating LLMs at Harness Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06301)
*Varun Ursekar,Apaar Shanker,Yash Maurya,Shehab Yasser,Vijay S. Kalmath,Veronica Chatrath,Yuan Xue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmarking framework to evaluate end-to-end harness optimization for LLM-powered agents, showing that optimizer models’ ability to edit or compose a harness can exceed improvements from the harness alone; results vary by task and seed, with native harnesses not consistently superior; establishes harness optimization as a measurable, discriminative capability with substantial room for improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs are embedded in agentic systems, performance hinges on the surrounding harness (prompts, tools, control flow, memory, orchestration). There is no standardized protocol to measure frontier LLMs’ capability to optimize such harnesses, hindering progress.

Method: A benchmark where an optimizer (an LLM paired with a coding harness) edits a seed harness using graded evaluation feedback within a fixed evaluation budget. The optimizer nominates a final candidate, which is scored by normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition unseen during search. A trusted execution environment enforces evaluation boundaries, meters resource use, and preserves candidate versions for auditing. The study evaluates 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers across 4 downstream tasks, using either a shared coding harness or native harnesses, over 111 scored runs.

Result: Optimizer models exhibit greater impact than harness-level changes; native harnesses are not consistently better than shared-harness baselines; gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes; harness optimization is a distinct, measurable capability with substantial growth potential.

Conclusion: Harness optimization constitutes a separable and discriminative capability in AI systems, warranting standardized benchmarking and further research to improve optimization algorithms, harness representations, and evaluation protocols.

Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed within agentic systems, their capabilities depend not only on the model weights but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, control flow, memory, and orchestration code surrounding them. This makes automated harness optimization -- the iterative and evaluation-guided improvement of a harness by an AI system -- both an important route to improving AI systems and a demanding capability for AI systems themselves. Yet the community lacks a common protocol for measuring how well frontier LLMs perform at this task. We introduce HarnessOpt-Bench, a benchmark for end-to-end harness optimization under expensive and stochastic evaluation. An optimizer, an LLM paired with a coding harness, receives a target agent's seed harness, graded evaluation feedback, and a fixed target-evaluation budget. It edits the harness and nominates a final candidate, which is scored by its normalized gain over the seed on a held-out test partition that remains inaccessible throughout search. A trusted execution environment enforces the evaluation boundary, meters target-agent resource use, and preserves candidate versions for audit. We evaluate 5 frontier LLMs as optimizers both under a shared coding harness and under their native harnesses across 4 downstream tasks, over 111 scored runs. Experiment results show that optimizer models separate more than the coding harnesses they act through, native harnesses are not consistently superior, and gains vary substantially across tasks and seed regimes. These results establish harness optimization as a measurable and discriminative capability with large space for improvement.

</details>


### [316] [Beyond Top-K: Replacing Black-Box Retrieval with Interpretable Agentic Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06305)
*Sagar Tamang,Ayush Vyas,Tabarakul Hazarika*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Embedding-free, deterministic retrieval (READ) improves QA on long financial documents, outperforming embedding-based dense retrieval on a 51-question test; BM25 is indistinguishable from READ, suggesting gains come from retrieval interface rather than iteration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Chunking+embedding retrieval struggles with long, structurally rich documents (e.g., financial statements with tables and units). A reliable, auditable retrieval approach is needed for accuracy and transparency in such documents.

Method: Introduce READ: Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search, using three deterministic operations—normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads—exposed via the Model Context Protocol to produce a replayable audit trail. Compare against dense retrieval and BM25; evaluate on 51 verified questions; also assess a table-aware chunker and a top-k tool variant.

Result: READ achieves 58.8% accuracy on 51 questions versus 15.7% for dense retrieval (Holm-corrected p = 2e-5). When tuned, 35.3% with READ, still leading by 23.5 points (p = 0.017). A top-k tool variant reaches 27.5%. A table-aware chunker reduces unit errors but yields 27–30% numeric chunks missing fiscal-year headers. BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, indicating the advantage lies with embedding-free retrieval rather than agentic vs lexical search.

Conclusion: Embedding-free, deterministic retrieval with a transparent audit trail can surpass embedding-based retrieval on long, structurally complex documents, but the observed gains may be driven by interface design. BM25 performs comparably to READ in this setting, suggesting that future work should disentangle retrieval interface from true agentic capabilities and test on broader datasets.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation over long documents is dominated by one design: chunk the text, embed the chunks, and surface the top-k nearest neighbours of the query. We argue that for an important class of documents -- financial statements, audit reports, regulatory returns -- this design is structurally unsound, and we make the argument measurable. On a 780-page government financial report, 86.8% of content lines are table rows, thousands of near-identical figures compete in one embedding space, and a figure inherits its unit from a header a median of 13 lines above it -- so a chunk boundary routinely separates a number from whether it is in lakh or crore, an error of two orders of magnitude. A table-aware chunker built as a steelman fixes the unit problem but leaves 27-30% of numeric chunks with no fiscal-year header at every chunk size we tried. We propose READ (Reliable Embedding-free Agentic Document-search), in which an agent reads the raw document through three deterministic operations -- normalized lexical search, structural navigation, and bounded span reads -- exposed over the Model Context Protocol, so a trajectory is a replayable audit trail, not an opaque similarity score. On 51 verified questions READ answers 58.8% against dense retrieval's 15.7% (p_Holm = 2 x 10^-5) -- or 35.3% tuned, which READ still leads by 23.5 points (p_Holm = 0.017). An agent given the same loop but a top-k tool reaches only 27.5%, locating the gain in the interface rather than in iteration. We also report what the evidence does not support: BM25 is statistically indistinguishable from READ, so our result separates embedding-based from embedding-free retrieval, not agentic from lexical search.

</details>


### [317] [TRAJDEBUG: Tracing Error Lifecycle to Identify Critical Failures in Long-Horizon Agent Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06346)
*Yunjia Qi,Zehua Yin,Xintong Shi,Hao Peng,Songyuanyi Lu,Yixian Liu,Richeng Xuan,Yuhong Liu,Zhichao Hu,Xiaozhi Wang,Lei Hou,Bin Xu,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces TrajDebug, a framework for error-lifecycle tracing in long LLM agent trajectories, and TrajErrBench, a 486-trajectory benchmark; achieves superior error localization and attribution; data/code to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cascading errors in agentic systems and difficulty localizing earliest error steps in long trajectories; multiple local errors complicate attribution.

Method: TrajDebug uses multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification to locate earliest responsible error and trace each error's resolution status and terminal impact; TrajErrBench assembled from Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro; evaluated across diverse benchmarks.

Result: TrajDebug achieves best overall performance against baselines; provides actionable feedback for improving success; 486 annotated trajectories; code/data release.

Conclusion: The framework and benchmark address long-trajectory error discovery and attribution, enabling better debugging and improvement of agentic systems; release to the community.

Abstract: LLM-based agentic systems have shown remarkable capabilities in complex domains, while suffering from cascading errors and difficulty in debugging. Critical error detection aims to locate the earliest error step in a failed trajectory that is responsible for the final failure. However, progress faces two main challenges. First, long trajectories make it difficult to identify individual errors, since the evidence for judging a step may be scattered across distant instructions, observations, and prior context. Second, failed trajectories often contain multiple local errors with different downstream effects, only some of which remain responsible for the final failure. In this work, we propose TrajDebug, an error-lifecycle tracing framework that addresses long-trajectory error discovery with multi-granularity history compression and evidence-based error identification, and supports critical attribution by tracing each error's resolution status and terminal impact. We further construct TrajErrBench, a benchmark of 486 manually annotated failed trajectories from Tau2Bench and SWE-Bench Pro, covering realistic tool-use and coding scenarios. Experiments across diverse agent benchmarks show that TrajDebug achieves the best overall performance over existing baselines, and application studies further demonstrate that its diagnoses provide actionable feedback for improving downstream agent success. We will release the codes and data to facilitate further research.

</details>


### [318] [Challenges in Evaluating Explanation Methods for Static and Evolving Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06351)
*Jerzy Stefanowski*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Survey-style abstract linking several XAI evaluation challenges: bias detection with DetoxAI, human-grounded evaluation, drift-aware explanations, counterfactual adaptation, and co-evolution of data/models/explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address insufficient XAI evaluation and the need to adapt explanations to changing data and models.

Method: Illustrative case (DetoxAI) for bias/concept unlearning; human-grounded evaluation example; discussion of drift adaptation and counterfactuals; framing co-evolution challenges.

Result: Raises concerns about current evaluation gaps; provides experiential insights and a roadmap for dynamic, human-aligned XAI evaluation; no concrete empirical results presented in the abstract.

Conclusion: Advocates for ongoing, integrated evaluation frameworks that track data, model, and explanation co-evolution; suggests directions for future research in adaptive explanations and counterfactuals.

Abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) with respect to insufficient evaluation. They are illustrated through the DetoxAI image recognition system for bias detection and concept unlearning. Then, an example of a human-grounded evaluation of methods for explaining image classification is presented. The paper further explores methods for adapting explanations to evolving data streams with concept drift. Experiences with adapting counterfactuals for this problem are discussed. Finally it is related to the challenges of tracking the co-evolution of data, models, and explanations.\footnote{This paper has been accepted for a publication in J.Nalepa (ed) Explainable AI in Space. Proceedings of EASi 2026 Workshop at IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Bremen, Springer CCIS vol 3107 (2016).}

</details>


### [319] [The Low Frequency Trap: Video Language Models Fail at Simple Event Bookkeeping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06361)
*Sarvesh Baskar,Zikui Cai,Shayan Shabihi,Anirudh Satheesh,Muhammad R. Islam,Udari Madhushani Sehwag,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trace-grounded parametric profiling audits event counting in controlled video tasks using executable event traces, revealing major temporal-reasoning failures in current models, especially for high-count/high-frequency and transient events; gains from more frames or prompts are limited.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridging the gap between real-world video benchmarks (which entangle event count, rate, duration, and complexity) and programmatic benchmarks (which optimize final answers) by auditing reported events against executable ground-truth traces.

Method: Three tasks (bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, categorical state transitions) with varied event count N and frequency F while keeping rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace for capability-surface estimation and timestamp-level evaluation. Evaluate a model (Gemini 3.6 Flash) across regimes; analyze sampling-rate effects and prompting strategies.

Result: At 80% reliability, persistent state transitions are correctly counted up to 12 events at 0.5 and 1 Hz; no reliable positive-count region for transient blinking. In high-count/high-frequency regimes, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and 18.1% of true events are recovered. Increasing sampling rate raises bounce-ball accuracy (19.6% to 29.3%), but the reported sequence aligns with ground truth only 3.7% of the time. Prompting strategies offer limited gains; real-world evaluations show similar low-event-count success.

Conclusion: Trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy to diagnosing where temporal reasoning fails, highlighting bottlenecks in event representation and evidence access and providing a diagnostic framework for temporal reasoning in video understanding.

Abstract: Real-world video benchmarks provide broad coverage, but their fixed clips entangle event count, rate, duration, and visual complexity, making failure modes hard to isolate. While existing programmatic benchmarks offer better control, they score only the final answer rather than auditing reported events against executable ground truth. To bridge this gap, we introduce trace-grounded parametric profiling for event counting in three controlled video tasks: bouncing-ball wall contacts, visual blinks, and categorical state transitions. Across 2,190 videos, we vary event count N and frequency F while holding rendering fixed. Each video includes an executable event trace for capability-surface estimation and timestamp-level evaluation. Our results reveal a staged temporal failure. At an 80% reliability threshold, Gemini 3.6 Flash reliably counts persistent state transitions up to 12 events at 0.5 and 1.0 Hz, yet demonstrates no reliable positive-count region for transient blinking events. Thus, event representation dictates whether a model initially accesses evidence -- a limitation that compounds as count and frequency increase. In the high-count, high-frequency regime, only 0.2% of final counts are correct and the model recovers just 18.1% of true events. To test if visual access is the primary bottleneck, we increase sampling rate. Although this boosts Bounce Ball accuracy from 19.6% to 29.3%, the reported sequence agrees with ground truth only 3.7% of the time. Extra frames can therefore inflate final scores without producing faithful event recovery. Different prompting strategies yield similarly limited gains, and real-world video evaluations show the same concentration of success at low event counts. Ultimately, trace-grounded profiling shifts video evaluation from aggregate accuracy metrics to a detailed diagnostic of where temporal reasoning fails.

</details>


### [320] [Tracing the Heart: An Evidence-Linked Pipeline for Heart-Failure Feature Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06366)
*Soorya Ram Shimgekar,Michelle Hu,Dorisa Shehi,Daniel Kang,Roy Ka-Wei Lee,Koustuv Saha,Christian Poellabauer,Christopher Lee,Sajeev Singh,Piyum Zonooz,Navin Kumar,Zeeshan Ahmed,Priyadarshini Kachroo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Automated, auditable EHR feature engineering for heart failure using a multi-agent system improves phenotyping AUROC; evaluation on dummy records shows strong performance but needs external validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EHR feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI, accounting for 39-45% of data scientists' workload. Heart failure requires integrating fragmented EHR data with disease-specific, guideline-based reasoning. Existing rule-based and LLM-based approaches offer partial automation with limited maintainability and traceability.

Method: Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS): an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering. Evaluated on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM.

Result: Held-out AUROC improved from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping. Independent LLM-based rubric assessment scored features at 81.5% of maximum. 500 dummy records, nine EHR source tables, 132 structured features and 70 rubric-scored features.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data; evaluation limited to a single-institution cohort with dummy data; external validation is needed.

Abstract: Electronic health record (EHR) feature engineering is a major bottleneck in clinical research and AI, accounting for 39-45% of data scientists' workload. This is especially pronounced in heart failure, which affects an estimated 6.7 million U.S. adults and requires integrating fragmented EHR data with disease-specific, guideline-based clinical reasoning. Existing rule-based and large language model (LLM)-based approaches offer only partial automation with limited maintainability and evidence traceability. We developed the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), an evidence-linked, rubric-grounded pipeline for automated heart-failure feature engineering, and evaluated it on 500 dummy patient records from nine EHR source tables. nMAS generated 132 structured and 70 rubric-scored aggregated features, verified for structural integrity, rubric compliance, and provenance, and audited by a restricted LLM. Adding the aggregated features improved held-out AUROC from 0.895 to 0.963 for HFrEF and 0.870 to 0.910 for HFpEF phenotyping, and an independent LLM-based rubric assessment of evidence support and methodological soundness scored the features at 81.5% of maximum points. These results demonstrate the feasibility of automated, auditable feature engineering for complex cardiovascular EHR data, though evaluation was limited to a single-institution cohort and external validation is needed.

</details>

### [321] [NP-Hardness of Non-Crossing Hamiltonian Path and Cycle in Non-Planar Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06255)
*Randal Tuggle,Jack Snoeyink*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Direct 3-SAT reduction to non-crossing Hamiltonian path/cycle on non-planar graphs, separating non-crossing constraints from Hamiltonicity and avoiding planar gadget constructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle two sources of hardness—the problem of finding a Hamiltonian path/cycle and the constraint that the path be non-crossing—so as to attribute the difficulty specifically to the non-crossing requirement and to avoid confounding it with planarity.

Method: Construct a direct reduction from 3-SAT to the non-crossing Hamiltonian path and cycle problems on non-planar graphs, using non-planar gadgets tailored to enforce non-crossing constraints without resorting to planar gadgetry; establish a bijection between 3-SAT instances and non-crossing Hamiltonian structures.

Result: Demonstrates NP-hardness of non-crossing Hamiltonian path and cycle on non-planar graphs via a direct 3-SAT reduction, clarifying the source of difficulty and yielding a more transparent proof.

Conclusion: The non-crossing constraint is a distinct hardness source that can be targeted directly; the approach yields a cleaner reduction framework and is amenable to extension to related non-crossing problems.

Abstract: We seek to disentangle the hardness of finding a Hamiltonian path or cycle from the hardness of finding a non-crossing path or cycle by giving a direct reduction from 3-SAT to the non-crossing Hamiltonian path and cycle problems on non-planar graphs. Prior hardness proofs proceed by reduction to planar graphs, where every path is automatically non-crossing; this conflates the two sources of difficulty and leaves unclear why forbidding crossings on the path alone makes the problem hard. Our reduction places the difficulty squarely in the non-crossing constraint, avoids planar gadget constructions, and yields a more transparent proof that may be easier to extend to related problems.

</details>
